teile.einleitung: Osmosis is the movement of water through a fine partition that lets only water through. It plays an important role in all living things. Plants, for example, take up water from the soil by osmosis.
wichtigste: In osmosis, water flows through a semipermeable membrane.
Overall, the water flows towards the higher concentration of dissolved particles.
Water moves from the higher to the lower water potential.
Two solutions with the same osmotic pressure are called isotonic.
Wilhelm Pfeffer studied osmotic pressure with the Pfeffer cell.
In reverse osmosis, a pressure is needed that is greater than the osmotic pressure.

abschnitte.text: Imagine two solutions separated by a **semipermeable membrane**. This partition lets water molecules through, but not larger dissolved particles such as sugar. The water then flows overall **to the side with the higher concentration**. You can also say: water moves from the **higher to the lower water potential**. The pressure that arises in this way is called **osmotic pressure**.

The German botanist **Wilhelm Pfeffer** studied osmotic pressure in the 19th century. For this he used a measuring cell called the **Pfeffer cell**. The chemist **van ’t Hoff** found a formula for it: the pressure depends on the particle concentration and the temperature. A sugar solution of 0.1 mol per litre has an osmotic pressure of **about 2.5 bar** at 300 kelvin. A **salt solution** of the same concentration has a greater pressure, because each salt particle splits into two ions.

**Root hairs** take up water from the soil by osmosis. Their cell sap is **more concentrated** than the soil water, so water flows into the cells. The water presses from inside against the cell wall and keeps the plant firm. If water is lacking, this pressure falls and the plant wilts. Two solutions with the same osmotic pressure are called **isotonic**. Then no water flows overall.

Osmosis can also be reversed. In **reverse osmosis**, salty water is pressed with great force against a membrane. The pressure has to be **greater than the osmotic pressure**. Then water is pressed through the membrane and the salt stays behind. In this way, in many dry countries, drinking water is obtained from **sea water**.

gewusst: Cherries often burst after heavy rain because water flows into the fruit by osmosis.
Salt on slices of cucumber draws water out of the cells by osmosis.

teile.einleitung: Many animal and plant species do not live in one single large group, but spread over many small habitats. When these groups are linked by migration, we speak of a metapopulation. The concept helps in nature conservation.
wichtigste: A metapopulation consists of spatially separate subpopulations that are linked by migration.
The term was coined by Richard Levins in 1969.
Subpopulations can die out and later be settled anew.
Immigrants can save a small subpopulation from dying out: the rescue effect.
A subpopulation that would die out without immigration is called a sink.
In Switzerland, wildlife overpasses link separated habitats again.

abschnitte.text: A **population** is a group of living things of the same species in one place. Often suitable habitats such as ponds, meadows or patches of woodland are scattered across the landscape like islands. On each island lives a **subpopulation**. Individual animals travel from patch to patch. All the subpopulations together form a **metapopulation**, a “population of populations”.

The ecologist **Richard Levins** described metapopulations in 1969 with a simple formula. Here e is the rate at which subpopulations die out, and c is the rate at which empty patches are settled anew. At equilibrium, the share of occupied patches is **p = 1 minus e/c**. With e = 0.2 and c = 0.5, p = 1 minus 0.4 = **0.6**. So six out of ten patches are occupied.

The Finnish researcher **Ilkka Hanski** studied the **Glanville fritillary** on the **Åland Islands** for decades. There the butterflies live on many small meadows. Hanski showed that individual groups keep disappearing while others appear anew. The species survives as long as enough meadows can be reached.

In the **mainland-island model** there is one large, stable main population that supplies the small subpopulations around it with immigrants. A subpopulation that has more young than needed is called a **source**. One that would die out without constant immigration is called a **sink**. When immigrants strengthen a shrinking group, this is called the **rescue effect**.

Roads, settlements and railway lines cut up the landscape. Animals such as deer, foxes or amphibians then can no longer reach other groups. In Switzerland, **wildlife overpasses** are therefore built over motorways and **wildlife corridors** are set aside. In this way separated subpopulations are linked again, and the metapopulation stays viable.

gewusst: A species can survive in a landscape even though each of its subpopulations will sooner or later die out.
Even small ponds lying close together can work like a network of stepping stones for frogs and newts.

teile.einleitung: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, and at the same time the smallest planet in our Solar System. It races around the Sun once in only 88 days. On its surface, glowing heat and icy cold take turns.
wichtigste: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
It is the smallest of the eight planets in the Solar System.
It needs only 88 days for one trip around the Sun.
Mercury has no moon and almost no atmosphere.
In the day it gets over 400 degrees hot, at night far below minus 150 degrees cold.
Its surface is covered with craters and looks similar to our Moon.
It is named after Mercury, the swift messenger of the gods in Roman legend.

abschnitte.text: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and is one of the **rocky planets**. With a diameter of about 4,900 kilometres it is the smallest planet in the Solar System, only a little bigger than our Moon. It has a very large **iron core** that makes up a large part of its interior. It got its name from the Roman messenger of the gods Mercury, because it moves so quickly across the sky.

Mercury goes around the Sun in only **88 days**, faster than any other planet. It turns on its own axis very slowly, though, once in about 59 Earth days. As a result, a whole day from one sunrise to the next lasts about 176 Earth days. So on Mercury a day is twice as long as a year.

Because Mercury has almost no **atmosphere**, it cannot hold on to heat. On the day side it gets over 400 degrees hot, hot enough to melt lead. On the night side the temperature falls to about minus 170 degrees. In deep craters at the poles, where sunlight never falls, researchers have even discovered **water ice**.

The surface of Mercury is grey and covered with countless **craters**, like the surface of the Moon. The biggest known impact crater is the **Caloris Basin**, about 1,500 kilometres across. Long steep slopes run for hundreds of kilometres; they probably formed when the planet shrank as it cooled. Many craters are named after famous artists, musicians and writers.

Because Mercury is so close to the Sun, it is hard to reach with space probes. The American probe Mariner 10 was the first to fly past it, in the 1970s. The probe **MESSENGER** orbited it from 2011 to 2015 and mapped the whole surface. The European-Japanese mission **BepiColombo** launched in 2018 and is due to enter orbit around Mercury at the end of 2026.

From Earth, Mercury is hard to see, because it always stands close to the Sun. You can only spot it briefly after sunset in the evening sky or shortly before sunrise in the morning sky, low above the horizon. Sometimes Mercury, seen from Earth, passes exactly in front of the Sun’s disc; this is called a **transit of Mercury**. The next transit of Mercury can be seen in November 2032.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large heavenly body that orbits a star such as the Sun.
The envelope of gas that surrounds a planet.
When Mercury, seen from Earth, passes in front of the Sun.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores other heavenly bodies.

gewusst: Although Mercury is closest to the Sun, Venus is the hottest planet, because its dense atmosphere holds in the heat.
On Mercury, at some places you can see the Sun rise briefly, set again and rise again.
Mercury is smaller than the biggest moons of Jupiter and Saturn, Ganymede and Titan.

teile.einleitung: A magnifying glass is a simple lens for enlarging things. With it you can look closely at small things in nature, for example leaves, stones or beetles.
wichtigste: The most important part of a magnifying glass is a curved lens.
The lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge.
Never look at the sun with a magnifying glass, it injures the eyes.
In the sun, a magnifying glass can set dry leaves alight.
You see sharply when you find the right distance.

abschnitte.titel: How a magnifying glass is built
abschnitte.text: A magnifying glass consists mainly of a **lens** made of glass or plastic. The lens is **curved**: in the middle it is thicker than at the edge. This is called a **converging lens**. It bends the light so that things behind it look bigger. Usually the magnifying glass has a handle or a frame.

Hold the magnifying glass close to the thing you want to look at. Then move it **slowly closer or further away**. At a particular **distance** the image becomes sharp. On a leaf you discover in this way the fine **leaf veins** through which water flows. On a beetle you can count the **six legs**, for all insects have six legs.

A magnifying glass **focuses** sunlight onto a small, very bright and hot spot. That is why you must **never look at the sun** with a magnifying glass. The focused light can seriously injure the eyes. Do not leave the magnifying glass lying in the blazing sun either. Dry leaves or paper there can **catch fire**.

gewusst: A very long time ago, people already used ground stones or glass to see things bigger.
Drops of water on a leaf also act like small magnifying glasses.

teile.einleitung: To grow, plants need light, water and **nutrients** from the soil. The three most important main nutrients are in **NPK fertiliser**. The letters stand for their chemical symbols.
wichtigste: N stands for nitrogen, P for phosphorus and K for potassium.
Nitrogen above all promotes the growth of leaves and stems.
The plant needs phosphorus for roots, flowers and its energy balance.
Potassium is important for the plant’s water balance.
The three numbers on the fertiliser give the content of the main nutrients in per cent.
Farmyard manure is dung or slurry from farm animals.
If too much fertiliser gets into lakes, algae grow far too strongly.

abschnitte.titel: What N, P and K mean
abschnitte.text: The letters come from the periodic table of the elements. **N** is the symbol for **nitrogen**, **P** for **phosphorus** and **K** for **potassium**. The K comes from the Latin word “kalium”. Plants take up these substances as dissolved salts with their roots. Because they need a lot of them, they are called **main nutrients**.

abschnitte.titel: What the plant needs them for
abschnitte.text: **Nitrogen** above all promotes the growth of **leaves and stems**. If it is lacking, the leaves turn light green to yellow. The plant needs **phosphorus** for strong **roots**, for **flowers** and for its **energy balance** in the cells. **Potassium** controls the **water balance**. It helps the plant to hold water and to survive drought or frost better.

On many fertiliser packs there are three numbers, for example **15-15-15**. They show how many **per cent** of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are in the fertiliser, always in this order. A fertiliser 15-15-15 therefore contains 15 per cent of each main nutrient. A lawn fertiliser often contains more nitrogen, a fertiliser for flowers more phosphorus.

There are different kinds of fertiliser. **Mineral fertiliser** is made in factories or obtained from rock. **Farmyard manure** is **dung or slurry** from farm animals such as cows and pigs. In Switzerland farmyard manure is very common, because there are many farms with animals. Compost from the garden and kitchen is also a natural fertiliser.

If too much fertiliser gets into water, for example through rain, lakes become **over-fertilised**. Then **algae grow far too strongly**. When they die, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen in breaking them down, and fish can suffocate. In Switzerland several lakes on the Central Plateau were affected. Some, such as Lake Sempach and Lake Baldegg, have therefore been supplied with oxygen artificially for decades.

gewusst: Besides N, P and K, plants also need small amounts of substances such as iron or magnesium.
Clover and peas can get nitrogen from the air thanks to bacteria on their roots.

teile.einleitung: Aerial roots are roots that grow not in the ground but above ground from the trunk, branches or stem. Depending on the plant, they hold on, support, fetch water or even air.
wichtigste: Aerial roots arise above the ground from the shoot.
Ivy holds on to walls and trees with adhesive roots.
Orchids take up rainwater and moisture with their aerial roots.
Mangroves fetch oxygen from the air with breathing roots.
Maize forms prop roots against the wind.
In the banyan tree, aerial roots become new trunks.

abschnitte.text: **Ivy** forms many short **adhesive roots**. They claw into the smallest unevenness of walls and tree bark. In this way the ivy can climb high. Water and nutrients, however, it takes up through its normal roots in the ground.

Many **orchids** such as the popular houseplant **Phalaenopsis** grow in nature in the rainforest on branches. Their silvery-green aerial roots take up **rainwater** and moisture from the air. Such plants, which grow on other plants without contact with the ground, are called **epiphytes**. Unlike parasites, they do not draw nutrients from what they sit on.

The mud in **mangrove forests** contains hardly any oxygen. Many mangroves therefore form **breathing roots** that stick up vertically out of the mud. Through them air reaches the roots in the ground. In this way the trees can survive in the wet soil by the sea.

**Maize** forms aerial roots on the lower nodes of the stem, which grow obliquely into the ground. These **prop roots** keep the tall plant upright in the wind. Even more impressive is the **banyan tree**, a kind of fig from India. Its aerial roots grow down from the branches, thicken in the ground and become **supporting trunks**.

The **strangler fig** germinates high up on a tree. From there it sends aerial roots down to the ground. In time these roots enclose the trunk of the **host tree** and take away its light and space. Often the host tree then dies, and the fig stands alone.

gewusst: A single banyan tree with its many supporting trunks can look like a small forest.
The aerial roots of orchids turn green when they are wet.

teile.einleitung: The ox-eye daisy is a well-known meadow flower with white petals and a yellow centre. In early summer, whole fields of ox-eye daisies shine on many meadows.
wichtigste: The ox-eye daisy has white petals and a yellow centre.
The centre is made up of many tiny tubular flowers.
It looks like a big daisy.
It grows to about 30 to 60 centimetres tall.
Ox-eye daisies bloom mainly in May and June.
In Switzerland people often say “Margritli”.

abschnitte.text: The **ox-eye daisy** has a ring of long, **white** petals and a **yellow centre**. It looks very like the small **daisy**, but is much bigger and has a long stem. It grows to about **30 to 60 centimetres** tall and stands well above the grass.

What looks like a single flower is really very many. The yellow centre is made of very many tiny **tubular flowers**. The white “petals” at the edge are also little flowers. Together they form a **flower head**. That is why the ox-eye daisy belongs to the **daisy family**.

Ox-eye daisies bloom mainly in **May and June**, often later in summer too. They like **poor meadows** that get little fertiliser. There they have enough light and room. The open flower is easy to reach. That is why many **beetles, flies and bees** land on it.

In Switzerland the ox-eye daisy is often lovingly called **“Margritli”**. The first name **Margrit** comes from the same word. Children like to play a counting game with the ox-eye daisy: they **pluck** one petal after another and say a line in turn. The last petal decides the result.

gewusst: The name Margerite, as the plant is known in German, comes from the Greek word for pearl.
The sunflower and the dandelion are also members of the daisy family.

teile.einleitung: Lignin is the substance that makes wood hard and firm. It is deposited in the cell walls of plants and makes them woody. After cellulose, lignin is one of the most common organic substances on Earth.
wichtigste: Lignin makes the cell wall resistant to pressure and stiff.
The name comes from the Latin lignum for wood.
Lignin is built from phenylpropane units, the monolignols.
White-rot fungi can break down lignin effectively.
Cheap newsprint turns yellow because its lignin oxidises in the light.
Softwood generally contains more lignin than hardwood.

abschnitte.text: Lignin is deposited between the **cellulose fibres** of the cell wall. This process is called **lignification**. The name comes from the Latin **lignum** for wood. Cellulose carries mainly **tension**, lignin mainly **compression**. Together they make wood so stable that trees can grow many metres tall. You can compare it with reinforced concrete: the fibres are like the steel, the lignin like the concrete.

Lignin is made from three building blocks, the **monolignols**. They are called coumaryl alcohol, **coniferyl alcohol** and sinapyl alcohol. They are **phenylpropane units**. They link up into an irregular, three-dimensional network. **Softwood** usually contains about 26 to 32 per cent lignin, native hardwood often about 18 to 25 per cent. In softwood lignin, coniferyl alcohol predominates; hardwood lignin additionally contains a lot of sinapyl alcohol.

Lignin is hard to break down. Only a few living things manage it well. Especially effective are **white-rot fungi**. They break down the lignin, and pale, fibrous wood is left behind. **Brown-rot fungi**, by contrast, decompose mainly the cellulose. They leave the brown lignin, and the wood breaks up into cube-shaped pieces.

Paper consists of wood fibres. **Groundwood paper**, such as cheap newsprint, still contains almost all of the lignin. Under light and oxygen it **oxidises**, and yellow compounds form. That is why such paper **turns yellow**. For bright, lasting paper, the lignin is dissolved out. In the **sulphate process**, also called the kraft process, a hot liquor dissolves the lignin out of the wood. What is left are the cellulose fibres, the **pulp**.

gewusst: Without lignin, trees could not grow so tall, because their trunks would not withstand the pressure.
Old newspapers turn yellow because the lignin in them reacts with light and air.

teile.einleitung: Light pollution means that the night becomes too bright through artificial light. Street lamps, lit buildings and advertisements light up the sky. This disturbs animals, plants and people too.
wichtigste: Many insects circle lamps until they are exhausted.
Migratory birds can lose their orientation through bright light.
Warm-white light attracts fewer insects.
Over cities a bright dome of light forms.
The Bortle scale rates the darkness of the night sky in nine levels.
Light at night inhibits the sleep hormone melatonin.
Lamps that shine only downwards reduce light pollution.

abschnitte.text: Many **nocturnal insects** are attracted by light. They circle around street lamps and cannot get away. They die of **exhaustion** or are eaten by predators. Insects react especially strongly to short-wave **blue and ultraviolet light**. **Warm-white** lamps with little blue content attract clearly fewer insects.

Many **migratory birds** fly at night. They orient themselves, among other things, by the **stars**. Brightly lit cities and buildings can distract them. Then they lose their **orientation** and circle the lights or crash into buildings. Bats, fish and plants too are affected by artificial light at night.

abschnitte.titel: The dome of light over the city
abschnitte.text: Light that shines upwards is scattered by particles in the air. In this way a bright **dome of light** arises over cities, which you can see from far away. It outshines the **starry sky**. In many places you can no longer see the Milky Way. The darkness of the sky is measured with the **Bortle scale**. It runs from 1 for a very dark sky to 9 for the sky in a city centre.

Our body needs the dark. In darkness it makes the hormone **melatonin**. It controls the **sleep-wake rhythm**. Bright light at night, especially blue, suppresses its production. That is why you sleep better in a dark room.

Very effective are **shielded lights** that shine the light **only downwards**. In this way hardly any light reaches the sky. You can also switch on light only when it is needed, for example with motion sensors. Warm-white lamps spare insects. In Switzerland, some municipalities partly switch off or dim the street lighting at night.

gewusst: Many children in cities have never seen the Milky Way with their own eyes.
A single street lamp can attract a great many insects on a summer night.

teile.einleitung: The daffodil, in German “Osterglocke”, is a yellow spring flower from the group of narcissi. It blooms around Easter, which is how it got its German name, meaning “Easter bell”. Its flower has a trumpet in the middle.
wichtigste: The daffodil is mostly yellow.
It belongs to the narcissi.
Its German name comes from the fact that it blooms around Easter, mostly in March and April.
The middle of the flower looks like a trumpet.
All parts of the daffodil are poisonous.
Above Montreux, in May the meadows are famous for wild white narcissi.

abschnitte.text: The **daffodil** belongs to the **narcissi**. It is mostly **yellow**. Its flower has a ring of six petals on the outside. In the middle sits a long tube that looks like a **trumpet**. The plant grows from a **bulb** in the ground. There it stores nutrients for the next year.

The daffodil blooms in **March and April**, so often around **Easter**. That is where its German name comes from. It is one of the first flowers in the garden and announces spring. After flowering it withdraws into its bulb again. You should cut off the leaves only when they have turned yellow, so that the bulb gathers enough strength.

abschnitte.titel: Poisonous and bad for other flowers
abschnitte.text: **All parts** of the daffodil are poisonous, especially the bulb. You must not mistake it for a kitchen onion. In a vase it is better to put daffodils **on their own**. Their **sap** makes other flowers such as tulips wilt faster. If you want to mix them anyway, first stand them in water on their own for a few hours.

In Switzerland there are also **wild narcissi**. Famous are the meadows **above Montreux**. In **May** countless white narcissi bloom there, and the slopes look as if covered with snow. People also speak of “May snow”. These meadows are a popular destination for outings. You should leave the wild narcissi standing and only look at them.

gewusst: The name narcissus goes back to a figure from a Greek legend.
The daffodil is the national flower of Wales.

teile.einleitung: Sequoias are huge conifers from California. They are among the largest and oldest living things on Earth, and today they also grow in Swiss parks.
wichtigste: The giant sequoia comes from the Sierra Nevada in California.
Sequoias are conifers with scale-like needles and cones.
Giant sequoias grow over 80 metres tall and live for over 3000 years.
The thick, reddish-brown bark protects them from forest fires.
The cones are only about as big as a hen’s egg.
The tallest tree in the world is a coast redwood.

abschnitte.text: The **giant sequoia** grows wild on the mountain slopes of the **Sierra Nevada** in **California** in the USA. It is a **conifer**: it has small, scale-like needles and bears cones. The biggest giant sequoias are **over 80 metres** tall. Their trunks are so thick at the bottom that many people would have to link arms to reach around them.
The oldest giant sequoias are **over 3000 years** old. That makes them some of the oldest living things on Earth. Some were already standing when emperors still ruled in ancient Rome.

The **bark** of the giant sequoia is fibrous, soft and **reddish brown**. That is why the trunks glow red in the sun. It can grow more than half a metre thick and does not burn easily. In this way the trees survive many **forest fires**.
Although the tree is huge, its **cones** are small. They are only about 5 to 8 centimetres long, roughly as big as a **hen’s egg**. The seeds inside are tiny.

Around **1850**, the first seeds came from California to Europe. Soon afterwards, sequoias were also planted in Switzerland, in **parks** and gardens. So they have been growing here for over 150 years. A close relative is the **coast redwood**. It is the tallest tree in the world: the tallest known tree in California is over **115 metres** tall.

gewusst: The giant sequoia is one of the trees with the greatest volume of wood in the world.
Fire even helps the cones to open and release their seeds.

teile.einleitung: Ergot is a dark, elongated body that can stick out of an ear of cereal in place of a grain. It is formed by a fungus and is poisonous. In the past it led to severe poisoning; today its active substances are also used in medicine.
wichtigste: Ergot is formed by the fungus Claviceps purpurea.
Biologically it is a sclerotium, a resting body of the fungus.
The fungus especially often attacks rye.
In the Middle Ages, poisoning from ergot was called St Anthony’s fire.
The effect is caused by the ergot alkaloids.
In 1938 the Basel chemist Albert Hofmann made LSD from an active substance in ergot.

abschnitte.text: Ergot is formed by the fungus **Claviceps purpurea**. It attacks the flowers of grasses and cereals, especially often **rye**. In the flower the fungus first makes a sweet juice, the **honeydew**. It **attracts insects**, which carry the **fungal spores** on to other flowers. Later a dark violet, hard body grows out in the place of the grain.

Biologically, ergot is a **sclerotium**, that is, a **resting body** of the fungus. It is made of densely interwoven fungal threads. With it the fungus survives the winter in the soil. In spring, small stalked heads grow from it and form new spores. So the cycle starts again.

In the past, grain was hardly cleaned. If a lot of ergot got into the flour, people fell ill. This poisoning is called **ergotism**, and in the **Middle Ages** it was called **St Anthony’s fire**. The poisons **narrow the blood vessels**. In severe poisoning, fingers and toes no longer got enough blood and died. The sick were looked after by, among others, the Order of St Anthony.

The effect is caused by the **ergot alkaloids**, a group of substances that the fungus makes. In the right dose, some of them can help as a medicine. **Ergotamine**, for example, was used **against migraine attacks**. In Basel, the company Sandoz researched these substances. There the chemist **Albert Hofmann** made **LSD** from an active substance in ergot in **1938**, a drug that strongly changes perception and thinking.

Today ergot poisoning is very rare here. After the harvest, grain is thoroughly **cleaned**, and modern machines sort out dark grains. **Limits** apply for food. Farmers can reduce infestation by rotating fields and keeping grasses at the field edge short.

gewusst: A single piece of ergot can be much bigger than a normal grain of rye.
Albert Hofmann lived to be over 100 years old.

teile.einleitung: Limnology is the science of inland waters, that is of lakes, ponds, rivers and streams. It studies how the water, the plants and the animals in it interact. It was founded by a researcher from Switzerland.
wichtigste: Limnology studies inland waters such as lakes and rivers.
François-Alphonse Forel from Morges is regarded as its founder.
Forel dedicated his main work “Le Léman” to Lake Geneva.
A seiche is a standing wave in which the whole lake surface swings.
The pelagic zone is the open water, the profundal zone the lightless deep bottom.
Water clarity is measured with the Secchi disc.
Flowing waters are called lotic, standing waters lentic.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Vaud as founder
abschnitte.text: **François-Alphonse Forel** from **Morges** in the canton of Vaud is regarded as the founder of limnology. In the 19th century he studied **Lake Geneva** comprehensively and coined the term limnology. His three-volume main work is called **“Le Léman”**. It describes the lake in physics, chemistry and biology and is regarded as the first comprehensive monograph on a lake. Today in Switzerland, among others, the water research institute **Eawag** carries out research on waters.

In a **seiche** the water of a whole lake sloshes back and forth as in a bathtub. It is a **standing wave**: the lake surface rises at one end and falls at the other. It is set off, for example, by wind or changes in air pressure. Forel was one of the first to study this phenomenon exactly, on Lake Geneva.

A lake has different habitats. The shore zone is called the **littoral**. The open water far from shore and bottom is the **pelagic zone**, the open-water zone. There live plankton and freely swimming fish such as **whitefish**. The deep lake bottom, on which no longer enough light for plants falls, is called the **profundal zone**. There bacteria and bottom animals mainly decompose material that has sunk down.

How deep the light reaches is decisive for life in the lake. **Water clarity** is measured with a **Secchi disc**. A white or black-and-white disc is lowered on a line. The depth at which it just disappears is the water clarity. At the **compensation level** the photosynthesis of the algae just balances their own respiration. Above it more oxygen is made than is used up, below it less.

Technical language distinguishes two kinds of waters. **Lotic** waters are flowing waters such as streams and rivers. **Lentic** waters are standing waters such as lakes and ponds. Both have quite different inhabitants. In streams live many animals that hold on to stones so that the current does not carry them away.

gewusst: The term limnology comes from the Greek word limne for lake.
Even on Lake Geneva, in a seiche the water level swings slowly back and forth.

teile.einleitung: Without a **mill** there would be no flour, no bread and no pasta. In a mill, grains of cereal are finely ground. Mills have existed for thousands of years.
wichtigste: In a mill, flour is made from grains of cereal.
Someone who grinds grain is a miller.
In the past, a water wheel on a stream drove the mill, or the wind turned the sails of a windmill.
Old mills crushed the grain with millstones.
Modern mills grind with steel rollers.
Before grinding, the grain is cleaned.
What is left over is the parts of the husk, the bran.

abschnitte.text: In the past many mills stood on streams. The flowing water turned a large **water wheel**. The power was carried to the millstones by gears. In flat, windy regions, **windmills** with big sails were built. In Switzerland water mills were much more common, because there are many streams here. Some old mills can still be visited today.

In old mills the grain was crushed between two heavy, round **millstones**. The lower stone lay still, and the upper one turned above it. The grains came through a hole in the middle and were crushed finer and finer as they moved outwards. The stones had to be sharpened again regularly. The **miller** knew a lot about this.

Today most mills work with **steel rollers**. First the grain is **cleaned**: small stones, dust and weed seeds are removed. Then the grain runs several times through pairs of rollers, which make it finer step by step. Between the passes, sieves separate the fine flour from coarser parts. Most modern mills run on electricity.

Pale **flour** is made from the inside of the grain. The parts of the husk that are left over are called **bran**. They contain a lot of fibre and go, for example, into wholemeal flour or into animal feed. Coarsely ground grain is called **semolina**. From it you can cook, for example, a fine semolina porridge.

gewusst: Many family names such as the German Müller or the English Miller recall the old trade.
Coffee, pepper or maize are also ground in mills.

teile.einleitung: Storm Lothar swept across Western Europe and Switzerland on 26 December 1999. It was one of the severest storms that Switzerland has ever experienced. It hit the forests especially hard.
wichtigste: Lothar passed over Switzerland on 26 December 1999.
In Switzerland it blew down about 13 million cubic metres of timber.
The Central Plateau and the Pre-Alps were hit hardest.
Especially many spruces fell, because they have shallow roots.
In the years afterwards, bark beetles multiplied in huge numbers in the storm-felled wood.
As early as 1990, Storm Vivian had caused great forest damage.

abschnitte.titel: The storm on St Stephen’s Day
abschnitte.text: On **26 December 1999**, St Stephen’s Day, Storm Lothar passed over France, Switzerland and southern Germany. In a few hours the gusts in Switzerland reached hurricane force. The **Central Plateau** and the **Pre-Alps** were hit hardest. Roofs were stripped off, roads and railway lines were blocked. Many people lost their lives, in Switzerland too.

In Switzerland Lothar blew down about **13 million cubic metres** of timber. That was roughly as much as is otherwise harvested in several years. Especially many **spruces** fell. They have **shallow roots** and offer the wind a large surface. As early as 1990, Storm **Vivian** had caused great damage, mainly in mountain forests.

Clearing up was dangerous. Fallen trees are often under tension and can suddenly spring back. This led to **fatal accidents**. Because so much timber came at once, the **timber price fell sharply**. Much storm-felled wood was **sprinkled with water continuously** in large storage yards. In this way it stayed damp and was not attacked by fungi and insects.

In the years after the storm, **bark beetles** multiplied in huge numbers in the lying wood. They then also attacked healthy spruces. On many storm areas, though, **young forest grew back without planting**. Often more broadleaved trees came up than before. Researchers are still observing these areas today. Since then many foresters have relied on mixed forests, which withstand storms better.

gewusst: In Switzerland Lothar blew down more timber than was used in an average year at the time.
On the Lothar Trail in Baden-Württemberg you can still visit a storm area today.

teile.einleitung: Mangroves are forests of trees and shrubs that grow in salt water on tropical coasts. At high tide they stand in the sea, at low tide in mud.
wichtigste: Mangroves can cope with salty sea water.
At high tide they are flooded, at low tide the ground dries out.
Many mangroves get air through breathing roots.
On Borneo, the proboscis monkey lives in mangroves.
Male fiddler crabs wave one big claw.

abschnitte.text: Most plants die if they get salty water. **Mangroves** can live with it. They grow on flat, warm coasts in the **tropics**, often at river mouths. Some species keep the salt back at the roots, others get rid of it again through their leaves.

At **high tide** the sea rises and floods the mangroves. At **low tide** the ground dries out again. The muddy ground contains hardly any oxygen. That is why many mangroves grow **stilt roots**, which hold them in the soft ground, and **breathing roots**, which stick out of the mud and take in air.
On the island of **Borneo**, the **proboscis monkey** lives in mangroves and in forests along rivers. It has a very large nose and is a good **swimmer**. It eats mainly leaves.
Many **crabs** live on the mud of the mangroves. In the **fiddler crab**, the male has one very large claw. He waves it as if he were greeting someone. The other claw is small.

Between the roots of the mangroves, many young **fish** find shelter from enemies. Mangroves hold the mud in place and protect the **coast** from waves and storms. That is why they are important for people and animals.

gewusst: Mangrove forests are found on the coasts of many tropical countries in Asia, Africa and the Americas.

teile.einleitung: Plants need light to live. With light they make their own food in their green leaves. That is why they always grow towards the light.
wichtigste: Plants need light to make food.
Outdoors they get their light from the sun.
Plants grow towards the light.
A houseplant is best placed near a window.
Ferns grow well in the shade of the forest.
Tomatoes need a lot of sun so that their fruits ripen.

abschnitte.text: Plants cannot eat like us. They make their **food themselves**. For this they need **light**, water and air. This happens in the **green leaves**. Outdoors the **sun** supplies the light. The plant makes sugar from it, on which it lives and grows. In doing so it gives off oxygen, which we need for breathing.

Plants grow in the direction from which the light comes. That is why plants at a window lean **towards the light**. A houseplant is best placed **near a window**. There it gets enough daylight. If you turn the pot **now and then**, the plant grows evenly and straight. Without light plants become pale and form long, thin shoots.

In the forest it is often shady. **Ferns** need less light and like to grow in the shady, damp forest. Many woodland flowers such as the **wood anemone** bloom already **in spring**. Then the deciduous trees have no leaves yet, and a lot of light falls on the forest floor. When the trees get their leaves, the spring flowers have already done their work.

Some plants need an especially large amount of sun. **Tomatoes** love a sunny, warm spot. There their fruits become **ripe and red**. Sunflowers, strawberries and many herbs also like it bright. Anyone planting a garden or balcony therefore first looks at how much sun a spot gets.

gewusst: Young sunflowers turn their heads to follow the sun in the course of the day.
Potatoes that sprout in a dark cellar form long, pale shoots in search of light.

teile.einleitung: Many animals and plants need habitats that are large enough and linked with one another. Switzerland is therefore building up an Ecological Infrastructure, a network of protected areas and links between them. The Confederation, cantons and municipalities work together on it.
wichtigste: The Ecological Infrastructure consists of core areas and connecting areas.
The Federal Council set the goal in 2012 in the Biodiversity Strategy Switzerland.
Connecting areas are important because isolated populations are more prone to inbreeding and dying out.
Fragmentation means the cutting up of habitats into small pieces.
Wildlife overpasses help animals to cross motorways safely.
Gardens, parks and green roofs can also be part of the network.
The Confederation supports the cantons mainly through programme agreements.

abschnitte.text: The **Ecological Infrastructure** is a network of habitats for animals and plants. It consists of **core areas** and **connecting areas**. Core areas are valuable habitats such as nature reserves, moors or floodplains. Connecting areas link them with one another so that animals and plants can get from one area to another. Just as people need roads and railway lines, nature too needs a working network.

In **2012**, in the **Biodiversity Strategy Switzerland**, the **Federal Council** set out that an Ecological Infrastructure should be built up. Biodiversity means the variety of life: species, habitats and genes. The cantons plan which areas belong to it. The **Confederation** supports them mainly with money through **programme agreements**, which are contracts on goals and contributions for several years.

Roads, railway lines and settlements cut up the landscape. This is called **fragmentation**: habitats are divided into **small, isolated pieces**. Animals living in such a piece can hardly exchange with other groups. **Isolated populations** are more prone to **inbreeding** and can **die out** more easily, for example after a hard winter or a disease.

So that animals can move again, **wildlife overpasses** are built. These are wide, planted bridges on which roe deer, red deer or foxes can cross a **motorway** safely. **Stepping-stone biotopes** are also important: small habitats such as ponds, hedges or flower meadows that serve species as a **stopover** on their way, like stones you use to cross a stream.

The Ecological Infrastructure does not end at the edge of the village. **Near-natural gardens**, **parks** and **green roofs** can also serve as **linking elements**. Native shrubs, flower meadows, piles of branches or small gaps in fences help hedgehogs, insects and birds. In this way every municipality and even every garden can make a small contribution.

gewusst: For hedgehogs, a hole of about 10 by 10 centimetres in the garden fence is enough for them to move from garden to garden.
Switzerland has built several wildlife overpasses over motorways, and more are planned.

teile.einleitung: A food chain shows who eats whom in nature. It usually begins with a green plant and leads through plant-eaters to meat-eaters. Because almost every living thing has several enemies and several sources of food, many chains are linked into a food web.
wichtigste: A food chain is the sequence of who eats whom in nature.
On land, a typical food chain begins with a green plant.
Plants are called producers because they make their own food with sunlight.
Animals are consumers and are divided into orders.
In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, stork, the frog is the secondary consumer.
From step to step, only about 10 per cent of the energy is passed on.
Decomposers break down dead animals and plants; several linked chains form a food web.

abschnitte.text: A **food chain** describes how energy and nutrients are passed on from one living thing to the next. An example from the meadow: grass is eaten by the grasshopper, the grasshopper by the frog and the frog by the stork. Each link in the chain is food for the next. The arrows in a food chain always point in the direction in which the energy flows.

At the start of almost every food chain stand the **producers**, the makers. These are green plants, algae and some bacteria. With the energy of sunlight they make sugar from water and carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. All other living things depend on them, directly or indirectly.

Animals are **consumers**, that is, users. Plant-eaters such as grasshopper, deer or cow are primary consumers. Whoever eats plant-eaters, like the frog, is a secondary consumer. Next come tertiary consumers such as the stork; at the top are animals with no natural enemies, such as the golden eagle, the wolf or the lynx.

At each step, a large part of the energy is used for movement, heat and respiration. Only about 10 per cent reaches the next step. If the plants of a meadow store 10,000 kilojoules, about 1,000 arrive at the primary consumers and only about 100 kilojoules at the secondary consumers. That is why there are many more plants than plant-eaters and many more plant-eaters than predators; this is called a **food pyramid**.

Dead plants and animals are broken down by the **decomposers**. These include bacteria, fungi, earthworms, woodlice and many small creatures in the soil. They turn the remains back into nutrients that plants can take up. In this way the cycle of materials in nature closes.

In nature a fox does not eat only mice, but also berries, beetles and birds. That is why many food chains are linked into a **food web**. If one species drops out, others can often switch, but sometimes the whole web gets out of balance. Poisons such as the insecticide DDT used to build up along the chain and mainly harmed birds of prey at the top.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that makes its own food, usually a green plant.
A living thing that eats other living things, that is, an animal.
A breaker-down such as fungi or bacteria that decomposes dead living things.
Several food chains linked with one another.

gewusst: The blue whale, the biggest animal on Earth, feeds on tiny crustaceans called krill.
In the deep sea there are food chains that begin not with sunlight but with bacteria at hot springs.
Humans are also part of food chains, depending on what they eat as primary consumers or higher.

teile.einleitung: Conifers are trees that carry narrow, hard needles instead of broad leaves. Most of them stay green in winter too. Spruce, fir, pine, larch and Swiss stone pine are among the most important conifers in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Conifers carry needle-shaped leaves instead of broad leaves.
Unlike most broadleaved trees, they often keep their needles in winter too.
The larch is an exception and loses its needles in autumn.
In the pine, the long needles always grow together in twos.
Sticky resin often oozes from the bark of conifers.
The Swiss stone pine grows high in the Alps and has edible nuts.
Their seeds usually ripen in cones.

abschnitte.text: **Conifers** are trees with narrow, needle-shaped leaves. Botanically they belong to the **gymnosperms**, because their seeds lie open on the scales of the cones and are not enclosed in a fruit. They have existed for over 300 million years, longer than broadleaved trees. There are about 600 species worldwide.

Most conifers do not drop their needles every autumn, but renew them bit by bit over several years. Needles have a thick **layer of wax** and a small surface, so they lose little water. In this way they survive winters in which the ground is frozen. The sloping branches and flexible twigs also let snow slide off.

The **spruce** has sharp, prickly needles all around the twig and hanging cones. The silver fir has soft needles with two white stripes underneath and upright cones. In the **pine**, long needles always grow in twos, in the Swiss stone pine in fives. The larch has soft needles in tufts and drops them in autumn after they have turned golden yellow.

The **Swiss stone pine** is a conifer of the high Alps and in Switzerland grows to over 2,000 metres, for example in the Engadine and in the Valais. It can live for several hundred years and withstands great cold. Its nuts are edible. The nutcracker, a bird, hides the nuts in the ground as a winter store and forgets some of them, so new Swiss stone pines grow.

If the bark of a conifer is injured, **resin** oozes out. The sticky sap seals the wound and keeps fungi and insects away. Amber was formed from resin millions of years old, and in it you sometimes find trapped insects. In the past, pitch, turpentine and rosin for violin bows were obtained from resin.

Softwood is light, grows straight and is easy to work, so it is used a lot for building. The spruce is Switzerland’s most important supplier of wood. From larch wood people make weatherproof shingles and balconies, from Swiss stone pine wood fragrant furniture. As **Christmas trees**, mainly Nordmann firs and spruces are put up today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plants whose seeds lie open on the scales of cones.
The woody fruiting structure of a conifer in which the seeds ripen.
A sticky sap with which conifers seal their wounds.
A plant that has green leaves or needles all year round.

gewusst: Some bristlecone pines in California are over 4,500 years old.
The tallest trees in the world are conifers; the coast redwoods in California grow over 110 metres tall.
The yew is a conifer without cones; almost all its parts are poisonous.

teile.einleitung: Sustainable agriculture means producing food in a way that spares soil, water, animals and the climate. Future generations should still find fertile fields and varied nature. At the same time, farmers have to be able to make a living from their work.
wichtigste: Sustainable agriculture protects soil, water, biodiversity and the climate.
A varied crop rotation reduces pests and diseases in the soil.
To receive direct payments, Swiss farms have to provide proof of ecological performance.
As a rule, at least 7 per cent of the farmland has to be biodiversity promotion areas.
In integrated pest management, beneficial insects such as ladybirds and their larvae are used against aphids.
Direct seeding without ploughing protects arable soils especially effectively from erosion.
Green manuring and agroforestry improve the soil and promote diversity.

abschnitte.text: **Sustainability** means not using up more than can grow back. The term originally comes from forestry: you should only fell as much wood as grows back. In agriculture, this means keeping soils healthy, water clean and many species alive. It also means that farms survive economically and animals are kept well.

Almost all Swiss farms receive **direct payments** from the Confederation. In return they have to provide the proof of ecological performance, **ÖLN** for short. This includes a regulated crop rotation, a balanced use of fertiliser, targeted plant protection and animal-friendly housing. As a rule, at least 7 per cent of the farmland has to be **biodiversity promotion areas**, such as flower meadows, hedges or standard fruit trees.

In **crop rotation**, the plants in a field change from year to year, for example wheat, oilseed rape, maize and temporary grass. In this way pests and diseases in the soil cannot multiply so strongly. In **green manuring**, plants such as clover or mustard are sown and later worked into the soil. They provide humus and nutrients and cover the soil in winter.

In **integrated pest management**, chemical agents are only used when really necessary. Before that, beneficial insects help: ladybirds and their larvae eat large numbers of aphids. Parasitic wasps, lacewings and birds help too. Hedges and flower strips offer these helpers a habitat.

A fertile soil takes hundreds of years to form. When ploughed, it is turned over and lies open, and rain can easily wash it away. In **direct seeding**, seed is sown straight into the remains of the previous crop without ploughing. In this way the soil stays covered and protected from erosion, and earthworms are spared.

In organic farming, chemical-synthetic fertilisers and pesticides are not used. In Switzerland there is the **Knospe** (“bud”) label of Bio Suisse for this, while the label of IP-Suisse with the ladybird stands for integrated production. In agroforestry, trees grow together with arable crops or on pastures. The trees give shade, protect against wind, store carbon and provide fruit or wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money from the Confederation to farms for services to nature and society.
The proof of ecological performance: environmental rules that farms must follow to receive direct payments.
Animals that eat pests and so help the plants.
Growing plants that are worked into the soil to improve it.
A kind of land use in which trees are combined with arable farming or pasture.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development.
Under one square metre of healthy meadow there often live over a hundred earthworms.
Standard fruit trees once shaped the landscape in Thurgau and other cantons.

teile.einleitung: Nectar is a sweet liquid that many flowers make. With it plants attract animals that carry pollen from flower to flower when they visit. For bees, butterflies and hummingbirds, nectar is an important food.
wichtigste: Nectar is sugar water made by flowers.
It is a reward for animals that visit the flower and pollinate it as they do so.
The nectar usually lies deep down in the flower.
Butterflies drink nectar with their long proboscis.
Bees make nectar into honey by letting a lot of water evaporate.
Plants with a lot of nectar and pollen are called bee pasture.

abschnitte.text: Nectar is a sweet liquid of water and sugar. It is made in small glands, the **nectaries**. They usually lie deep down in the flower. An animal that wants the nectar therefore has to move far inside. As it does so, it brushes off **pollen**, that is, flower dust, and picks up new.

abschnitte.titel: An exchange between flower and animal
abschnitte.text: Flowers offer nectar as a **reward** for a visit. The animal gets food, and the plant is **pollinated**: the pollen reaches another flower of the same species. In this way the plant can form seeds and fruit. Some flowers have coloured lines pointing to the centre. These **nectar guides** show visitors the way to the nectar.

Butterflies unroll their long **proboscis** and suck up the nectar as if with a straw. The **hummingbird hawk-moth** is a moth that seems to stand still in the air while it drinks. In America live the **hummingbirds**. These small birds beat their wings very fast and hover in front of the flower. Bumblebees, flies and beetles also visit flowers for the nectar.

Honey bees collect nectar and carry it into the hive. There they add substances from their bodies and let a lot of **water evaporate**. The nectar becomes thicker and sweeter until it turns into **honey**. Plants that offer bees a lot of nectar and pollen are called **bee pasture**. They include, for example, fruit trees, lime trees, clover and lavender.

gewusst: Bees have to visit millions of flowers for a single jar of honey.
The hummingbird hawk-moth, because of its hovering flight, is often taken for a hummingbird, even in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a huge collection of stars, gas and dust. Our Sun and the Earth belong to it too. On dark nights you can see it as a bright, milky band across the sky.
wichtigste: The Milky Way is the galaxy that our Solar System belongs to.
It has the shape of a spiral with several arms.
There are estimated to be 100 to 400 billion stars in the Milky Way.
Its diameter is about 100,000 light years or more.
The Sun lies in a spiral arm, about 26,000 light years from the centre.
At the centre is a huge black hole.
Because of light pollution, the Milky Way can hardly be seen in cities any more.

abschnitte.text: A **galaxy** is a huge collection of stars held together by gravity. Our galaxy is called the Milky Way. Besides billions of stars, it contains clouds of gas, dust and planets. In the Universe there are billions more galaxies.

The Milky Way is a **spiral galaxy**: seen from above, it would look like a flat, glowing wheel with curved arms. To be more precise, it has a long bar in the middle, so it is a barred spiral galaxy. Its diameter is about 100,000 light years or more. A **light year** is the distance that light travels in a year, which is almost 10 trillion kilometres.

Our Sun does not lie at the centre, but in a spiral arm, about 26,000 light years from the middle. The Sun and its planets orbit the centre of the Milky Way. It needs about 230 million years for one lap. The last time the Sun was in the same place, the first dinosaurs were living on Earth.

abschnitte.titel: The heart of the Milky Way
abschnitte.text: At the centre of the Milky Way sits a **black hole** called Sagittarius A*. It is about four million times as heavy as the Sun. You cannot see it directly, but stars orbit around it very fast. In 2022 a first picture of its surroundings was published.

Because we sit in the middle of the flat disc, we see the Milky Way from the side as a bright band across the sky. In summer the brightest part, towards the constellation Sagittarius, is easy to see. Around 1610, Galileo Galilei realised with his telescope that the milky band is made up of countless individual stars. In Switzerland you see it best far from cities, for example in the mountains or in the Gantrisch Nature Park, where people fight **light pollution**.

The name comes from a Greek legend in which milk from the goddess Hera was splashed across the sky. The word galaxy also comes from the Greek word for milk. The Milky Way belongs to the **Local Group**, together with the Andromeda Galaxy and many smaller galaxies. In a few billion years, the Milky Way and Andromeda will probably merge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge collection of billions of stars, gas and dust.
The distance light travels in a year, almost 10 trillion kilometres.
A curved arm of a spiral galaxy, rich in stars.
Artificial light that brightens the night sky and hides the stars.

gewusst: Light from the other end of the Milky Way takes tens of thousands of years to reach us.
The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light years away and can be seen with the naked eye.
Nobody has ever seen the Milky Way from outside; all pictures of it are drawings or models.

teile.einleitung: Invasive neophytes spread strongly and push out native plants. That is why in Switzerland they are fought by municipalities, cantons, nature conservation groups and private individuals. What matters is to act early and to choose the right method.
wichtigste: Small stands can still be removed completely, so acting early pays off.
Young seedlings of trees and shrubs are pulled out with their roots.
Flowering neophytes do not belong in the garden compost.
Herbicides are rarely used, because they also harm other plants and waters.
Areas have to be checked for several years, because seeds in the soil stay able to germinate for a long time.
With giant hogweed you must protect your skin.

abschnitte.text: A small stand can often still be **removed completely**. Once a species has spread, controlling it becomes expensive and laborious. That is why it is important to spot new occurrences quickly. Many municipalities and cantons collect reports. Volunteers help with campaigns, for example on stream banks or at the edges of woods.

Young **seedlings** of trees and shrubs are best pulled out **with their roots** while the soil is damp. Other plants are mown several times a year before they form seeds. Larger trees such as the tree of heaven are sometimes **ringed**: the bark is removed all the way round, and the tree slowly dies. **Herbicides**, that is, plant poisons, are used only rarely. They also harm other plants and can get into waters.

The sap of **giant hogweed** is dangerous. If it gets on the skin and the sun then shines on it, painful **burns** with blisters appear. Anyone fighting the plant therefore wears gloves, long clothing and safety glasses. It is best to work on a cloudy day. Children should never touch the plant themselves.

Flowering plants do **not belong in the garden compost**. Their seeds can survive and spread further. You dispose of them in the household rubbish so that they are burned. After control you have to check the area for **several years**, because seeds in the soil can still germinate for a long time. In your own garden it helps to plant **native plants**.

gewusst: A single giant hogweed can produce many thousands of seeds.
Some municipalities in Switzerland organise action days against neophytes every year.

teile.einleitung: Ladybirds are small, round beetles with bright wing cases and black spots. They eat aphids and are seen as bringers of good luck.
wichtigste: The seven-spot ladybird is the best known in Switzerland.
The number of spots shows the species, not the age.
Beetles and larvae eat very many aphids.
When in danger, the ladybird gives off a yellow, bitter fluid.
The red colour warns birds.
In winter, many ladybirds often hide together.

abschnitte.text: The best known here is the **seven-spot ladybird**. It has red **wing cases** with **seven** black spots. But there are many other species with other colours and numbers of spots. The number of spots depends on the **species**. It does not show the age and does not change as the beetle gets older.

Ladybirds like to eat **aphids**. Their **larvae** also eat very many of them. The larvae look quite different from the beetles: they are long, dark and often have pale patches. Because they gobble up aphids, ladybirds are very welcome in the garden. That is why they are called **beneficial insects**.

The red colour is a **warning**. It tells birds: I do not taste good. That is why they rarely eat ladybirds. When in danger, the ladybird also gives off a **yellow, bitter fluid** from its legs. It often plays dead too.
In autumn, ladybirds look for sheltered hiding places, such as **crevices**, leaves or gaps in walls. Often **many lie together** there. In spring, when it gets warmer, they come out again.
The ladybird is a popular **lucky charm**. In German it is also called the **Glückskäfer**, the “lucky beetle”. It is often pictured on New Year or birthday cards.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development.
The harlequin ladybird was introduced into Europe and is now also widespread in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Nikolai Vavilov was a Russian botanist and geneticist. On journeys all over the world he collected seed and built up one of the largest seed collections in Leningrad. In the Soviet Union he was persecuted and died in custody.
wichtigste: Nikolai Vavilov did research in botany and genetics.
He formulated the law of homologous series.
On many research journeys he collected seed and wild forms of crop plants.
In Leningrad he built up one of the largest seed collections in the world.
His opponent Trofim Lysenko contributed greatly to his persecution.
Vavilov died in 1943 in Saratov in custody of malnutrition.

abschnitte.text: Nikolai Vavilov lived from 1887 to 1943. He worked on **botany**, the study of plants, and on **genetics**, the study of heredity. His aim was to breed better crop plants so that fewer people would go hungry. For this he wanted to know as many varieties as possible and their wild relatives. In Leningrad, now Saint Petersburg, he headed a large institute for plant growing.

Vavilov made numerous **research journeys** to many countries, for example to Afghanistan, Ethiopia and America. He collected **seed** and **wild forms** of wheat, barley, maize and many other plants. In doing so he recognised that crop plants are especially varied in certain regions. He concluded that they originally come from there. These regions are now called **Vavilov centres**.

Vavilov compared related plant species with one another. He found that they often form similar variants, for example in grain colour or growth form. He described this in the **law of homologous series**. With it you could predict which variants you might still find in a species. This helped in the targeted search for useful traits.

In the Soviet Union, **Trofim Lysenko** gained great influence. He rejected modern genetics and was supported by the state leadership. Vavilov was arrested in 1940 and died in 1943 in **Saratov** in custody of **malnutrition**. During the **siege of Leningrad** in the Second World War, staff of his institute guarded the collection. They preferred to starve rather than eat the seed. Some of them died as a result.

gewusst: The institute in Saint Petersburg now bears Vavilov’s name.
The seed collection that Vavilov began is still one of the largest in the world.

teile.einleitung: Potatoes, tomatoes and peppers end up on our plates almost every day. They all belong to the same plant family, the **nightshade family**. But this family also includes very poisonous plants.
wichtigste: Tomato, potato, aubergine, pepper and physalis are nightshades.
From the potato we eat the tuber.
Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.
The deadly nightshade is a poisonous member of the family with black berries.
Capsaicin makes chillies hot.
The tobacco plant contains the addictive substance nicotine.

abschnitte.text: Many popular vegetables are **nightshades**. They include the **tomato**, the **aubergine** with its glossy, dark violet skin, and the **pepper**. The **physalis** also belongs. Its orange fruit sits in a papery husk. Tomato, potato and pepper come from the Americas and only came to Europe after 1500. The aubergine, on the other hand, comes from Asia.

From the potato we eat the **tuber**. This is a thickened part of the shoot that grows underground and stores starch. So it is not the root. If potatoes lie in the light, they turn green in places. There the poisonous **solanine** forms. That is why green patches and sprouts are cut away **generously**. The green berries and leaves of the potato plant are also poisonous.

The **deadly nightshade** grows in forest clearings and at the edges of woods, also in Switzerland. It bears **black, glossy berries** that look like cherries. Even a few berries can be life-threatening for children. **Henbane** and the **thorn apple** are also poisonous nightshades. That is why you only eat wild berries if you know them for certain.

Chillies are hot because of the substance **capsaicin**. It irritates nerves in the mouth that otherwise react to heat. That is why hot food feels hot. The **tobacco plant** is also a nightshade. It contains **nicotine**, a substance that is addictive and harms health.

gewusst: The petunia, a popular balcony flower, is also a nightshade.
Against the heat of chilli, milk helps better than water.

teile.einleitung: Ecology is the science of the relationships of living things with one another and with their environment. It asks, for example, who eats whom, and why a species occurs in one place and not in another. In this way it helps us to understand and protect nature.
wichtigste: Ecology is the study of the relationships between living things and their environment.
The term was coined in 1866 by the German researcher Ernst Haeckel.
The community of all organisms in a biotope is called a biocoenosis.
A distinction is made between abiotic factors such as light and temperature and biotic factors such as grazing pressure from plant-eaters.
According to the law of the minimum, the scarcest factor limits growth.
Carrying capacity is the largest population that a habitat can support permanently.
On a glacier foreland, a primary succession takes place.

abschnitte.text: The word **ecology** comes from the Greek “oikos”, which means house. So it is about the household of nature. The German zoologist Ernst Haeckel coined the term in 1866. Ecologists study single species, whole populations and communities. In everyday speech “ecological” is also often used in the sense of environmentally friendly.

Everything that acts on a living thing is an environmental factor. **Abiotic factors** come from non-living nature, such as light, temperature, water, wind and type of soil. **Biotic factors** come from other living things, for example competition, disease-causing organisms or grazing pressure from plant-eaters. The place where a community lives is called a **biotope**, the community itself a biocoenosis.

In the 19th century the chemist Justus von Liebig made the **law of the minimum** known. It says that the growth of a plant is limited by the factor that is scarcest. This is often compared with a barrel made of wooden staves: the water can only stand as high as the shortest stave. If a plant lacks nitrogen, for example, even a lot of water does not help.

Every species has its own **ecological niche**, that is, its particular way of finding food and living. According to the competitive exclusion principle, two species with exactly the same niche cannot live side by side permanently. That is why, for example, different species of tit feed in different parts of the trees. Energy flows through the food chains: by the 10 per cent rule, of 10,000 kilojoules of the producers only about 100 reach the secondary consumers.

A **population** is a group of living things of the same species in an area. It cannot grow without limit, because food and space are limited. The largest population that a habitat can support permanently is called the carrying capacity. **r-strategists** such as mice or aphids have many offspring and care little for them. K-strategists such as elephants or humans have few young, which they look after for a long time.

When a glacier melts, bare rock and scree are left behind. First lichens and mosses settle, then grasses and flowers, later shrubs and finally trees such as larches. This sequence on previously lifeless ground is called **primary succession**. On the foreland of the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine you can see from signboards how the ice has retreated and life moves in.

begriffe.erklaerung: A habitat with particular conditions, for example a pond or a meadow.
The community of all living things in a biotope.
Coming from non-living nature, such as light, water or temperature.
All living things of one species that live together in an area.
The natural sequence of different plant communities in one place.

gewusst: Ernst Haeckel was also a gifted draughtsman and painted famous pictures of tiny sea creatures.
On some glacier forelands in the Alps, the first trees grow only a few decades after the ice retreats.
With a good supply of food, mice can have a huge number of offspring in a year.

teile.einleitung: The seas take up a large part of the carbon dioxide that people blow into the air. As a result the sea water changes chemically and becomes somewhat more acidic. This process is called ocean acidification.
wichtigste: In ocean acidification, the pH of the seas falls because they take up CO2.
The main cause is the burning of coal, oil and natural gas.
The seas have taken up about a quarter of the CO2 emitted by humans.
Since the start of industrialisation, the pH of the sea surface has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1.
The sea is still slightly alkaline, but is becoming more acidic.
Mussels, snails and corals have difficulty building their shells and skeletons of lime.
Ocean acidification is often called the other CO2 effect besides global warming.

abschnitte.text: The **pH value** shows how acidic or alkaline a liquid is. Pure water has the value 7, lemon juice about 2. Sea water is at about 8.1 and so is slightly alkaline. If this value falls, we speak of **ocean acidification**, even though the sea is not yet really acidic.

When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, **carbonic acid** forms. You know this from sparkling mineral water, which tastes slightly sour. In the sea, the carbonic acid releases hydrogen ions, which lower the pH. At the same time the carbonate that animals need to build their shells becomes scarce.

Since about 1850, people have been burning large amounts of **fossil fuels**. Part of the CO2 produced stays in the air, another part is taken up by plants and by the sea. In this way the oceans act like a huge store that slows climate change. The price for this is acidification.

Corals, mussels, oysters, sea urchins and tiny **sea butterflies** build shells and skeletons of **lime**. In more acidic water this is harder for them, and thin shells can even dissolve. Many of these animals are food for fish and whales. That is why the whole food chain in the sea can be affected.

**Coral reefs** are home to about a quarter of all marine species, although they cover only a tiny part of the sea floor. They suffer twice over, because on top of acidification comes the warming of the water, which leads to **coral bleaching**. The best-known example is the Great Barrier Reef off Australia. Experts therefore watch such reefs very closely.

The most effective remedy is to emit less CO2. This includes renewable energies such as sun, wind and hydropower, as well as using energy sparingly. Marine protected areas also help, because healthy ecosystems are more resilient. The **Paris Climate Agreement** of 2015, which Switzerland also signed, is meant to cut CO2 emissions worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that tells how acidic or alkaline something is.
A weak acid that forms when CO2 dissolves in water.
The hard substance from which mussels, snails and corals build their shells.
Corals lose their colourful lodgers and turn white.

gewusst: Because the pH scale works in steps of ten, a fall of only 0.1 means about 30 per cent more acid in the water.
The seas are now becoming acidic faster than probably in many millions of years before.
You can see the effect in an experiment: an eggshell slowly dissolves in vinegar.

teile.einleitung: Lilies are large, splendid flowers with a strong scent. They grow from a bulb in the earth. Some species bloom wild in the Alps, others stand in gardens or in bunches of flowers.
wichtigste: Lilies grow from a bulb made of scales.
A lily flower has six petals.
Many lilies smell strong and sweet.
For cats, lilies are very poisonous.
The red lily beetle eats lily leaves.
The fire lily grows with orange flowers in the Alps.

abschnitte.text: Lilies form a **bulb** in the earth. It consists of many fleshy **scales**, in which the plant stores nutrients. From it a new **stem** with leaves and flowers grows every year. A lily flower has **six petals**. They often form a trumpet or a star. In the middle stand six stamens.

Many lilies have a very **strong, sweet scent**. For some people it is even too strong in a room. The **pollen** is orange-brown and stains strongly. On clothes it makes stubborn **stains**. That is why the anthers of cut flowers are often plucked off.

For **cats**, lilies are very poisonous. Even a little pollen or a piece of leaf can make them seriously ill. Cat owners should therefore not have lilies in the home. In the garden too, lilies have an enemy: the **lily beetle**. This small beetle is bright red. It and its larvae eat holes in the lily leaves.

The **Madonna lily** has large **white** flowers and is a very old garden plant. In the **Alps** the **fire lily** grows with bright orange flowers on sunny slopes. In mountain forests you find the **Turk’s cap lily** with nodding, pink flowers. Wild lilies have become rare. That is why you do not pick them, but enjoy them in nature.

gewusst: The lily is an old heraldic emblem, for example of the French kings.
The lily beetle can squeak when you touch it.

teile.einleitung: The mango tree is a large evergreen tree from the tropics. Its sweet, juicy fruit, the mango, is popular all over the world.
wichtigste: The mango is the national fruit of India.
Mango trees can grow over 30 metres tall.
The tree is evergreen and has leaves all year round.
In the middle of the mango is a large, flat stone.
Mango and cashew belong to the same plant family.
Mango trees can live for over 100 years.

abschnitte.text: The mango has been grown in **India** for thousands of years. There it is the **national fruit**. Today mango trees grow in many warm countries around the world. In India **lassi** is also popular, a drink made from yoghurt. **Mango lassi** is a well-known kind.

Mango trees can grow very large and reach **over 30 metres**. On plantations they are usually kept smaller so that the fruit is easier to pick. The mango tree is **evergreen**: it never drops all its leaves at once and has leaves all year round. Mango trees live a long time. Some still bear fruit after **more than 100 years**.

The mango is a **stone fruit**. In its middle is a large, **flat stone**. Ripe mangoes have juicy, **yellow to orange** flesh. The skin can be green, yellow or red. So the colour of the skin does not always show whether a mango is ripe.
Mango and **cashew** belong to the same plant family, the **sumac family**. The pistachio also belongs to this family. You cannot tell from looking at the fruit, but the plants are closely related.

gewusst: There are very many different kinds of mango, with different shapes, colours and sweetness.

teile.einleitung: Neonicotinoids are insecticides that are chemically similar to nicotine. They act on the nervous system of insects. Because they also harm bees and other useful insects, they are now highly controversial and banned in many places.
wichtigste: Neonicotinoids bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the nervous system of insects.
They act systemically: the plant takes them up and spreads them to all parts.
They were often applied to seed as a seed dressing.
The first very successful neonicotinoid was imidacloprid.
Even small amounts can make it harder for honey bees to find their way.
In 2018 the EU banned three widely used neonicotinoids in the open.

abschnitte.text: In the nervous system, messenger substances pass signals from cell to cell. Neonicotinoids occupy certain docking sites there, the **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors**. The nerves are constantly excited, and the insect is paralysed and dies. In insects the substances act much more strongly than in mammals. The first commercially very successful product was **imidacloprid**.

Neonicotinoids act **systemically**. The plant takes up the substance and spreads it into stem, leaves and partly also into pollen and nectar. They were often used as a **seed dressing**: the seed is coated with it before it goes into the soil. In this way the young plant is protected from the start. The drawback: insects that do no harm also come into contact with the poison.

Researchers found that even small amounts harm honey bees. The bees find their way back to their **hive** less well. A study in the journal “Science” showed in 2012 that bumblebee colonies exposed to imidacloprid produced clearly fewer new **queens**. A study by the **University of Neuchâtel** in 2017 examined honey from all over the world. About three quarters of the samples contained neonicotinoids.

Because of these results, in 2018 the **EU** decided on a ban on use in the open for three widely used neonicotinoids: imidacloprid, clothianidin and thiamethoxam. **Switzerland** also restricted the use of these substances strongly. Since then farmers have been looking for other ways to protect their crops. The debate between crop protection and nature conservation goes on.

gewusst: The name neonicotinoids means roughly “new nicotine-like substances”.
Because neonicotinoids dissolve well in water, they are also found in streams and rivers.

teile.einleitung: A clearing is an open spot in the forest where no trees, or hardly any, stand. There a lot of sunlight reaches the ground. That is why especially many plants and animals live in clearings.
wichtigste: A clearing is an open spot in the forest.
In clearings there is more sunlight and therefore many flowers.
Clearings arise, for example, when a storm blows trees over.
Raspberries like to grow in clearings.
Butterflies, lizards and roe deer visit clearings.
If you leave a clearing in peace, forest grows again.

abschnitte.text: In dense forest the **tree crowns** hold back a lot of light. In a **clearing** no trees, or hardly any, stand. That is why a lot of **sunlight** falls on the ground there. It is warmer and brighter than in the forest all around. Clearings can be quite small or as large as a football pitch.

Strong **storms** can blow over many trees. In Switzerland, for example, the storm **Lothar** at Christmas 1999 flattened whole areas in many forests. Open areas also arise when foresters **fell** trees. Sometimes trees die from diseases or through beetles. Then the canopy opens up as well.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of life in the light
abschnitte.text: Without dense tree crowns, many **flowers** and grasses grow in clearings. **Raspberries** also need a lot of light and like to grow where trees are missing. **Butterflies** fly from flower to flower and drink nectar. **Lizards** bask on warm stones.
