At dusk **roe deer** often come out of the forest and graze in the clearing.

If you leave a clearing in peace, it changes slowly. First **herbs** grow, then **shrubs** and **young trees**. After many years **forest** stands there again. This development is called **succession**. Some clearings are therefore mown or grazed so that the variety of flowers is kept.

gewusst: On fresh clearings the pink rosebay willowherb often blooms in great numbers.
Roe deer are out and about mainly at dusk, in the morning and in the evening.

teile.einleitung: The dandelion is one of the best-known meadow flowers of Switzerland and colours whole meadows bright yellow in spring. When it has finished flowering, it forms a dandelion clock, whose seeds fly through the air with little parachutes. It gets its name from its jagged leaves, which recall a lion’s teeth.
wichtigste: The flower of the dandelion is bright yellow.
After flowering, the dandelion forms a dandelion clock.
The name comes from the jagged leaves, which recall lion’s teeth.
If you break off the stem, white milky sap comes out.
Rabbits and guinea pigs like to eat dandelion leaves.
A dandelion flower in reality consists of many small single flowers.
The dandelion belongs to the daisy family.

abschnitte.text: The common dandelion, scientifically **Taraxacum officinale**, is a perennial plant of the **daisy family**. Its leaves grow in a flat rosette close to the ground and are deeply jagged, which recalls a lion’s teeth. From the middle grows a hollow stem with a yellow flower. What looks like a single flower consists in reality of over a hundred small **ray florets**.

After flowering, the flower head closes, and the seeds ripen. After that it opens again as a round, white **dandelion clock**. Each seed hangs on a fine parachute of hairs, which experts call a **pappus**. Even a light gust of wind carries the seeds away, sometimes several kilometres.

If you break off a stem, a white, sticky **milky sap** comes out, which tastes bitter and can leave brown stains on the skin. It protects the plant from those that would eat it. The dandelion has a long, strong **taproot** that reaches deep into the ground. That is why it is hard to pull out, for even from a small piece of root a new plant grows.

Rabbits, guinea pigs and tortoises like to eat dandelion leaves, and cows too like it in their feed. For **bees** and bumblebees the dandelion is an important source of nectar and pollen in spring. Young leaves can be eaten as a slightly bitter salad, and from the flowers people cook a sweet syrup that is called dandelion honey. In folk medicine, dandelion was formerly used for digestive complaints.

The dandelion grows almost everywhere in Switzerland, from the Central Plateau up high into the Alps, on meadows, pastures, path edges and in gardens. It thrives especially well on **nutrient-rich**, fertilised meadows, which in April and May often glow entirely yellow. Its flowers open in the morning and close in the evening or in rain. In many regions it has its own dialect names, for example **Söiblueme**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family in which many small flowers together look like a single large flower.
The small parachute of hairs with which dandelion seeds fly.
A strong main root that grows vertically deep into the ground.
Leaves that grow in a circle flat on the ground around the middle.

gewusst: A single dandelion clock can carry well over a hundred seeds.
From the milky sap of a related species of dandelion, rubber for car tyres is today being made on a trial basis.
In flight, the seed parachutes of the dandelion form a small vortex of air above them, which keeps them in the air for longer.

teile.einleitung: Norman Borlaug was an agricultural scientist from the USA. He bred wheat varieties that gave much higher yields and were resistant to diseases. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
wichtigste: Norman Borlaug came from the USA and lived from 1914 to 2009.
In the 1940s he began breeding wheat in Mexico.
His varieties were especially resistant to stem rust.
In 1970 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
He is regarded as the father of the Green Revolution.
In 1986 he founded the World Food Prize.

abschnitte.text: Norman Borlaug was born in 1914 in the US state of Iowa. In the **1940s** he went to **Mexico** to breed better wheat there. A big problem was **stem rust**, a fungal disease that can destroy whole harvests. Borlaug crossed countless varieties and picked out those that could resist the fungus. Later he also bred varieties with short, strong stalks that carry more grain without falling over.

Borlaug used a quick method, **“shuttle breeding”**. He grew wheat in two places in Mexico with different climates. In this way he could raise **two generations of breeding a year** instead of just one. This doubled the speed of breeding. In addition the varieties adapted to different day lengths and later grew well in many countries.

In the 1960s Borlaug’s varieties came to India and Pakistan. Great famines threatened there at the time. With new varieties, fertiliser and irrigation, harvests rose strongly. This development is called the **Green Revolution**, and Borlaug is often called its **father**. From his programme in Mexico came the international research centre for maize and wheat, **CIMMYT**. Critics point out that the heavy use of fertiliser and water also brought environmental problems.

In **1970** Borlaug received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The committee honoured that he had spared many people hunger. In 1986 he founded the **World Food Prize**, a prize for achievements against hunger. In 2007 he received the **Congressional Gold Medal**, one of the highest awards of the US Congress. Borlaug died in 2009.

gewusst: Borlaug is one of the few people who have received the Nobel Peace Prize, the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Congressional Gold Medal.
He received the Nobel Peace Prize although he was not a politician but a plant breeder.

teile.einleitung: Light energy is the energy that is in light. Plants capture it in photosynthesis and store it as chemical energy in sugar. Almost all life on Earth depends on it.
wichtigste: In photosynthesis, light energy is converted into chemical energy.
Plants use light of about 400 to 700 nanometres.
In weak light, photosynthesis rises with more light.
In very strong light, other factors limit photosynthesis.
At the light compensation point, the uptake and release of carbon dioxide balance out.
The energy in coal, oil and natural gas comes from sunlight of long ago.

abschnitte.text: In **photosynthesis**, plants use light energy to make **sugar** from carbon dioxide and water. The energy of the light is stored in the bonds of the sugar molecules. This is **chemical energy**. The green pigment **chlorophyll** captures the light. It absorbs mainly blue and red light. Green light is reflected more strongly, which is why leaves look green.

Plants use roughly the visible light with a wavelength of **400 to 700 nanometres**. This range is called **photosynthetically active radiation**. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Plants hardly use ultraviolet and infrared light for photosynthesis.

In weak light, the light is the **limiting factor**. When it gets brighter, **photosynthesis increases**. In very strong light, however, it eventually stops rising further. Then other factors such as **carbon dioxide** or **temperature** become the bottleneck, and the curve levels off. At a certain light intensity the plant takes up exactly as much carbon dioxide as it gives off through respiration. This is the **light compensation point**.

**Shade plants** manage with little light and grow, for example, on the forest floor. They often have large, thin leaves and make good use of weak light. Examples are many ferns and **wood sorrel**. Plants also grow towards the light. On the shaded side of the shoot they grow more strongly, so that it bends towards the light. This is called **phototropism**.

**Coal, oil and natural gas** arose from the remains of living things that lived millions of years ago. Their energy came, through photosynthesis, from **sunlight**. When they are burned, this old light energy is released again. Today light energy is also used directly: **solar cells** on roofs convert sunlight into electric current, in Switzerland too more and more often.

gewusst: Leaves are green because chlorophyll uses green light less well and reflects it.
A piece of coal contains solar energy that plants captured millions of years ago.

teile.einleitung: In most Swiss forests, timber is harvested and the forest is looked after. In a **natural forest reserve** it is different. Here the forest may develop freely, without people stepping in.
wichtigste: In a natural forest reserve there is no forestry intervention.
In a special forest reserve, action is taken on purpose to help certain species.
By 2030 the Confederation wants to secure 10 per cent of the forest area as forest reserves.
Natural forest reserves are usually secured by contract for 50 years.
The spruce forest reserve Scatlè near Breil/Brigels has been protected since about 1910.
Pro Natura owns or looks after numerous forest reserves, including Derborence.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are two types of forest reserve. In a **natural forest reserve** there is **no forestry intervention**. No timber is harvested, and fallen trees stay where they lie. In a **special forest reserve**, on the other hand, **action is taken on purpose**. There, for example, the forest is thinned out to help certain plants or animals such as the capercaillie.

**By 2030**, the Confederation wants to secure **10 per cent** of the forest area in Switzerland as forest reserves. The reserves are mostly agreed with the forest owners, for example with municipalities or corporations. As a rule, natural forest reserves are secured by contract **for 50 years**. The owners receive compensation for this, because they give up income from timber.

In natural forest reserves there is a lot of **dead wood**, that is, dead trees and branches. What looks like rubbish is an important habitat. Beetles, fungi, mosses and lichens live in it. Woodpeckers look for food in it and build holes that other animals later move into. Many rare species depend on such wood.

Natural forest reserves are also valuable for **forestry research**. **They show how a forest develops without intervention.** Experts compare these forests with managed forests. In this way they learn how trees recover after storms and how the forest reacts to climate change. These findings help to look after managed forests better too.

The spruce forest reserve **Scatlè** in the municipality of **Breil/Brigels** in the Grisons has been protected **since about 1910**. It is regarded as one of the oldest forest reserves in Switzerland. The **Swiss National Park in the Engadine** was founded in **1914** and also protects large forests completely from use. **Pro Natura** owns or looks after numerous forest reserves. These include **Derborence** in the Valais, a primeval-like forest in a valley shaped by great rockfalls in the 18th century.

gewusst: In Derborence grow silver firs and spruces that are several hundred years old.
A fallen tree can take decades in the forest until it has completely rotted into soil.

teile.einleitung: A **nature trail** is a path on which you learn something as you walk. Along the way there are information boards and stops about animals, plants and the landscape. In Switzerland there are many such trails, in forests, by lakes or in the mountains.
wichtigste: A nature trail is a path with information boards about nature.
The boards give knowledge about animals and plants.
On a forest trail you often get to know different species of tree.
At listening posts you can listen to birdsong.
With flaps or rotating boards you can solve riddles.
Signposts and stops show where the trail goes on.

abschnitte.text: On a **nature trail** there are **information boards** along the way. They explain which **animals and plants** live here and how the landscape came about. You read a little, look around and walk on to the next stop. **Signposts and stops** show where to go next. In this way a walk becomes a small voyage of discovery.

On a **forest trail** you often get to know **different species of tree**. Small signs with their names hang on the trees. You can feel the bark and compare the leaves. In this way you learn to tell beech, oak, spruce and silver fir apart. Some trails also show how the forester looks after the forest.

Many nature trails invite you to join in. At a **listening post** you can **listen to birdsong** and guess which bird is singing. With **flaps or rotating boards** you can **solve riddles**: the answer is under the flap. Some trails have a **barefoot path**. There you walk without shoes over sand, bark, stones and moss and **feel the ground with your feet**.

A nature trail is especially suitable for **school classes**. **You learn outdoors in nature** and not only from a book. What you see, hear and touch yourself, you often remember better. It is important to stay on the path, not to pick anything and to take your rubbish home again. In this way the trail stays lovely for everyone.

gewusst: Some nature trails now also have stops with QR codes, through which you can call up texts or animal sounds on your phone.
There are trails on very different subjects, for example glaciers, moors or bees.

teile.einleitung: The oleander is a shrub with beautiful pink, white or red flowers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and is a popular tub plant with us. All its parts, however, are highly poisonous.
wichtigste: The oleander originally comes from the Mediterranean region.
It belongs to the dogbane family.
The oleander is evergreen.
All parts of the plant are poisonous.
The most important poison is called oleandrin and acts mainly on the heart.
In Switzerland it usually has to be protected from frost in winter.

abschnitte.text: The **oleander** grows wild in the **Mediterranean region**, often on river banks and in dry stream beds. It grows several metres tall and bears narrow, leathery leaves. The oleander is **evergreen**, so it keeps its leaves in winter too. Its flowers are pink, white, red or yellowish and some are scented. It belongs to the **dogbane family**.

In the oleander **all parts of the plant are poisonous**: leaves, flowers, stems and seeds. The most important poison is called **oleandrin**. It acts mainly on the **heart** and can dangerously disturb the heartbeat. The oleander is also poisonous to pets such as dogs, cats and horses. If you suspect that someone has eaten some, in Switzerland you immediately call the emergency number 145 of Tox Info Suisse.

In Switzerland the oleander usually stands in a **tub** on terraces and balconies. It cannot stand **hard frost**. So in winter it is put in a bright, cool place, for example a conservatory or an unheated stairwell. It can stand light frost for a short time. In Ticino it also grows outdoors in sheltered places.

When it is cut, plant sap comes out. So it is best to wear **gloves** and wash your hands afterwards. The cut twigs must **not be burned**, because the smoke can also do harm. They are also **not fed to animals**. It is best to put them in the green waste collection. Small children should not play near the plant.

gewusst: Even a few leaves of the oleander can be dangerous for humans.
The oleander is the flower of the Japanese city of Hiroshima, because it was one of the first plants to bloom there again after the atomic bomb in 1945.

teile.einleitung: The Lotka-Volterra rules describe how the numbers of predators and their prey influence each other. They are based on a simple mathematical model from the 1920s.
wichtigste: Alfred Lotka (1925) and Vito Volterra (1926) developed the model independently of each other.
First rule: predators and prey fluctuate periodically, the predators with a delay.
Second rule: the average values of both populations stay the same in the long term.
Third rule: after equally strong culling, the prey recovers faster.
The snowshoe hare and the Canada lynx show a cycle of about 10 years.
Real systems are more complicated than the model.

abschnitte.text: The biologist **Umberto D’Ancona** studied fishing data from the **Adriatic** from the time of the First World War. During the war little fishing was done, and the share of **predatory fish** had risen. The mathematician **Vito Volterra** looked for an explanation and in 1926 set up equations. **Alfred Lotka** had already published similar equations in 1925. That is why the model bears both names.

The **first rule**: the numbers of predators and prey fluctuate regularly, the predators following the prey with a time offset. If there is a lot of prey, the predators increase, then the prey decreases and afterwards the predators too. The **second rule**: the sizes of both populations averaged over a long time stay the same. The **third rule**: if predators and prey are **culled** equally strongly, the prey recovers faster, because it finds fewer enemies.

A well-known example is the **snowshoe hare** and the **Canada lynx**. The **Hudson’s Bay Company** in Canada recorded over many decades how many pelts were traded. These numbers show regular fluctuations. The populations reach a peak about every nine to eleven years, which is called the **ten-year cycle**.

The simple model knows only one predator species and one prey species. Without predators the prey in it grows **exponentially**, because unlimited food is assumed. In nature, however, predators often use **several prey species**. In addition there are diseases, weather and limited food. That is why real predator-prey systems often do not follow the rules exactly.

gewusst: The third rule explains why pests sometimes come back faster after poison is used than their natural enemies do.

teile.einleitung: Orchids are one of the plant families richest in species in the world. Their flowers are often especially beautiful and unusually shaped. You find them in the rainforest, but also on Swiss meadows and as house plants.
wichtigste: There are over 20,000 species of orchid.
Many orchids in the rainforest grow on the branches of trees.
The seeds of orchids are as tiny as dust.
A particularly striking petal is called the lip.
The spice vanilla comes from an orchid.
The lady’s slipper is a rare wild orchid of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: With **over 20,000 species**, orchids belong to the largest plant families. They grow almost everywhere in the world, except in deserts and ice regions. A typical feature is the **lip**. This is a particularly striking, reshaped petal. Insects land on it when they visit the flower. The seeds of orchids are **as tiny as dust** and are carried far by the wind.

In the **rainforest** many orchids do not grow in the ground but **on branches of trees**. They are called **epiphytes**. They do not harm the tree but only use it as a seat, to be nearer the light. With their **aerial roots** they take up water from rain and moist air. Many **pot orchids** also have aerial roots that stick out of the pot.

Many orchids have clever ways of attracting insects. The flower of the **bee orchid** looks like an insect and so attracts suitable insects. These then carry the pollen to the next flower. Other orchids attract with scent or colour. The popular **moth orchid** has flowers that recall butterflies. It is one of the most common house plants.

In **Switzerland**, too, dozens of wild orchid species grow, for example on poor meadows and in light woods. A particularly beautiful one is the **lady’s slipper**. It has a large, yellow, **shoe-shaped** lip and reddish-brown petals. It is rare and protected, and you must not pick it. A well-known spice also comes from an orchid: **vanilla**. People use its fermented seed pods, the vanilla pods.

gewusst: A single orchid capsule can contain hundreds of thousands of tiny seeds.
Orchid seeds need the help of a fungus in the soil to germinate.

teile.einleitung: Oregano is a spicy kitchen herb that you know above all from pizza. In German the plant is also called “Dost”. In Switzerland it even grows wild on sunny meadows.
wichtigste: Oregano is also called “Dost” in German.
It is closely related to marjoram.
It is often sprinkled on pizza and put in tomato sauce.
In the kitchen oregano is used dried especially often.
The flowers are mostly pink.
An oregano plant lives for several years.

abschnitte.text: Oregano, in German also called **“Dost”**, belongs to the **mint family**. This also includes thyme, sage and mint. Its closest relative is **marjoram**. The plant grows about knee-high and bears small, roundish leaves. In summer many small, mostly **pink** flowers appear. Oregano is a **perennial**: it sprouts anew every spring.

Oregano is a typical seasoning of Mediterranean cooking. You sprinkle it on **pizza** and put it in **tomato sauce**. It also goes well with vegetables, cheese and meat. Oregano is used especially often **dried**. In drying, its flavour even becomes stronger. Fresh leaves taste milder.

Oregano also grows **wild** in Switzerland. You find it on **dry, sunny meadows**, at the edges of paths and woods, often on chalky soil. Its flowers are very popular with bees, bumblebees and butterflies. That is why oregano is also a good plant for insects in the garden. It needs a lot of sun and little water.

Oregano is easy to grow in the garden or on the balcony. It needs a **sunny spot** and loose soil that is not wet. You can harvest the leaves all summer long. Just before flowering the aroma is strongest. To dry it, you hang the twigs upside down in an airy, shady place.

gewusst: The name oregano probably comes from Greek and means roughly “joy of the mountain”.
Dried oregano is one of the few herbs that taste stronger dried than fresh.

teile.einleitung: A meteor, also called a shooting star, is a short flash of light in the night sky. It happens when a piece of rock from space enters the atmosphere at high speed and burns up there. If you look up at the sky on a clear August night, you can often see many shooting stars.
wichtigste: A meteor is a piece of rock that burns up in the atmosphere, and is also called a shooting star.
The piece of rock in space is called a meteoroid.
If a remnant of it reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite.
Most shooting stars come from particles smaller than a grain of sand.
Meteors usually light up at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres.
In a meteor shower such as the Perseids in August, you see especially many shooting stars.
An especially bright meteor is called a fireball or bolide.

abschnitte.text: The term **meteor** really means the streak of light in the sky; in everyday speech we talk about a shooting star. But it has nothing to do with stars. It is caused by a small piece of rock or metal from space, a **meteoroid**. If a remnant of it falls to Earth, it is called a **meteorite**.

Meteoroids race into the Earth’s **atmosphere** at 11 to 72 kilometres per second. The air in front of them is squeezed and heated so strongly that the particle vaporises and makes the air all around it glow. This usually happens at a height of 80 to 120 kilometres, far above the clouds and aircraft. Most shooting stars come from particles smaller than a **grain of sand**.

Several times a year, the Earth flies through a trail of dust that a **comet** has left behind on its path. Then you see especially many shooting stars, which all seem to come from the same direction of the sky; this is called a **meteor shower**. The best known are the **Perseids** around 12 August, which come from the comet Swift-Tuttle. In December the Geminids follow, which often provide just as many shooting stars.

Bigger lumps produce especially bright meteors, which are called **fireballs** or bolides and sometimes burst with a bang. In February 2013, a lump about 20 metres across exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk and shattered thousands of window panes. Very rarely, large bodies hit the Earth and leave craters such as the Barringer Crater in Arizona. About 66 million years ago, a huge impact helped to wipe out the dinosaurs.

In Switzerland only a few meteorites have been found so far. The best-known site is the **Twannberg** above Lake Biel, where many pieces of an iron meteorite have been found since 1984. Today **camera networks** run by experts and amateur astronomers watch the sky over Switzerland and help to calculate where meteorites have fallen. Meteorites are valuable for research because they contain material from the time the Solar System formed.

To watch them you do not need a telescope, just a dark place far from city lights and a little patience. The best thing is to lie down comfortably and let your eyes get used to the dark for about 20 minutes. After midnight you usually see more shooting stars, because the Earth is then turning in the direction of its flight. According to an old **custom**, you may make a wish when you see a shooting star.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small lump of rock or metal flying through space.
The remnant of a meteoroid that has reached the ground.
Many shooting stars that come at the same time from the same direction of the sky.
An especially bright meteor, also called a bolide.

gewusst: Every day, tonnes of tiny dust particles fall from space onto the Earth.
The Perseids are named that because their shooting stars seem to come from the constellation Perseus.
A shooting star usually shines for less than a second.

teile.einleitung: A mire landscape is more than a single mire. It includes mires and the landscape around them. In Switzerland, the most beautiful mire landscapes are protected by the Confederation.
wichtigste: A mire landscape consists of mires and the surroundings that give them their character.
In 2025 there were 89 mire landscapes of national importance in Switzerland.
They cover about 2 per cent of the country’s area.
The Federal Inventory of Mire Landscapes came into force in 1996.
The Entlebuch in the canton of Lucerne is a UNESCO biosphere reserve with many mire landscapes.
Traditional farming is allowed if it does not harm the mire.

abschnitte.text: A **mire landscape** is a near-natural landscape that is strongly shaped by **mires**. It includes not only the raised bogs and fens, but also the woods, streams, pastures, hedges and old buildings in between. Only all together do they make up the typical picture. The protection therefore applies to the whole **surroundings**, not just the mires themselves.

Especially beautiful and valuable mire landscapes are of **national importance**. That means the **Confederation** protects them as important for the whole of Switzerland. They are listed in the **Federal Inventory of Mire Landscapes**, which came into force in **1996**. In 2025 it included **89** mire landscapes. Together they cover about **2 per cent** of the country’s area. The cantons see to putting the protection into practice.

In the **Entlebuch** in the canton of **Lucerne** there are especially many mire landscapes. The region was recognised by UNESCO in 2001 as a **biosphere reserve**. Today it is called the UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere. There, nature and people are meant to live well together: the landscape is protected, and the people still use it for farming and tourism.

In a protected mire landscape you may not simply build new houses, roads or facilities. But **traditional farming** is allowed, as long as it **does not harm** the mire. Many fens even need to be used: if they are mown regularly, they do not become overgrown with bushes. This litter was used in the past as bedding in the stable.

Mires work like a **sponge**. They **store water** and give it back **slowly**. In heavy rain this can soften floods, and in dry periods it can feed streams. Mire landscapes are also a habitat for rare plants and animals that occur only there.

gewusst: The protection of mire landscapes goes back to a popular initiative that was accepted in 1987.
One of the best-known mire landscapes in Switzerland lies near Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz.

teile.einleitung: In the garden you often see beds that are covered with bark, leaves or grass clippings. This layer is called mulch. It protects the soil and helps the plants to grow.
wichtigste: Mulch is a layer of organic material on the ground.
It keeps moisture in the soil.
Less weed grows under mulch, because it lacks light.
Bark mulch is made of chopped tree bark.
Mulch made of leaves rots with time into humus.
Fresh grass clippings are spread only thinly, because thick layers rot.

abschnitte.text: **Mulch** is a **layer** that you put on the ground between the plants. It usually consists of **organic material** such as leaves, straw, grass clippings, wood chips or **bark mulch** made of chopped tree bark. Covering the ground like this is called **mulching**. In nature this happens too: in the forest, a layer of leaves and needles covers the ground.

Mulch **keeps moisture** in the soil. The sun dries out the soil underneath less quickly. On **hot summer days** the layer gives **shade**, and the soil stays cooler. So you have to water less. In heavy rain, mulch also protects the soil from being turned to mud or washed away.

Weed seeds often need **light** to germinate. Under a thick layer of mulch it is dark. That is why **fewer weeds** grow there, and you have to do less weeding. For paths and shrubs, **bark mulch** is especially suitable, because it rots slowly. For vegetable beds, people prefer soft material such as leaves or straw.

abschnitte.titel: Food for life in the soil
abschnitte.text: Under a layer of mulch, **earthworms** and other soil animals like to work. They pull the remains into the soil and eat them. A layer of **leaves** in this way **rots** with time into **humus**. This makes the soil loose and fertile. That is why mulch has to be renewed again and again.

**Fresh grass clippings** are spread only **thinly**. In a **thick layer** they get no air, begin to **rot** and smell unpleasant. It is better to let them dry out a little first. In damp regions, mulch can also attract slugs, which like to hide under it. That is why it should not be put right next to young lettuce plants.

gewusst: Some lawnmowers mulch too: they chop the grass so finely that it can stay where it falls and work as fertiliser.
In the forest, the ground is covered all year round by a natural layer of mulch made of leaves.

teile.einleitung: The mint family is a large plant family with many well-known culinary and medicinal herbs. Their flowers look like an open mouth with an upper and a lower lip.
wichtigste: The flower has an upper lip and a lower lip.
Basil, thyme, rosemary, oregano and lavender belong to the mint family.
Many species have a square stem.
Essential oils make up the strong scent.
The fruit mostly splits into four small nutlets.
Menthol gives peppermint the coolness in the mouth.

abschnitte.text: In the mint family the petals are fused into a **tube**. At the front, the tube opens into an **upper lip** and a **lower lip**. That is where the family gets its German name, “Lippenblütler”, lip-flowerers. The lower lip serves insects such as bumblebees as a **landing place**. Many species also have a **square stem** and leaves in opposite pairs.

The mint family includes many **culinary herbs**: basil, thyme, rosemary, oregano and sage. **Peppermint** and **lemon balm** also belong to it. The violet-flowering **lavender** is grown in Provence in big fields. Dried, it is put into scented sachets for the wardrobe.

Many members of the mint family smell strongly. The reason is **essential oils**, which are stored in tiny **glandular hairs** on leaves and stems. These oils protect the plant from those that would eat it. In peppermint, **menthol** is the main component of the oil. It stimulates the cold receptors in the mouth, which is why it feels cool.

Some members of the mint family are drunk as tea. Tea from **lemon balm** is regarded as mildly calming. The name **sage** comes from the Latin Salvia, derived from salvare, which means to heal. Sage tea is drunk, for example, for a sore throat.
After flowering, a special fruit forms that splits into parts. When ripe, it mostly breaks up into **four** one-seeded nutlets. In this way the plant can reproduce through its seeds.

gewusst: Thyme, rosemary and lavender grow wild in the dry scrubland by the Mediterranean.
Catmint is also a member of the mint family, and its scent attracts many cats.

teile.einleitung: Mendel’s laws describe how characteristics are passed on from parents to offspring. The monk Gregor Mendel found them through crossing experiments with peas. They are among the foundations of the study of heredity, genetics.
wichtigste: Gregor Mendel published his results in 1866.
Law of uniformity: if you cross two pure-bred parents, all the offspring of the F1 generation are the same.
Law of segregation: in the F2 generation of a dominant-recessive inheritance, the characteristics appear in the ratio 3 to 1.
The genotypes of the F2 generation are distributed 1 AA to 2 Aa to 1 aa.
Law of independent assortment: with two characteristics, the F2 generation splits in the ratio 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
One exception is gene linkage: genes on the same chromosome are often inherited together.

abschnitte.text: **Gregor Mendel** lived in the 19th century as a monk in the monastery in Brno, in what is now the Czech Republic. In the monastery garden he crossed **pea plants** with different characteristics for many years, such as yellow and green seeds. He counted the offspring carefully and worked with number ratios. His work was hardly noticed for a long time. Only around **1900** did other researchers rediscover it.

Each characteristic is determined by two **hereditary factors**, one from each parent. They are written with letters, for example A and a. A capital letter stands for a **dominant** factor, which wins out. A small letter stands for a **recessive** factor, which only shows if it is present twice. **Pure-bred** means AA or aa, **hybrid** means Aa. The hereditary factors are called the **genotype**, and the visible characteristic the **phenotype** or appearance.

If you cross two hybrid plants Aa times Aa, you get AA, Aa, aA and aa. Three out of four show the dominant characteristic, so **3 to 1**. For the genotypes the result is **1 to 2 to 1**. If you look at two characteristics at the same time, they combine freely: (3 to 1) times (3 to 1) gives **9 to 3 to 3 to 1**. The genotype aabb occurs in only **1 of 16** offspring.

A plant with the dominant characteristic can be AA or Aa. To find out which, you cross it with a **pure-bred recessive** partner aa. This is called a **backcross** or **test cross**. If the plant is Aa, the offspring show both characteristics in the ratio **1 to 1**. If it is AA, all the offspring look the same.

A factor does not always win out completely. In the **four o’clock flower**, the offspring of a red and a white pure-bred plant bloom **pink**. This is called **intermediate inheritance**. Also, the law of independent assortment only applies to genes that lie on different chromosomes. If they lie on the same chromosome, this is called **gene linkage**.

gewusst: In his experiments, Mendel studied many thousands of pea plants.
The word “gene” did not yet exist in Mendel’s time. It was only introduced at the start of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Maize is a large cereal plant that originally comes from the Americas. Its kernels are used to make popcorn, polenta, cornflakes and animal feed.
wichtigste: The kernels sit in rows on the cob.
Most maize kernels are yellow, but there are also white, red and blue ones.
Maize was grown in Mexico thousands of years ago.
A maize plant often grows taller than 2 metres.
In Ticino, polenta is cooked from maize semolina.
Popcorn maize bursts open into popcorn when it is heated.

abschnitte.text: On maize, the kernels sit in rows on the **cob**. The cob is wrapped in green leaves, and fine threads stick out at the top. Most kernels are **yellow**. But there are also varieties with white, red or blue kernels.

Maize comes from the **Americas**. People were already growing it in **Mexico** thousands of years ago. After the discovery of America, sailors brought it to **Europe**. Today maize is grown all over the world, including in Switzerland.

Maize grows quickly in summer and often reaches **over 2 metres**, which is taller than a person. To stop it falling over, it grows **prop roots** at the bottom of the stalk. You cannot see into a field of maize. In summer, some farmers cut paths into it and turn it into a **maize maze**, where you have to find the way out.

**Popcorn maize** has a little water locked inside. When the kernel is heated, the water turns to steam and the kernel bursts open: that is how **popcorn** is made. To make **cornflakes**, maize is cooked, rolled flat and toasted. The English word “corn” means maize here.

**Polenta** is a porridge made from **maize semolina**. In **Ticino** it is a well-known dish and is often eaten with meat, mushrooms or cheese. In Switzerland a lot of maize is also grown as **feed** for cows.

gewusst: Maize belongs to the sweet grasses, like wheat and rice.
A single maize cob often carries several hundred kernels.

teile.einleitung: In the garden, not all plants have to grow in separate rows. In companion planting, different species are put side by side on purpose. Good neighbours can help each other.
wichtigste: In companion planting, different plant species grow together in one bed.
Onions next to carrots can distract the carrot fly.
The “three sisters” of the milpa are maize, beans and squash.
Marigolds can push back harmful roundworms in the soil.
Deep-rooted and shallow-rooted plants use different layers of soil.
The opposite is monoculture, where only one plant species grows.

abschnitte.text: **Companion planting** means that different plant species grow together in one bed. A well-known pair is **carrots** and **onions**. The smell of the onions can confuse the **carrot fly**, whose larvae eat carrots. In return, carrots are said to distract the onion fly. Between **tomatoes**, **basil** is often planted, which has similar needs for warmth and water.

In Central America, farmers have grown the **milpa** for a very long time. There **maize**, **beans** and **squash** grow together, the “three sisters”. The maize serves as a **climbing frame** for the beans. With the help of bacteria on their roots, the beans can fix **nitrogen** from the air and so improve the soil. The big leaves of the squash shade the ground, keep it damp and suppress weeds.

The **marigold** is often planted among vegetables. Its roots give off substances that can push back harmful **roundworms** in the soil. Roundworms, also called nematodes, are tiny worms that suck at roots. Flowering plants also attract useful insects such as bees and hoverflies.

Plants root to different depths. Lettuce has rather shallow roots, other vegetables reach deeper. When **deep-rooted and shallow-rooted** plants grow side by side, they use **different layers of soil**. So they compete less for water and nutrients. The space in the bed is used better.

The opposite of companion planting is **monoculture**. Here only plants of one species grow over large areas, for example only maize or only wheat. This is easier to farm with machines. But pests and diseases can spread more easily. Mixed plantings are seen as more varied, but need more hand work and knowledge.

gewusst: The milpa has been grown in Central America for several thousand years.
Not all plants are good neighbours: some hold back each other’s growth.

teile.einleitung: The Earth has very different landscapes: hot deserts, wet rainforests, cold tundra. An **ecozone** is a large belt of the Earth in which climate, soils, plants and animals are similar. The geographer Jürgen Schultz divided the land surface into nine such zones.
wichtigste: An ecozone is a large habitat with a similar climate, similar soils and similar plant life.
The German geographer Jürgen Schultz distinguishes nine ecozones of the Earth.
The ecozones run roughly like belts from the equator to the poles.
The Swiss Central Plateau belongs to the humid mid-latitudes.
The permanently wet tropics have the most plant mass per area.
The taiga is the coniferous forest of the boreal zone.

abschnitte.text: The word **ecozone** is made up of “eco” (household of nature) and “zone” (area). In an ecozone many things are connected: the **climate**, the **relief** (the shape of the landscape), the **soils**, the **vegetation** (plant life) and also the way people use the land. Jürgen Schultz described this in his book “Die Ökozonen der Erde” (“The Ecozones of the Earth”). The borders between the zones are not sharp but blend into one another.

In the far north and south lies the **polar and subpolar zone**. It includes the **tundra** with mosses, lichens and low shrubs and the polar cold deserts of ice and rock. South of it follows the **boreal zone**. It stretches as a broad belt through North America, Scandinavia and Siberia. There the **taiga** grows, a huge coniferous forest of spruces, pines and larches, for the winters are long and cold and the summers short.

In the **humid mid-latitudes** it rains all year round, the summers are warm and the winters cool. Without humans, there would mainly be summer-green **deciduous forest** here. The Swiss Central Plateau also belongs to this. In the **dry mid-latitudes** less rain falls. There lie the **steppes** of Central Asia and the **prairies** of North America with wide grasslands. Today grain is often grown there.

The Mediterranean region belongs to the **winter-wet subtropics**: the summers are hot and dry, rain falls mainly in winter. Typical plants are olive trees and tough, evergreen shrubs. Around the tropics lie the **tropical and subtropical dry regions** such as the Sahara and the Arabian Desert. There dry air sinks, and hardly any clouds form. There are also the **permanently wet subtropics**, for example in the south-east of the USA or in parts of China.

Near the equator lie two tropical zones. In the **summer-wet tropics** there is a rainy season and a dry season. Here lie most of the **savannas** of Africa with grass and scattered trees. In the **permanently wet tropics** it is warm and wet all year round. There the tropical **rainforests** grow, for example on the Amazon and in the Congo Basin. No other zone has so much plant mass on one area.

gewusst: The taiga is the largest continuous forest area on Earth.
Although the rainforest is so lush, its soils are often rather poor in nutrients, because the plants take up the nutrients quickly.

teile.einleitung: A forest can renew itself. Old trees scatter their seeds, and young trees grow from them. This is called **natural regeneration**. In Switzerland it is the most common way in which new forest comes about.
wichtigste: In natural regeneration, young trees grow from the seeds of old trees.
Young trees above all need enough light.
The silver fir is a shade-tolerant species and can also grow up under a dense canopy.
As a pioneer, the birch often grows first on open ground.
In a selection forest, trees of all ages grow mixed together.
Natural regeneration is usually cheaper than planting.
A mast year is a year with especially many seeds.

abschnitte.text: In **natural regeneration**, **young trees grow from the seeds of old trees**. The seeds fall down or are spread by the wind, by birds and by squirrels. For the seedlings to grow well, they above all need **enough light**. That is why foresters often fell individual old trees on purpose. This creates gaps in the canopy through which light falls on the ground.

Tree species have very different needs. The **silver fir** is a **shade-tolerant species**. It can grow up slowly even under a dense canopy and wait for many years. The **birch**, on the other hand, is a **pioneer**. It often grows **first on open ground**, for example after a storm. Its light seeds fly far, and it grows quickly in full light.

In a **selection forest**, trees of **all ages** grow mixed together on a small area: seedlings, young trees and mighty old trees. Only single trees are ever harvested. The forest **constantly regenerates itself** and always stays closed. In Switzerland there are well-known selection forests, for example in the **Emmental**. There mainly silver fir, spruce and beech grow.

Natural regeneration is usually **cheaper** than planting, because **you do not have to buy and plant young trees**. Also, the young trees are usually **well adapted to their site**. Their **parents already grew in the same place** and coped well with the soil and climate. When felling timber, foresters therefore sometimes leave **seed trees** standing on purpose. They supply the area with their seeds.

Beeches and oaks do not bear the same number of seeds every year. In a **mast year** they produce **especially many seeds**, that is, beechnuts or acorns. Then especially many seedlings grow in the following year. A danger for young trees is roe deer and red deer. They like to eat buds and shoots, above all of young silver firs. This is called **browsing damage**.

gewusst: In mast years there are often also more mice, because they find so much food.
A young silver fir can stay small in the shade for decades and then grow quickly as soon as it gets light.

teile.einleitung: Mould on bread or fruit does not just look unappetising. Many moulds make poisonous substances called **mycotoxins**. They can make people and animals ill, so it is worth knowing about them.
wichtigste: Mycotoxins are poisonous metabolic products of moulds.
Most mycotoxins are heat-stable; cooking hardly makes them harmless.
Patulin occurs mainly in mouldy apples and apple juice.
Fusarium fungi often make deoxynivalenol (DON) on cereals and fumonisins in maize.
Ochratoxin A mainly damages the kidney.
An illness caused by mycotoxins is called mycotoxicosis.
Warm and damp storage promotes the formation of mycotoxins most.

abschnitte.text: The word **mycotoxin** is put together from “myco” for fungus and “toxin” for poison. Moulds make these substances in their metabolism. You cannot see or taste them. An illness caused by mycotoxins is called **mycotoxicosis**. Depending on the poison, the liver, kidney, gut or nerves can be affected.

Most mycotoxins are **heat-stable**. They are hardly destroyed by boiling, baking or frying. That is why you should not simply boil up and eat mouldy food. In soft foods such as bread, jam or yoghurt, the fungal threads can spread invisibly through the whole food. Such foods must be thrown away completely, not just the mouldy spot.

**Patulin** is found mainly in rotten apples and apple juice pressed from them. Fungi of the genus **Fusarium** attack cereals as early as in the field. They make, for example, **deoxynivalenol**, DON for short, and in maize the **fumonisins**. **Ochratoxin A** can occur in cereals, coffee or dried fruit and mainly damages the **kidney**. Among the most powerful poisons are the **aflatoxins**, which can form, for example, in badly stored nuts.

Moulds grow best when it is **warm and damp**. Cereals, nuts and spices should therefore be stored dry and cool. Farmers dry their grain after harvest before it goes into silos. At home it helps to seal food well and check supplies regularly. In Switzerland, maximum levels of mycotoxins apply to many foods and are checked.

gewusst: In the Middle Ages, many people fell ill with “St Anthony’s fire” because rye was contaminated with ergot, a poisonous fungus.
Animals can also fall ill if their feed is contaminated with mycotoxins.

teile.einleitung: The lime tree is a large broadleaved tree with heart-shaped leaves. In early summer it smells wonderful, and for centuries it has stood on village squares, by fountains and beside churches.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the large-leaved lime and the small-leaved lime grow wild.
Limes bloom in June and July and attract many bees.
Lime wood is soft and pale and well suited to carving.
The fruits sail through the air with a flat wing-like bract.
Aphids on limes let sticky, sweet sap drip down.
Even in the Stone Age, ropes were plaited from lime bast.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland two species of lime grow wild: the **large-leaved lime** and the **small-leaved lime**. Both have heart-shaped leaves with a toothed edge. The large-leaved lime has bigger leaves and blooms a little earlier than the small-leaved lime. Limes can grow very old and very big. That is why people liked to plant them as shade trees on squares and along paths.

Limes bloom in **June and July**. The yellowish flowers smell strongly and contain a lot of sweet **nectar**. Bees collect it and make lime blossom honey from it. On the leaves there often live many **aphids**. They give off a sweet, sticky juice that is called honeydew. It drips onto bicycles, cars and benches standing under the tree.

The flowers turn into small **nutlets**. Several hang together on a pale, flat **wing-like bract**. When the fruits fall, this bract spins like a propeller. In this way the wind carries the seeds far from the tree.

The wood of the lime is soft, pale and even. That is why it is very popular with **woodcarvers**: many nativity figures and figures of saints are made of lime wood. Under the bark lies a tough, fibrous layer, the **lime bast**. Even in the Stone Age people plaited ropes, cords and mats from it.

In the well-known song “Der Lindenbaum”, “The Linden Tree”, it says: “By the well before the gate stands a linden tree”. The words were written by **Wilhelm Müller**, the music by **Franz Schubert** in 1827. In **Fribourg** people tell the legend of the **Murten lime**: after the Battle of Murten in 1476 a messenger is said to have run to Fribourg with a lime twig. From the twig a big lime tree is said to have grown.

gewusst: In many places in Europe, people used to meet under the village lime to celebrate or to hold court.
Limes can become several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: The Neolithic Revolution is one of the biggest upheavals in human history. People moved from hunting and gathering to farming and keeping livestock, and settled down. Neolithic is the technical term for the New Stone Age.
wichtigste: At its centre is the move to farming and keeping livestock.
In the Near East the change began about 12,000 years ago.
People built permanent villages and laid in stores.
Stores made specialisation and differences between rich and poor possible.
Living closely with animals brought more infectious diseases.
Typical tools were polished stone axes for clearing forest.

abschnitte.text: For a long time all people lived as **hunters and gatherers** and moved about. About 12,000 years ago, people in the **Near East** began to grow plants such as wheat and barley on purpose. They tamed animals such as sheep, goats and cattle. Because fields have to be looked after, people **settled down**. Because of its good soils, this region is also called the **Fertile Crescent**.

In present-day Turkey lies the site of **Göbekli Tepe**. There stand large stone pillars that were probably put up by hunters and gatherers. This shows that large communal buildings were possible even before farming. In central Anatolia lies **Çatalhöyük**, one of the biggest settlements of the New Stone Age. The houses stood close together and were entered through the roof.

Typical of the New Stone Age is the **polished stone axe**. With it people cleared forest for fields and settlements. They made **pottery**, that is, vessels of fired clay, to store supplies. Weaving of cloth also arose. Farming spread to Europe over thousands of years. In Switzerland the **pile dwellings** on lake shores bear witness to this time, and they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Farmers could harvest more than they needed straight away. With these **surpluses** they laid in stores. Not everyone had to get food any more, and some became craftsmen or leaders. In this way differences between people arose, which is called **social differentiation**. The way of life also had drawbacks: through close living with animals, **diseases** passed on from animals increased, and diet was often more one-sided.

gewusst: Göbekli Tepe is older than the pyramids of Egypt and older than Stonehenge.
The term Neolithic Revolution comes from the archaeologist Vere Gordon Childe.

teile.einleitung: Crop plants are plants that people grow on purpose because they supply food, fodder, fibres, oil, timber or medicines. Without them there would be neither bread nor chips nor cotton T-shirts. Many of our crop plants originally come from distant countries.
wichtigste: Crop plants are grown by humans because they bring a benefit.
They supply food, animal feed, fibres, oil, sugar, timber and medicines.
The potato originally comes from the Andes in South America.
Maize is the cereal harvested in the largest quantity worldwide today.
In Switzerland, sugar is mainly made from sugar beet.
In spring, rape makes fields flower bright yellow and supplies cooking oil.
In cotton, the seed hairs are made into cloth.

abschnitte.text: **Crop plants** are plants that humans grow and look after on purpose. They are divided by their use: food plants such as cereals and vegetables, fodder plants for animals, fibre plants such as cotton and flax, oil plants such as rape and sunflower, and medicinal and spice plants. Trees for timber and fruit belong here too.

About 10,000 years ago, people in the **Fertile Crescent**, a region in what is now the Near East, began to grow wild grasses. They sowed again and again the grains of the best plants. In this way, over many generations, wheat and barley with bigger grains came about. This process is called **domestication** or breeding. In China rice, and in Central America maize, were bred in a similar way.

Many crop plants came to Europe only after the discovery of America. The **potato** comes from the Andes in South America and came to Europe in the 16th century. In Switzerland it became an important food in the 18th century, and today we think of rösti. Maize, tomatoes, beans and cocoa also come from America, coffee on the other hand from Ethiopia.

Maize is today the most harvested cereal in the world, used mainly as animal feed and for biofuel. For more than half of humankind, rice is the most important **staple food**. Wheat is made into bread, pasta and baked goods. Soya beans supply protein for animal feed, tofu and oil.

In Switzerland the fields grow mainly wheat, barley, maize, potatoes, rape and **sugar beet**. Swiss sugar is made from the beet in the sugar factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld. **Rape** colours whole fields yellow in April and May and supplies cooking oil. But meadows and pastures take up the largest part of the area, because grass is the fodder plant for cows.

In **cotton**, the seeds form long, white hairs that are spun into yarn and woven into cloth. From flax you make linen, from hemp ropes and fabrics. Plants such as camomile, peppermint or marigold are used as tea and medicines. Rubber from the rubber tree is made into rubber goods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant that humans grow because it supplies them with food or raw materials.
The slow change of a wild plant into a cultivated plant through breeding.
The most important food that people eat daily in large amounts.
A plant whose fibres are used to make cloth or ropes.

gewusst: In the Andes there are still thousands of different potato varieties in many colours today.
Popcorn pops because the water in the maize kernel turns to steam when heated and bursts the shell.
The largest part of the maize harvested worldwide is not eaten by humans.

teile.einleitung: **NADPH** is a small molecule with a big job. It carries high-energy electrons in the cell. In **photosynthesis** it is made in the light reaction and used in the Calvin cycle.
wichtigste: NADP stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate.
NADP+ takes up two electrons and one proton and becomes NADPH.
The electrons are taken up by the nicotinamide ring.
Ferredoxin takes over the electrons from photosystem I.
The enzyme ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase makes NADPH at the end of the light reaction.
NADPH is made on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane.
In the Calvin cycle, NADPH supplies electrons for reduction.

abschnitte.text: NADP is the abbreviation for **nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate**. The molecule is a **coenzyme**, that is, a helper of enzymes. It occurs in two forms: as **NADP+** without extra electrons and as **NADPH** with two extra electrons. In reduction, NADP+ takes up **two electrons and a proton**. The electrons end up at the **nicotinamide ring**, a part of the molecule that is derived from the vitamin niacin.

In the light reaction of photosynthesis, light excites the photosystems in the **thylakoid membrane** of the chloroplasts. At the end of the electron transport chain, **photosystem I** passes electrons on to **ferredoxin**. Ferredoxin is a small electron carrier with iron and sulphur. The enzyme **ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase** then transfers the electrons to NADP+. This is how NADPH is made, on the **stroma side** of the membrane.

The NADPH passes directly into the **stroma**, where the **Calvin cycle** takes place. There carbon dioxide from the air is built into sugar. For this building up, energy from ATP and electrons from NADPH are needed. NADPH **reduces** an intermediate product, which is then processed further into sugar. The NADP+ that is left returns to the light reaction and is loaded up again.

NADPH has a close relative: **NADH**. Chemically the two differ only by **one extra phosphate group** in NADPH. This small difference is important. The cell’s enzymes recognise it and each work only with one of the two forms. NADH serves mainly to gain energy, NADPH mainly to build up substances.

gewusst: Animals and humans also need NADPH, for example to build up fats.
Per molecule of NADPH, two electrons are transferred in the light reaction.

teile.einleitung: In the water of streams, rivers and lakes, tiny amounts of medicines, pesticides and other chemicals are found. They are called micropollutants. Even at very low concentrations they can harm water animals.
wichtigste: Micropollutants are substances that can cause harm even at very low concentrations.
They usually occur in the range of nanograms to micrograms per litre.
Conventional sewage treatment plants remove them poorly, because bacteria can hardly break them down.
Switzerland is equipping selected sewage treatment plants with an additional cleaning stage.
This stage is meant to remove about 80 per cent of the micropollutants.
The ARA Neugut in Dübendorf was the first sewage treatment plant in Switzerland to use ozonation in full operation.

abschnitte.text: Micropollutants come from many sources: from **medicines**, **pesticides**, cosmetics, cleaning products and industrial chemicals. A well-known example is the painkiller **diclofenac**. Part of the active ingredient leaves the body again and gets into the sewage treatment plant with the waste water. Pesticides, on the other hand, are often washed from fields into streams by the rain.

The substances occur in **nanograms to micrograms per litre**. A nanogram is a billionth of a gram, a microgram a millionth of a gram. An example: a river contains 200 nanograms of a medicine per litre. A cubic metre has 1,000 litres, so that makes 200,000 nanograms. That is **200 micrograms** per cubic metre. Even with such small amounts, fish, crayfish or water insects can be harmed.

abschnitte.titel: The limits of the sewage plant
abschnitte.text: In an ordinary **sewage treatment plant** (ARA), **bacteria** break down dirt and nutrients. But many micropollutants are **hard for bacteria to break down** and flow on almost unchanged into the waters. That is why extra processes are needed. In **ozonation**, the substances are broken up with the gas ozone. In treatment with **activated carbon**, they stick to tiny particles of carbon.

Switzerland has decided to upgrade selected large sewage treatment plants with an **additional cleaning stage**. The aim is to remove **about 80 per cent** of the micropollutants. The first to put ozonation into full operation was the **ARA Neugut** in **Dübendorf**. The upgrade is paid for mainly through a **waste water charge**, which is collected per connected person.

**Groundwater**, which supplies a large part of our drinking water, can also be affected. The fungicide **chlorothalonil** was used against fungal diseases on fields. Its breakdown products turned up in groundwater in many places. The substance was then **banned** in Switzerland. Cases like this show how long substances can stay in water.

gewusst: Modern measuring devices can still detect individual substances when only a few nanograms of them are in a litre of water.
Ozone is the same gas that, high up in the atmosphere, protects the Earth from UV radiation.

teile.einleitung: The mole is a small mammal that spends almost its whole life underground. Everyone knows its molehills on meadows and in gardens.
wichtigste: The mole lives in tunnels under the ground.
It eats mainly earthworms and insect larvae, not plants.
It digs with broad, spade-like front paws.
It sees very badly, but smells and feels very well.
It does not hibernate.
Without its tail it is about 11 to 16 centimetres long.

abschnitte.text: The **mole** almost always lives in its **tunnels** under the ground. It only rarely comes up to the surface. It is about **11 to 16 centimetres** long, plus a short tail of 2 to 4 centimetres. Its short, **black fur** is as soft as velvet. It can be stroked in any direction, so the mole can get forwards and backwards through the narrow tunnels.

The mole’s **front paws** are as broad as **spades** and have strong claws. With them it pushes the soil aside. It pushes the rest of the soil up out of the ground. That is how **molehills** are made.
It is dark underground. The mole’s **eyes** are tiny, and it sees only very badly. But it can **smell** and **feel** very well. Its sensitive snout picks up the smallest movements.
The mole eats **no plants**. It catches **earthworms** and **insect larvae** in its tunnels. It does not **hibernate**. In winter it digs deeper, because that is where the worms live then.

Many molehills on a meadow annoy **farmers**. When mowing and making hay, the soil from the hills gets mixed into the grass. **Dirty feed** is bad for the animals. In the garden, on the other hand, the mole loosens the soil and eats the larvae of pests.

gewusst: The mole is more closely related to the hedgehog and the shrews than to mice.
A mole can dig many metres of new tunnels in a short time.

teile.einleitung: Who eats whom? This question shows a food chain. In nature, though, most animals eat several kinds of food. That is why many chains link up into a **food web**.
wichtigste: A food web shows nature better than a chain, because most animals have several sources of food.
If a prey species becomes rare, predators often switch to other prey.
Many species and many links make an ecosystem more stable.
A species whose disappearance greatly changes the web is called a keystone species.
In 1995, wolves were reintroduced in Yellowstone National Park.
If sea otters are missing, sea urchins eat the kelp forests bare.
The wood mouse is both prey and predator in the Swiss forest.

abschnitte.text: A **food chain** is a simple row, for example: grass, grasshopper, frog, grey heron. In reality, though, most animals eat **several kinds** of food. Besides fish, the **grey heron** often eats **frogs** and mice. If you draw all the links, a dense **food web** results. It shows much better how the species depend on one another.

abschnitte.titel: A web in the Swiss forest
abschnitte.text: In the Swiss forest, the **wood mouse** is a good example. It eats seeds, berries, buds and also insects and snails. In this way it is a **predator**. At the same time it is **prey** for the fox, the tawny owl, the weasel and the marten. If a prey species becomes rare, **predators** often **switch to other prey**. The fox then eats more beetles, fruit or birds.

An ecosystem with **many species** and many links is usually **more stable** against disturbances. If one species drops out, others can partly take its place. In a web with few species, on the other hand, a loss has big consequences. Some species are especially important. If such a **keystone species** disappears, the whole food web changes greatly.

In **Yellowstone National Park** in the USA, the wolves had been wiped out. Without them the deer became very numerous and ate many young trees along the rivers. In **1995**, **wolves** were brought back. The deer became fewer and avoided some places. In many places willows and poplars could grow again, which beavers and birds also benefited from. Just how strong these changes are is still being studied by experts.

On the Pacific coast of North America live **sea otters**. They like to eat **sea urchins**. Sea urchins in turn eat **kelp**, large brown algae that form whole forests under water. If the sea otters disappear, the sea urchins multiply strongly and **eat the kelp forests bare**. Then many fish and other sea animals lose their habitat. The sea otter is therefore a typical keystone species.

gewusst: Bacteria, fungi and worms are also part of the food web: they break down dead plants and animals.
Sea otters used to be hunted heavily for their dense fur.

teile.einleitung: Between the cities of Bern, Fribourg and Thun lies a landscape of hills, forests, moors and mountains. This is the **Gantrisch Nature Park**. It is a regional nature park and spreads over the cantons of **Bern and Fribourg**.
wichtigste: The Gantrisch Nature Park lies in the cantons of Bern and Fribourg.
It lies between the cities of Bern, Fribourg and Thun.
It is named after the mountain Gantrisch, which is about 2,200 metres high.
Lake Schwarzsee in the canton of Fribourg lies in the park area.
The pass road over the Gurnigel Pass leads through the Gantrisch area.
With a Dark Sky Park project, the park campaigns against light pollution.

abschnitte.titel: A park named after a mountain
abschnitte.text: The nature park is named **after a mountain**: the **Gantrisch**. It is **about 2,200 metres** high and belongs to the Pre-Alps. The park stretches from gentle hills with farms to rocky mountains. It lies **between Bern, Fribourg and Thun** and so is quickly reached from many places. Many people come to hike, cycle and, in winter, to go sledging.

The pass road over the **Gurnigel Pass** leads through the Gantrisch area. From there you can see far across the Central Plateau and into the Alps. In the canton of Fribourg lies the well-known mountain lake **Schwarzsee**. It is a popular destination for outings in summer and winter. The park also has many **moors**, pastures and large forests.

In many areas the night sky is never really dark because of street lamps, advertising and lit-up houses. This is called **light pollution**. In the Gantrisch area it is still comparatively dark at night. With its **Dark Sky Park project**, the park campaigns **against light pollution**. Municipalities and residents are encouraged to avoid unnecessary light. So there you can still see many stars and the Milky Way.

Too much artificial light at night harms many animals. **Moths and other insects** suffer especially. They fly around lamps until they are exhausted, and are then missing when it comes to pollinating plants and as food for bats and birds. Migratory birds can also lose their bearings in bright light. So dark nights help the whole of nature.

gewusst: A regional nature park is not a strict protected area: people carry on living, building and farming there.
One reason for protecting the night: people also sleep better on dark nights.

teile.einleitung: The **spring snowflake** is one of the first flowers of the year. It often blooms as early as March, when it is still cool in the woods. With its little white bells it looks pretty and delicate. In German it is called the “Märzenbecher”, the “March cup”.
wichtigste: The spring snowflake often starts to bloom in March.
Its flowers are white.
At the tips of the petals there are green or yellow spots.
All six petals are the same length.
It likes to grow in damp woods.
Another German name is “Frühlings-Knotenblume”.

abschnitte.text: The flower of the spring snowflake is **white** and hangs down like a little bell. It has six petals. At each **tip** there is a small **green or yellow spot**. A stem usually carries **one or two flowers**. The flowers have a light scent. The plant grows to about the height of a hand or a little more.

The spring snowflake looks like the **snowdrop**. But you can easily tell the two apart. In the spring snowflake **all the petals are the same length**. In the snowdrop the three outer petals are long and the three inner ones short. Another German name for the spring snowflake is **“Frühlings-Knotenblume”**.

The spring snowflake likes to grow in **damp woods**, in floodplains and on stream banks. There the soil is loose and rich in nutrients. In spring the trees are still bare, and plenty of light reaches the ground. The spring snowflake uses this time to bloom. It spends the rest of the year as a **bulb** in the soil.

Wild spring snowflakes should be **left standing**. In many Swiss cantons they are protected. Anyone who picks or digs them up harms the populations. In addition, the whole plant is **poisonous**, especially the bulb. If you want them in your garden, buy them from a garden centre.

gewusst: The spring snowflake belongs to the amaryllis family, as do the snowdrop and the daffodil.
Sometimes it is already in bloom when snow still lies in the woods.

teile.einleitung: Logistic growth describes how a population grows when space and food are limited. At first it goes quickly, then ever more slowly, until the population reaches an upper limit.
wichtigste: The model comes from the Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst (1838).
The upper limit is called the carrying capacity K.
The curve of population size is S-shaped.
The population grows fastest at half the carrying capacity.
If the population is bigger than K, it decreases again.
Raymond Pearl and Lowell Reed made the model known in biology around 1920.

abschnitte.text: The Belgian mathematician **Pierre-François Verhulst** set up the **logistic equation** in 1838. He wanted to describe how a population grows whose growth is slowed down. His work was long forgotten. Around 1920 **Raymond Pearl** and **Lowell Reed** rediscovered the equation independently. They applied it to population data and made it known in biology.

The equation reads: dN/dt = r · N · (1 minus N/K). Here **N** is the size of the population, **r** the growth rate and **K** the **carrying capacity**, that is the largest population that a habitat can feed permanently. An example: with r = 0.4 per year, K = 1,000 and N = 500 you get 0.4 · 500 · 0.5 = an increase of **100 animals** per year.

As long as N is much smaller than K, the bracketed factor is close to 1. Then the population grows **almost exponentially**. The denser it becomes, the more strongly the factor brakes the growth. Close to K the curve levels off, which is called the **saturation phase**. In this way an **S-shaped** or **sigmoid** curve arises.

Unlike the exponential model, the logistic model contains a **density-dependent brake on growth**. It reflects the competition for limited food and space. The absolute increase is greatest at **N = K/2**. If N is greater than K, the bracketed factor becomes negative, and the population **decreases** until it settles around K again.

gewusst: The same S-curve also describes how some new inventions spread in a population.
Bacteria in a nutrient solution often show a similar growth in the laboratory.

teile.einleitung: Mowing is the cutting of a meadow. From the cut grass, farmers make hay, aftermath hay or silage as fodder for their animals.
wichtigste: Large meadows are mostly mown with a mower on the tractor.
On steep slopes you often need the motor mower.
Before mowing, people look for hidden roe deer fawns with drones.
Hay from the first cut is called hay, that from the second cut Emd.
Silage is grass that is packed airtight in foil.
Flower meadows are mown only when the flowers have formed seeds.

abschnitte.text: Today the farmer mows large meadows mostly with a **mower** that is mounted on the **tractor**. It cuts a wide swathe of grass in a short time. On **steep slopes** you often need the **motor mower**. It is small and light, is guided by hand and does not tip over so easily. In the garden you mow the lawn with the **lawn mower**.

After mowing or raking together, the grass lies in long rows, the **windrows**. Dried, it becomes **hay**. In Switzerland the hay from the second and following cuts is called **Emd**. You can also let the grass wilt only briefly and then pack it airtight in foil. In this way it keeps, and is called **silage**.

In early summer roe deer mothers lay their **fawns** in the tall grass. In danger the fawns do not run away but press themselves to the ground. That is why they are at risk when mowing. Today the meadows are often searched beforehand with **drones**. A **thermal imaging camera** shows the warm animals in the grass, so they can be brought to safety beforehand.

After flowering, flowers need time to form **seeds**. From the seeds new plants grow the following year. If a flower meadow is mown too early, many flowers cannot sow themselves. In time they disappear. That is why species-rich meadows are mown only after flowering.

gewusst: In the past all meadows were mown by hand with the scythe.
Meadows with many flowers are important for bees, butterflies and grasshoppers.

teile.einleitung: The ecological footprint shows how much of nature a person, a country or the whole of humankind uses up. It is compared with what the Earth can supply in return. The concept was co-developed by the Swiss Mathis Wackernagel.
wichtigste: The ecological footprint measures how much area our way of life requires.
Mathis Wackernagel developed it together with William Rees.
Biocapacity is the ability of ecosystems to produce resources and to absorb waste such as CO2.
If the footprint is larger than a country’s own biocapacity, the country has an ecological deficit.
In industrial countries, the CO2 share from fossil energy is usually the largest part.
If everyone lived like the Swiss population, almost three Earths would be needed.

abschnitte.text: For food, clothes, housing, electricity and travel we need areas: fields, pastures, forests and seas. The **ecological footprint** calculates **how much area** is needed to produce everything we use and to absorb our waste. It is measured in **global hectares**. The concept was developed in the 1990s by the Swiss **Mathis Wackernagel** and the Canadian **William Rees**.

The footprint is set against the **biocapacity**. This is the **ability of ecosystems** to produce resources such as timber and food and to absorb **waste such as CO2**. If a country’s footprint is **larger than its own biocapacity**, it has an **ecological deficit**. It then uses more than its own nature can supply, and depends on other countries or overuses nature.

In **industrial countries**, the **CO2 footprint from fossil energy** usually makes up the largest share. It comes from burning oil, natural gas and coal, for example for heating, cars, aeroplanes and making goods. For the calculation, it is estimated how much forest would be needed to absorb this CO2 again. Food and housing also contribute a lot.

If all people in the world lived like the **Swiss population**, according to calculations **almost three Earths** would be needed. So Switzerland has a clear ecological deficit. A large part of it comes from goods and energy that are imported. The footprint is an estimate and depends on the calculation methods, but it shows the order of magnitude well.

The **Global Footprint Network**, an organisation that Wackernagel co-founded, calculates every year the **Earth Overshoot Day**. On this day humankind has used up as much nature as the Earth can renew in a whole year. For the rest of the year it is living, as it were, on credit. In recent decades this day has mostly fallen in summer.

gewusst: Mathis Wackernagel comes from Basel and studied at ETH Zurich.
You can estimate your own footprint with online calculators that ask about food, housing and travel.

teile.einleitung: Every animal and plant species has its own role in nature. The ecological niche describes how a species lives: what it eats, when it is active and which conditions it needs. This helps to understand why many species can live side by side.
wichtigste: The ecological niche describes the role and requirements of a species in the ecosystem.
The niche is the way of life, the habitat is the place where it lives.
Blue tit and great tit look for food in different parts of the trees.
Swallows hunt by day, bats by night.
The beak shapes of Darwin’s finches show different sources of food.
Similar niches on different continents are called ecological equivalence.
Because of competition and predators, the niche used is usually smaller than the possible one.

abschnitte.text: The **ecological niche** is not a cave or a corner, but the **role and requirements of a species** in the ecosystem. This includes what it eats, when it is active, what temperature it can stand and where it finds shelter. The **habitat**, on the other hand, is the **place where it lives**, for example a deciduous wood or a pond. You could say: the habitat is the address, the niche is the job.

abschnitte.titel: Side by side in the woods
abschnitte.text: In the same deciduous wood live the **blue tit** and the **great tit**. Both eat insects but hardly get in each other’s way. The light blue tit often looks for its **food** on thin twigs and in the crown, the larger great tit more on thicker branches and on the ground. The **woodpecker** takes yet another niche: it looks for **insects in the wood** of the trees. In this way many species share one habitat.

Species can also keep out of each other’s way through the time of day. **Swallows** hunt insects **by day**, **bats** by **night**. So they hardly disturb each other in hunting, although they eat similar prey. It is similar with birds of prey and owls. The more different the niches of two species are, the less **competition** there is between them.

A famous example is **Darwin’s finches** on the **Galápagos Islands**. The different species have very different **beak shapes**: thick beaks for cracking hard seeds, slender beaks for insects. So the finches use **different sources of food** and occupy different niches. Charles Darwin observed these birds on his voyage round the world.

On different continents there are often species that occupy a very similar niche without being closely related. This is called **ecological equivalence**. An example is grass-eaters in the steppes of different parts of the world. It is also true that the niche a species actually uses is usually **smaller than the possible one**.
