The reasons are **competition** from other species and **predators**.

gewusst: The concept of the ecological niche was shaped by several researchers in the first half of the 20th century.
According to a well-known rule of ecology, two species with exactly the same niche cannot live together in the same place permanently.

teile.einleitung: The privet is a shrub that grows at forest edges in Switzerland and is often planted as a hedge. In early summer it blooms white and smells strongly. In autumn it bears black berries, which are poisonous for people.
wichtigste: The privet bears glossy black berries.
The berries are poisonous for people.
The flowers are white and smell strongly and sweetly.
Privet is often planted for clipped hedges.
Many leaves stay green well into winter.
Birds eat the berries in winter.

abschnitte.text: The **wild privet** is native to Switzerland. It grows at **forest edges**, in hedgerows and on sunny slopes, preferably on chalky soil. It belongs to the **olive family**, like the olive tree, the ash and the lilac. Its leaves are oblong and smooth. Many of them stay **green well into winter**. In mild winters the shrub stays almost entirely green.

In **early summer** the privet blooms with small **white flowers**. They stand together in panicles. The flowers have a **strong, sweet scent**. It attracts many insects, such as bees, beetles and butterflies. The large **privet hawk-moth** is also named after the shrub. Its big green caterpillar likes to eat privet leaves.

In autumn the privet bears **glossy black berries**. They often hang until winter. For people the berries are **poisonous**, and you should never eat them. **Birds** such as thrushes, however, like to eat them, especially in winter, when there is little food. In this way the birds spread the seeds across the landscape.

Privet **tolerates cutting** very well. It sprouts again densely after every cut. That is why it is a popular **hedge plant** in gardens. A privet hedge offers birds shelter and nesting places. Because the privet is native, it is more valuable to nature than many foreign hedge plants.

gewusst: The privet is related to the olive tree.
The caterpillar of the privet hawk-moth can grow almost as long as a finger.

teile.einleitung: In summer big machines hum across the golden grain fields. These are **combine harvesters**. They cut the grain and at once separate the kernels from the straw.
wichtigste: A combine harvester reaps and threshes grain in one pass.
At the front the wide cutter bar cuts off the stalks.
The reel turns and presses the stalks to the knife.
The kernels collect in the grain tank.
Through a long tube the kernels go into the trailer.
Combine harvesters also harvest rape and are out and about mainly in summer.

abschnitte.text: The name already says what the machine does: it **reaps** and **threshes**. Reaping means cutting off the stalks. Threshing means loosening the kernels from the ears. In the past many people did this with scythe and flail, and it took a very long time. Today a combine harvester manages a whole field in a short time.

At the front sits the wide **cutter bar** with a knife. Above it turns the **reel**, a roller with tines. It presses the stalks to the knife. Inside, a fast-turning **threshing drum** beats the kernels out of the ears. After that shakers and sieves separate the kernels from straw and chaff. The straw falls out at the back onto the field.

The clean kernels collect in the **grain tank** at the top of the machine. When the tank is full, a tractor with a **grain trailer** drives alongside. Through a long, swivelling **tube** the kernels flow into the trailer. This often even happens while moving. After that the tractor takes the grain to the collection point or to the mill.

Combine harvesters are seen mainly **in summer**, when wheat, barley and rye are ripe and dry. Besides grain they can also harvest **rape**, whose small black seeds supply oil. With a special attachment they also harvest maize. On the road a combine harvester drives **slowly and carefully**, because it is very wide. Often the cutter bar is taken off for this and towed behind on a trailer.

gewusst: A combine harvester has a cab high up so that the driver can see well over the field.
Many farmers in Switzerland do not own a combine harvester, but have their grain threshed by a contractor.

teile.einleitung: The needles of a conifer look quite different from the leaves of a beech. But in botanical terms they are also **leaves**, only very narrow ones. They are called **needle leaves**.
wichtigste: From a botanical point of view, a needle is a narrow leaf.
The needles of the silver fir have two white stripes underneath.
On most twigs, silver fir needles are parted to two sides.
Spruce needles are four-sided in cross-section and stay on the tree for several years.
The yew has soft, flat needles and is poisonous almost everywhere.
In the juniper, the prickly needles usually stand in threes in a whorl.
In many needles, the stomata lie sunk in hollows.

abschnitte.text: A needle is a **narrow leaf**. Like every leaf, it carries out **photosynthesis** and makes sugar. Needles have a thick, waxy skin. Their **stomata**, through which gases and water vapour flow, often lie **sunk in hollows**. In this way little water evaporates. This is important in winter, when the ground is frozen and the roots can hardly take up any water.

You can easily tell spruce and silver fir apart by their needles. **Spruce needles** are sharp and **four-sided** in cross-section. You can roll them between your fingers. They stand all around the twig. The needles of the **silver fir** are flat and slightly notched at the tip. Underneath they have **two white stripes**. On most twigs they stand **parted to two sides**, like a comb.

Most conifers are **evergreen**. But that does not mean that their needles last for ever. A **spruce needle** normally stays on the tree for **several years** and then falls. Because not all the needles fall at the same time, the tree always stays green. One exception is the **larch**. Its needles turn golden yellow in autumn and fall.

The **yew** has **soft, flat needles** that do not prick. Almost all parts of the yew are **poisonous**. In the **juniper**, on the other hand, the needles are hard and **prickly**. They usually stand **in threes in a whorl**, that is, at the same height all around the twig. In the **pine** the needles stand in twos, in the **Swiss stone pine** in fives in a bunch.

gewusst: A saying helps you remember: in German, “Die Fichte sticht, die Tanne nicht”, meaning “the spruce pricks, the fir does not”.
The larch is the only native conifer that is bare in winter.

teile.einleitung: Fruit growing is the growing of fruit trees and fruit bushes in order to harvest fruit. In Switzerland, mainly apples are grown, but also pears, cherries and plums. Fruit growers look after their trees all year round.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, most apples are grown.
In winter fruit growers prune the trees so that more light gets into the crown.
In thinning, part of the young fruit is removed.
Bees are especially important for the pollination of fruit blossom.
Nets over the trees protect against hail.
Fire blight is a dangerous bacterial disease of apple and pear trees.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **apple** is the most important fruit. Large growing areas lie, for example, in Thurgau, in the Valais and in the region around Lake Constance. There are also pears, **cherries**, plums and apricots. In the past large **standard trees** shaped the landscape. Today most farms have **low-trunk orchards**: many small, low apple trees in long rows. They are easier to look after and to harvest.

In winter fruit growers **prune** their trees. In this way more **light** gets into the crown, and the fruit ripens better. In spring the trees blossom. For **pollination**, **bees** are especially important, so many farms set up bee colonies. If a tree bears too much fruit, part of it is removed. This **thinning** gives bigger fruit and regular harvests.

A hailstorm can destroy a whole harvest. That is why many fruit growers stretch **hail nets** over their trees. Diseases are also a danger. **Fire blight** is a bacterial disease that attacks apple and pear trees. Affected twigs look as if they were burnt. Pests such as insects and fungi are also watched closely.

Apples are harvested in autumn, but you can buy them all year round. They are stored in **cool stores with little oxygen**. There the fruit breathes more slowly and stays **fresh for months**. Fruit is also made into cider, juice, dried fruit and spirits. Well known is **Zuger Kirsch**, a spirit made from **cherries**, which also goes into the Zug cherry cake.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are hundreds of old fruit varieties, which are kept alive by organisations such as Pro Specie Rara.
An apple tree in a modern orchard can bear fruit only a few years after planting.

teile.einleitung: Plants keep growing at certain places throughout their lives. These places are called meristems. There, cells divide again and again and form new tissue.
wichtigste: A meristem is a plant tissue that can divide and produces new growth.
The apical meristems at the tips of shoots and roots are responsible for growth in length.
The cambium is responsible for the growth of trees in thickness.
Annual rings form because the cambium is active to different degrees during the year.
The root cap protects the meristem at the root tip.
Grasses have meristems at the base of their leaves and grow quickly again after mowing.

abschnitte.text: A **meristem** is a **growth tissue**. Its cells are small, have thin walls and can divide again and again. The new cells later become the different tissues of the plant, for example vessels or leaf cells. These finished tissues are called **permanent tissue**. The word meristem comes from Greek and means roughly “divisible”.

At the tip of every shoot and every root sits an **apical meristem**, also called a **tip meristem**. It makes sure the plant grows **longer**. At the root tip, the meristem pushes its way through the soil. To keep it from being injured, it is protected by a cap of cells, the **root cap**. In grasses there are extra meristems at the **base of the leaves**. That is why they grow back quickly after being mown or grazed.

abschnitte.titel: Growth in thickness and annual rings
abschnitte.text: Trees get a little thicker every year. The **cambium** is responsible for this, a thin layer under the bark. It forms **wood** towards the inside and **bast** towards the outside. In spring light, loose wood forms, and in late summer darker, dense wood. This is how the **annual rings** become visible. Another layer, the **cork cambium**, forms the cork of the **bark** that protects the trunk.

Meristems that are already laid down in the seedling are called **primary meristems**. **Secondary meristems** form later from cells that were already fully developed. These cells become able to divide again. One example is the cork cambium.

In laboratories, whole new plants can be grown from tiny pieces of a tip meristem. This is called **meristem culture**. In this way, for example, **virus-free potato plants** are obtained. Viruses hardly ever reach the meristem, because no vessels have formed there yet.

gewusst: Thanks to their meristems, some trees can live for several thousand years and still keep growing.
You can tell the age of a felled tree from its annual rings.

teile.einleitung: Nature does a great deal for us humans, often without our noticing. Forests protect against avalanches, insects pollinate fruit trees, soils filter water. Such services are called ecosystem services.
wichtigste: Ecosystem services are the benefit that people draw from ecosystems.
In 2005 the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment distinguished four categories.
They are provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting services.
The pollination of fruit trees is a regulating service.
The protective forest in the Alps protects against avalanches, rockfall and debris flows.
Recreation in the forest is a cultural service, soil formation a supporting service.
From 2007 the TEEB study examined the economic value of nature.

abschnitte.text: **Ecosystems** are communities of plants, animals and tiny organisms together with their habitat, such as a forest, a lake or a meadow. The **benefit** that people draw from them is called an **ecosystem service**. It includes food, clean water, fresh air and protection from natural hazards. Many of these services are free, but can hardly be replaced.

A big international report, the **Millennium Ecosystem Assessment**, distinguished four categories in **2005**. **Provisioning** services supply goods such as food, timber and drinking water. **Regulating** services control processes, for example the **pollination** of fruit trees by insects or protection from floods. **Cultural** services concern recreation and experiences. **Supporting** services such as **soil formation** are the basis for all the others.

In the Swiss Alps the **protective forest** is especially important. It protects villages, roads and railway lines from **avalanches**, **rockfall** and **debris flows**, that is, flows of mud and rubble. About half of the Swiss forest counts as protective forest. Replacing this protection with structures would be enormously expensive. That is why the protective forest is looked after on purpose.

Anyone who walks in the forest, swims in a lake or enjoys the view in the mountains is using a **cultural service**. Nature serves **recreation**, health and inspiration. Landscapes that are typical of a region and part of its identity also count. In Switzerland the landscape is also important for tourism.

Researchers try to express the value of ecosystem services in money. In **1997** the researcher **Robert Costanza** estimated the annual value of all global ecosystem services at **about 33 trillion US dollars**. From **2007** the international study **TEEB** examined the economic value of ecosystems and biodiversity. Such figures are uncertain, but they are meant to show how much we lose when nature is destroyed.

gewusst: A large part of the crop plants grown worldwide depend wholly or partly on pollination by animals.
In heavy rain a healthy forest soil can store a lot of water and so reduce floods.

t1vg0ctg.t: Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage

teile.einleitung: Lakes, moors, beautiful villages and old paths shape Switzerland. To keep them, there is the **Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage**, **NHG** for short. It was passed by the Federal Assembly in **1966**.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly passed the NHG in 1966.
According to the Federal Constitution (Art. 78), the cantons are in principle responsible for protecting nature and cultural heritage.
In its own tasks, the Confederation must spare the landscape and the appearance of places.
The ISOS lists village and town scenes worth protecting, the IVS historic transport routes.
The Federal Commission for the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage prepares expert opinions on federal projects.
Bank vegetation such as reeds and riverside woodland may in principle not be removed.
The Confederation designates biotopes of national importance.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Federal Constitution**, **Article 78**, the **cantons** are in principle responsible for protecting nature and cultural heritage. But the Confederation has important tasks. Under **Article 3 NHG**, in its own tasks it must **spare the landscape and the appearance of places**. This applies, for example, when it builds railway lines, national roads or military installations or approves such buildings.

By **protection of cultural heritage**, the NHG means **protecting the appearance of places, historic sites and cultural monuments**. This includes old village centres, castles, churches and bridges. For this the Confederation keeps lists, called **federal inventories**. The **ISOS** lists **village and town scenes** in Switzerland that are worth protecting. The **IVS** records **historic transport routes** such as old mule tracks and roads. For landscapes there is the BLN.

If a federal project could **seriously harm** an object in a federal inventory, an expert opinion is needed. It is prepared by the **Federal Commission for the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage**, ENHK for short. It judges whether and how strongly a project changes the landscape or the appearance of a place. Its opinion is an important basis for the authorities when they decide.

The NHG also protects habitats. Under **Article 18a**, the Confederation designates **biotopes of national importance**, for example moors, floodplains, dry meadows and spawning grounds of amphibians. The cantons then see to their protection and care. Especially protected is the **bank vegetation** along waters, that is, **reeds, rushes and riverside woodland**. It **may in principle not be removed**.

gewusst: The NHG gives certain nature and heritage organisations the right to appeal against building projects.
Since a popular vote in 1987, moors and moorland landscapes of special beauty have also been protected in the Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: A coniferous forest is a forest in which mainly conifers such as spruces, firs, pines or larches grow. It is green in winter too and often grows where it is cool, such as in the mountains or in the far north. The largest coniferous forest on Earth is the taiga.
wichtigste: In a coniferous forest, mainly conifers grow.
The spruce is the most common tree species in Swiss forests overall.
Fir cones stand upright, spruce cones hang down.
The larch is the only native conifer that loses its needles in autumn.
In the Swiss stone pine, five needles grow together in a bunch.
A layer of wax protects the needles from water loss in winter.
The taiga is a huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of Russia, Scandinavia and Canada.

abschnitte.text: A **coniferous forest** consists mainly of conifers. Conifers cope better with cold, short summers and poor soils than many broadleaved trees. That is why coniferous forests grow mainly in mountains and in the far north. In the Swiss Central Plateau, though, many spruce forests have also been planted by people, because spruces grow quickly and provide good building timber.

Spruce and silver fir are often mixed up. The simplest rule: the cones of the **spruce** hang down and fall to the ground whole. The cones of the **silver fir** stand upright on the branches and fall apart there, which is why you do not find whole fir cones on the ground. Also, spruce needles prick, while fir needles are soft and have two white stripes underneath.

The spruce is the most common tree species in Swiss forests. In the Alps there are dense spruce forests up to about 1,800 metres. Above that, at the tree line, light **larch and Swiss stone pine forests** grow in the Engadine and in the Valais. The larch drops its golden yellow needles in autumn, and in the Swiss stone pine five needles stand together. Many mountain forests are **protective forests** that shield villages and roads from avalanches and rockfall.

Needles have a thick layer of wax that protects them from drying out in winter, when the ground is frozen. In this way the trees can carry out photosynthesis straight away on warm winter days. Under the dense crowns it is dark, so often only mosses, ferns and **bilberries** grow on the ground. The falling needles rot slowly and make the soil acid.

In the coniferous forest live squirrels, which eat seeds from cones, and the crossbill, a bird with a crossed beak. The nutcracker collects Swiss stone pine nuts. In Swiss mountain forests there also live capercaillie, red deer and lynx. A feared pest is the **bark beetle**, which attacks weakened spruces.

The **taiga** is a huge belt of coniferous forest that stretches across Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska. It is the largest continuous area of forest on Earth. There the winters are long and icy, the summers short. In the taiga live elk, brown bears, wolves and wolverines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A forest in which mainly conifers grow.
A huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of the world.
The height in the mountains above which no closed forests grow.
A forest that protects people and buildings from avalanches, rockfall or landslides.

gewusst: The cones you find in the forest are almost always spruce cones, not fir cones.
In the Siberian taiga it can get colder than minus 50 degrees in winter.
A large part of the Swiss forest protects against natural hazards such as avalanches and rockfall.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is a heavenly body that orbits the Earth. It is our nearest neighbour in space and the brightest object in the night sky. To this day it is the only other heavenly body that people have set foot on.
wichtigste: The Moon is the Earth’s natural companion and orbits around it.
On average it is about 384,400 kilometres from the Earth.
Its diameter is about 3,474 kilometres, a good quarter of the Earth’s diameter.
The Moon does not shine by itself, but is lit up by the Sun.
It always shows the same side to the Earth.
In 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to set foot on the Moon.
The pull of the Moon causes the tides on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The **Moon** is a satellite, that is a heavenly body that orbits a planet. It is about 384,400 kilometres away; by car you would need more than half a year to get there without a break. For one lap around the Earth it needs about 27 days. Because it turns exactly once on its own axis in that time, we always see the same side. The far side was only photographed in 1959, by a space probe.

Researchers think that about 4.5 billion years ago, a heavenly body the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris that was thrown out. This heavenly body is called **Theia**. Since then the Moon has been slowly moving away from the Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.

On the Moon there is no air, no liquid water and no weather. The surface is covered with countless **craters** that come from impacts. The dark patches that we see are large plains of solidified lava, called **maria**, which means seas. In the day it gets over 100 degrees hot, at night far below minus 100 degrees cold.

On 20 July 1969, the American mission **Apollo 11** landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong was the first person to set foot on it. Up to 1972, twelve astronauts in all walked on the surface of the Moon and brought back about 380 kilograms of Moon rock. Because gravity is only about a sixth as strong as on Earth, they could make big jumps.

Switzerland was part of Apollo 11 too. The University of Bern, under Johannes Geiss, developed a **solar wind sail**, a foil that caught particles from the Sun. It was the only non-American experiment of the mission. Buzz Aldrin even put it up in front of the American flag.

The Moon’s gravity pulls on the water of the oceans. This causes **low tide** and **high tide** twice a day. On some coasts the sea rises and falls by several metres. The Moon also stabilises the tilt of the Earth’s axis and so makes for a calmer climate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavenly body that orbits a planet, also called a moon.
A bowl-shaped dip made by an impact.
Dark, flat plains of lava on the Moon, once thought to be seas.
The regular rising and falling of sea level, that is low tide and high tide.

gewusst: The astronauts’ footprints can probably still be seen today, because no wind blows on the Moon.
On the Moon, a child who weighs 30 kilograms would feel as light as if they weighed 5 kilograms.
The Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun, but also about 400 times closer, so both appear the same size in the sky.

teile.einleitung: The lily family is a plant family with many beautiful flowers. It includes lilies, tulips and the snake’s head fritillary. Most of them survive the winter in a bulb in the earth.
wichtigste: Tulips and lilies belong to the lily family.
They survive the winter in a bulb.
Their flowers have six tepals of the same colour.
The lily family belongs to the monocotyledons.
The wild ancestors of garden tulips come from Central Asia.
In 1637 the tulip mania in the Netherlands collapsed.

abschnitte.text: The lily family includes **lilies**, **tulips**, the **snake’s head fritillary** and the crown imperial. Other well-known spring flowers, by contrast, belong to other families. **Daffodils** and **snowdrops** count among the amaryllis family, the **crocus** among the iris family. In the past many more plants were counted in the lily family. New studies, however, have made the family smaller.

Tulips and lilies survive the winter in a **bulb**. It consists of thickened, fleshy leaves. In it the plant stores nutrients for sprouting in spring. Lily-family plants are **monocotyledons** with flowers in threes. They have two circles of three **tepals** of the same colour each, so **six** in all.

In mountain forests the **Turk’s cap lily** grows. Its nodding, pink flower has rolled-back, spotted petals and recalls a turban. On mountain meadows in the Alps the **fire lily** blooms with upright, orange-red flowers. It has become rare. On damp meadows you find the **snake’s head fritillary**. Its bell-shaped flowers carry a **chequered pattern** like a chessboard. It too is very rare.

Wild tulips grow in the steppes and mountains of **Central Asia**. Via the **Ottoman Empire** they came to central Europe in the 16th century. In the **Netherlands** they became fashionable. Single bulbs were traded for huge sums. People speak of the **tulip mania**. In February **1637** the prices suddenly collapsed, and many traders lost money.

gewusst: The Netherlands is still famous today for its huge tulip fields.
The Turk’s cap lily gets its name from the shape of a turban.

teile.einleitung: Many mires were drained in the past and dried out. In a mire restoration, people try to bring them back to a natural, wet state. This helps rare animals and plants and also the climate.
wichtigste: The most important aim of a mire restoration is to raise the water level again.
To do this, the old drainage ditches are closed.
Putting a dried-out mire under water again is called rewetting.
Trees and bushes are often removed because they draw water from the mire.
It takes many decades before a restored raised bog forms peat again.
In Switzerland, the Confederation and the cantons help to pay for the upgrading of mires.

abschnitte.text: A mire lives on **water**. If it is drained, the typical plants disappear, and the peat breaks down. In a **mire restoration**, the main aim is to **raise the water level again**. This is called **rewetting**. Only when the ground is permanently wet can the sphagnum mosses grow again.

To hold the water back, the old **drainage ditches are closed**. For this, small dams made of peat, wood or other materials are built in the ditches. The water builds up behind them and spreads out in the mire again. Sometimes old drainage pipes are also broken. Work like this is planned carefully so that neighbouring meadows and paths are not flooded.

On a dried-out mire, birches, pines or spruces often grow. With their roots, these **trees and bushes draw water** from the mire and **shade** it. The light-loving mire plants then have no chance. That is why, in a restoration, the woody plants are often felled and taken away.

A raised bog grows very slowly, often only about one millimetre of peat a year. It takes **many decades** until a restored mire really **forms peat** and grows again. But animals often return after just a few years. **Dragonflies** and **amphibians** such as frogs and newts especially benefit from the new areas of water.

Dry mires constantly give off **carbon dioxide**, because their peat breaks down. Once the mire is wet again, this breakdown is slowed. The peat gives off **less carbon dioxide** and goes on storing its carbon. In Switzerland, the **Confederation and the cantons** support the upgrading of mires of national importance with money.

gewusst: A layer of peat one metre thick can have taken several thousand years to form.
Sphagnum mosses can store many times their own weight in water.

teile.einleitung: The maquis, in Italian “macchia”, is a dense, evergreen scrubland on the coasts of the Mediterranean. It smells of herbs and is adapted to hot, dry summers.
wichtigste: The maquis consists of dense shrubs, mostly one to five metres tall.
It grows in the Mediterranean climate with dry summers and damp winters.
Many plants have small, hard, leathery leaves.
Rosemary, thyme, lavender and myrtle grow wild there.
The maquis often arose from cleared forests.
In summer the danger of bushfires is great.

abschnitte.text: The **maquis** is typical of the coastal countries around the **Mediterranean**. There a **Mediterranean climate** prevails: the summers are long, hot and dry, the winters mild and damp. Most of the rain falls in the winter half of the year. The dense shrubs mostly grow to about one to five metres tall.

Many plants of the maquis have small, hard and leathery leaves. They are called **sclerophyllous plants**. Their thick skin protects against too much **evaporation** in the dry summer. The plants stay green all year round.

In the maquis many fragrant plants grow wild, for example **rosemary**, **thyme**, **lavender** and **myrtle**. Rosemary tolerates drought especially well. The essential oils of the plants make the landscape smell strongly on warm days.

Originally, in many places **sclerophyllous forests** with **holm oaks** grew. People cleared, grazed and burned them over centuries. The maquis often arose from this. On barren chalky soils in southern France there is an even lower, more open form, the **garrigue**. There the stony ground shows between the bushes.

In summer the shrubs are parched and often contain essential oils that burn well. A spark or carelessness can therefore set off large **bushfires**. In French the maquis is called **“maquis”**. The word later also referred to resistance groups who hid in the scrubland in the Second World War.

gewusst: On Corsica the maquis covers large parts of the island.

teile.einleitung: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is called the “red planet” because of its colour. It is a rocky planet like Earth, but smaller, colder and with very thin air. No other planet has been explored so thoroughly with robots, and one day people may perhaps travel there.
wichtigste: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
It is called the “red planet” because of its colour.
The red colour comes from iron oxide, a kind of rust, in the dust and rock.
Mars is about half the size of Earth.
A Martian year lasts 687 Earth days, a Martian day a little over 24 hours.
On Mars stands Olympus Mons, the highest known volcano in the Solar System.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

abschnitte.text: After Earth, Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is one of the **rocky planets**. Its surface is covered with red dust that contains a lot of **iron oxide**, a kind of rust. That is why Mars glows reddish in the night sky and is called the red planet. It is named after the Roman god of war, Mars, because its colour reminded people of blood and fire.

Mars has a diameter of about 6,800 kilometres, which makes it about half the size of Earth. **Gravity** there is only a little over a third as strong: a child who weighs 30 kilograms on Earth would feel like 11 kilograms. A day on Mars, a **sol**, lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes. For one trip around the Sun, Mars needs 687 Earth days, which is almost two Earth years.

Mars has enormous landscapes: the volcano **Olympus Mons** rises more than 20 kilometres high, which is almost three times as high as Mount Everest. The system of canyons called Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometres long. The air is mostly carbon dioxide and is so thin that people could not breathe there. On average it is about minus 60 degrees cold, and at the poles there are **polar caps** of water ice and frozen CO2.

Dried-up riverbeds and lake deposits show that liquid **water** flowed on Mars billions of years ago. Today water exists almost only as ice in the ground and at the poles. Researchers are looking for traces of simple life that might once have existed there. So far, however, no sure proof of life on Mars has been found.

Space probes have been flying to Mars since the 1960s, and several **rovers** have driven across its surface. The rover Curiosity landed in 2012, and the rover **Perseverance** in February 2021, together with the little helicopter Ingenuity, which was the first aircraft to fly on another planet. Switzerland takes part in the research too: the University of Bern built the camera **CaSSIS**, which photographs Mars from orbit on board a European probe. Space agencies plan to send people to Mars in the future as well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet with a solid surface made of rock, like Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
A day on Mars. It lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes.
A remote-controlled vehicle that explores the surface of a heavenly body.
A cover of ice around the north or south pole of a planet.

gewusst: On Mars there are sometimes huge dust storms that can wrap the whole planet.
A sunset on Mars looks bluish, which is exactly the opposite of on Earth.
Depending on the distance, a radio signal from Earth takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to reach Mars.

teile.einleitung: A mire (in German a “Moor”) is a permanently wet habitat in which dead plants do not rot completely but slowly pile up into peat. Mires are home to rare plants and animals. They are also important for the climate, because they store large amounts of carbon in the ground.
wichtigste: A mire is a wetland with waterlogged ground in which peat forms.
Peat forms from plant remains that are hardly broken down because of wetness and lack of oxygen.
A distinction is made between raised bogs, which receive only rainwater, and fens, which are fed by groundwater.
Mires store large amounts of carbon in the ground and are therefore important for the climate.
Rare plants such as the carnivorous sundew grow in mires.
In Switzerland, mires have been protected in the constitution since the Rothenthurm initiative of 1987.
A large part of the former Swiss mires has been drained or mined.

abschnitte.text: A **mire** is an area in which the ground is wet all year round. Dead plants sink into the water, where there is hardly any oxygen. That is why they do not rot completely, but form a dark, spongy mass, the **peat**. Peat grows only about a millimetre a year, so a metre of peat takes about a thousand years.

A **raised bog** is supplied with water only by rain and is very poor in nutrients. Here mainly sphagnum moss grows, which slowly curves upwards like a watch glass. A **fen**, also called a low bog, lies by groundwater or on lake shores and is richer in nutrients. There sedges, rushes and orchids grow.

Mires cover only about three per cent of the Earth’s land area, but store about twice as much **carbon** as all the forests put together. If a mire is drained, air gets into the peat. Then it breaks down and releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. That is why it is good for the climate when drained mires are made wet again.

In the nutrient-poor raised bog, plants have developed special tricks. The **sundew** catches small insects with sticky droplets and digests them. The cotton grass stands out with its white, fluffy heads. Dragonflies, moor frogs, adders and rare butterflies also live here.

In the past, many Swiss mires were drained to gain farmland, or peat was mined as fuel. As a result, a large part of the mire areas has been lost since 1800. In 1987 the Swiss voters accepted the **Rothenthurm initiative**, and since then mires and mire landscapes of special beauty have been protected in the Federal Constitution. Well-known mire landscapes lie near Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz and in the UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere.

Because hardly anything rots in a mire, things are preserved for a very long time. Pollen in the peat tells researchers which plants grew thousands of years ago. In Northern Europe, even **bog bodies** have been found, people from the Iron Age whose skin and hair were still preserved. Mires are therefore like a history book of nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark mass of hardly decomposed plant remains that forms in a mire.
A mire that is fed only by rainwater and is very poor in nutrients.
A mire that is fed by groundwater or a body of water.
A habitat with very wet ground, for example a mire, a marsh or a reedbed.

gewusst: Sphagnum moss can store many times its own weight in water, like a sponge.
For a long time, peat was cut in Switzerland as a fuel for heating.
The mire protection initiative was named after the place Rothenthurm, where an army training ground was planned in a mire landscape.

teile.einleitung: The red-backed shrike is a songbird that lives in hedges and thorny bushes. It is famous for a special habit: it impales its prey on thorns. It spends the winter far away in Africa.
wichtigste: The red-backed shrike is a bird from the shrike family.
It impales prey on thorns and so lays in stores.
The male wears a black eye mask.
It eats mainly large insects.
It builds its nest in thorny bushes.
It spends the winter in Africa and comes back in May.

abschnitte.text: The red-backed shrike is a little bigger than a sparrow. The **male** has a grey head, a reddish-brown back and a **black eye mask**. The female is a plainer brown. The beak is strong and hooked at the tip, like that of a bird of prey. The red-backed shrike belongs to the family of the **shrikes**.

The red-backed shrike eats mainly **large insects** such as beetles, grasshoppers and bumblebees. Sometimes it also catches a mouse or a lizard. Surplus prey it impales on **thorns** or pointed twigs. In this way it lays in **stores**, for example for days of bad weather. The German name “Neuntöter”, meaning “nine-killer”, comes from the old idea that it first kills nine animals before it eats one. But that is not true.

The red-backed shrike likes open landscapes with **hedges**, pastures and meadows. It likes to sit on a bush or fence post and look out for prey. It builds its **nest** well hidden in **thorny bushes** such as blackthorn, hawthorn or dog roses. The thorns protect the young from enemies. In Switzerland you find it mainly in landscapes rich in structure, also in the Jura and in the Alpine valleys.

The red-backed shrike is a **migratory bird**. In late summer it flies to **Africa** and spends the winter in the south of the continent. Only in **May** does it come back to us, so rather late in spring. Then there are enough large insects. Because hedges and flower-rich meadows have disappeared in many places, the red-backed shrike has become rarer. New hedges help it.

gewusst: The scientific name Lanius means “butcher”, because of the impaled prey.
Every year a red-backed shrike flies many thousands of kilometres on migration.

teile.einleitung: An oasis is a green place in the middle of the desert. There is water there, and so palms and other plants grow. For thousands of years people have lived in oases, and caravans stop there.
wichtigste: The water of an oasis mostly comes from groundwater.
In oases mainly date palms grow, which give shade.
A caravan is a group of travellers with camels.
Caravans stop at oases to fetch water.
A thirsty dromedary can drink up to about 100 litres at once.
A well-known oasis is Siwa in Egypt.

abschnitte.text: In the desert it hardly ever rains. Even so, there is water deep in the ground, the **groundwater**. In some places it comes to the surface as a spring or lies so near that wells can be dug. There an **oasis** forms. Some oases are as small as a garden, others so big that whole towns have room in them.

In oases mainly **date palms** grow. Their fruits are sweet and keep for a long time. The palms also give **shade**. Underneath, people plant fruit trees, vegetables and cereals. The water is led to the fields in small channels. In this way one green storey grows beneath another.

A **caravan** is a group of travellers with **camels**. In the past caravans travelled through the desert with goods such as salt, cloth and spices. At the oases they stopped to fetch **water** and rest. The **dromedary**, the camel with one hump, can go a long time without water. At an oasis a thirsty dromedary can drink **up to about 100 litres** in a short time.

A famous oasis is **Siwa** in **Egypt**, near the border with Libya. There are salt lakes, springs and many date palms. In the desert, travellers sometimes see a lake where there is none at all. This is a **mirage**, an **optical illusion**. It arises because hot air above the ground bends the light, so that you see a mirror image of the sky.

gewusst: In the oasis of Siwa, Alexander the Great visited a famous oracle.
The hump of a dromedary stores fat, not water.

teile.einleitung: The light reaction is the first part of photosynthesis. In the thylakoid membrane of the chloroplasts, light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH. In the process water is split and oxygen is released.
wichtigste: The light reaction supplies ATP and NADPH to the Calvin cycle.
In non-cyclic electron transport, electrons flow from water through both photosystems to NADP+.
Plastoquinone carries electrons from photosystem II to the cytochrome b6f complex.
The cytochrome b6f complex additionally pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen.
Plastocyanin is a copper protein and carries electrons to photosystem I.
In cyclic electron transport, only ATP is made.
The Z scheme shows the energy levels of the electrons.

abschnitte.titel: Where the light reaction takes place
abschnitte.text: The light reaction takes place in the **thylakoids** of the chloroplasts. These are flat membrane sacs. In their membrane sit large protein complexes with pigments, the **photosystems**. They capture light and use it to excite electrons. The result is two high-energy substances: **ATP** as chemical energy and **NADPH** as reducing power. Both are used up in the **Calvin cycle** to make sugar.

In **non-cyclic electron transport**, the electrons travel from **water** through **photosystem II** and **photosystem I** to NADP+. At photosystem II water is split, and **oxygen** is produced. The mobile, fat-soluble **plastoquinone** carries electrons and protons to the **cytochrome b6f complex**. This additionally pumps **protons** into the thylakoid lumen. The copper-containing **plastocyanin** carries the electrons on to photosystem I.

Through the splitting of water and the work of the cytochrome b6f complex, many protons collect in the lumen. In this way a **proton gradient** arises, a slope like that of a reservoir. The protons flow back through the enzyme **ATP synthase**. In the process ATP is made. In **cyclic electron transport**, the electrons return to the transport chain after photosystem I. Then **only ATP** is made, but neither NADPH nor oxygen.

abschnitte.titel: The Z scheme and the numbers
abschnitte.text: If you plot the energy levels of the electron carriers, you get a zigzag line like a Z lying on its side. This is called the **Z scheme**. The two rises correspond to the excitation by light in the two photosystems. The photosystems were numbered in the **order of their discovery**. Photosystem I was known first, although the electrons run first through **photosystem II**.

gewusst: The oxygen that we breathe comes from the splitting of water in the light reaction.
Plastocyanin contains a copper atom that can take up electrons and give them off again.

teile.einleitung: Methane is a colourless, odourless gas that burns and is the main component of natural gas. It is produced, among other places, in cows’ stomachs, in swamps and on rice fields. As a greenhouse gas, methane has an especially strong effect on the climate.
wichtigste: Methane is a gas made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms; its formula is CH4.
Methane is the main component of natural gas and biogas.
It is a powerful greenhouse gas and contributes to global warming.
Methane is produced, among other ways, by livestock farming, because cows make it in their stomachs and belch it out.
Swamps, rice fields and rubbish tips also release methane.
Methane stays in the atmosphere for only about twelve years, but has a much stronger effect than carbon dioxide.
Mixed with air, methane can explode.

abschnitte.text: **Methane** is the simplest hydrocarbon: one carbon atom is joined to four hydrogen atoms. At room temperature it is a gas that you can neither see nor smell. Because it is lighter than air, it rises. The Italian researcher Alessandro Volta discovered it in 1776 in the marsh gas at Lake Maggiore.

Methane is produced when **bacteria** break down plant remains without oxygen. This happens in the rumen of cows, sheep and goats, in swamps and bogs, on flooded rice fields and in rubbish tips. A cow belches out several hundred litres of methane a day. Methane also escapes when coal, oil and natural gas are extracted. In Switzerland, most of the methane comes from agriculture.

Methane holds back heat in the atmosphere, like carbon dioxide. But it has a much stronger effect: calculated over 20 years, about 80 times as strong as the same amount of **carbon dioxide**. On the other hand, it is broken down again after about twelve years. Since industrialisation began, the amount of methane in the air has more than doubled. Releasing less methane therefore slows warming quickly.

Because methane burns well, it is used as **natural gas** for heating, cooking and generating electricity. So that leaks can be noticed, a substance with a strong smell is added to natural gas. In **biogas plants**, methane is obtained from slurry, manure and green waste. This biogas can also be used as a fuel for cars and buses.

In coal mines, methane sometimes collects, and there it is called firedamp. If it mixes with air, a spark can set off a serious explosion, called a **firedamp explosion**. In the past, miners therefore took canaries with them, which showed signs first when the air was bad. Today, electronic measuring devices give the warning.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat and warms up the Earth.
A flammable gas from the ground that is mostly methane.
A gas that bacteria produce from manure, slurry or waste.
The largest part of a cow’s stomach, where bacteria break down the grass.

gewusst: On Saturn’s moon Titan there are whole lakes of liquid methane.
Natural gas only smells because a scent is deliberately added to it.
Researchers are testing feed additives so that cows belch out less methane.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, mires and mire landscapes are protected by the Federal Constitution. This protection goes back to a popular initiative of 1987. Mires are valuable habitats and important stores of carbon.
wichtigste: The mire protection article was added to the Federal Constitution in 1987 through the Rothenthurm initiative.
The occasion was a planned army training ground near Rothenthurm.
Today mire protection is in Article 78, paragraph 5 of the Federal Constitution.
Buildings that go against the protection and were put up after 1 June 1983 must be removed.
The first step in putting it into practice was the Raised Bog Ordinance, which came into force in 1991.
Mires store large amounts of carbon in their peat.

abschnitte.text: Near **Rothenthurm** in the canton of Schwyz lies a large mire landscape. The army planned a **training ground** there, that is, an area for military exercises. People from the region and nature conservation groups fought against it. They submitted a **popular initiative**. On 6 December **1987**, the people and the cantons accepted the **Rothenthurm initiative**. In this way mire protection came into the Federal Constitution.

Today the protection is in **Article 78, paragraph 5** of the Federal Constitution. Mires and mire landscapes of special beauty and national importance are protected. No facilities may be built there and no changes made to the ground, unless they serve the protection or the farming use as before. A special **retroactive** rule said that facilities built **after 1 June 1983** that go against the protection must be **removed**.

For the Constitution article to work, precise rules are needed. The first to come into force, in **1991**, was the **Raised Bog Ordinance**, with a list of the important raised bogs. The Fen Ordinance followed in **1994** and the Mire Landscape Ordinance in **1996**. A **mire landscape** is a near-natural landscape that is strongly shaped by mires.

A **raised bog** gets its water only from rain and snow. It is very poor in nutrients, and sphagnum mosses slowly grow upwards. A **fen**, on the other hand, is fed by **groundwater or slope water rich in minerals**. That is why more different plants grow there, such as sedges, rushes and orchids. Many fens are mown as litter meadows.

In mires, dead plants are hardly broken down because of the wetness. They pile up as **peat**. This peat **stores large amounts of carbon**. If mires are drained, the peat breaks down and carbon dioxide gets into the air. Healthy, wet mires are therefore also important for **climate protection**.

gewusst: The Rothenthurm initiative was one of the few popular initiatives to be accepted by the people and the cantons.
Mires cover only a small part of the Earth, but store a great deal of carbon.

teile.einleitung: A neophyte is a plant that has reached an area only through humans. Most neophytes are harmless, and some are even important crop plants. A few, however, spread strongly and push out native plants.
wichtigste: The Greek word “neos” means new, “phyton” means plant.
Plants that occur naturally in an area are called native.
Neophytes that spread strongly and cause damage are called invasive neophytes.
Many came to Switzerland as ornamental plants for gardens.
They often lack natural enemies here.
Alien animals are called neozoa.

abschnitte.text: Plants that have grown by themselves in an area for a long time are called **native**. A **neophyte**, on the other hand, is a plant that humans have brought along. The word comes from Greek: “neos” means new, “phyton” means plant. For animals we speak of **neozoa**. Many neophytes are useful. The **potato**, for example, comes from America and is not regarded as invasive.

Many neophytes came to Switzerland as **ornamental plants** for gardens and parks. Others travelled unnoticed with seed, soil or goods. Some have escaped from gardens and are now spreading in the wild. One example is the **staghorn sumac** from North America. In autumn it has bright red foliage and cone-shaped, red fruit clusters.

Some neophytes spread very fast. They often lack **natural enemies** here, such as insects or fungi that keep them in check in their homeland. Such species are called **invasive neophytes**. They form dense stands and **push out native plants**. In this way animals that depend on these plants also lose their food. Some species also harm buildings or health.

Through **climate change** winters are becoming milder. Warmth-loving species that used to freeze can now survive here. In Switzerland, Info Flora keeps a list of invasive neophytes. Certain species may no longer be sold or planted. If you plant **native plants** in your garden, you help to slow their spread.

gewusst: Tomato, maize and sunflower are also plants that originally come from America.
Only a small part of all neophytes becomes invasive.

teile.einleitung: The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, NDVI for short, is a measure of how dense and healthy the plants in an area are. It is calculated from satellite images. In doing so, you compare how much red light and how much near infrared an area reflects.
wichtigste: NDVI is calculated like this: (NIR minus red) divided by (NIR plus red).
Chlorophyll in green plants absorbs red light.
Healthy leaves reflect near infrared strongly, because of the cell structure inside the leaf.
NDVI always lies between -1 and +1.
Open water typically shows negative values.
With very dense vegetation, NDVI saturates and hardly responds any more.

abschnitte.text: Satellites measure how much light the Earth’s surface reflects. In doing so they distinguish different **wavelengths**, for example red light and **near infrared (NIR)**. Near infrared is invisible to our eyes. From these measurements you calculate the **NDVI**. In this way you can monitor large areas without being on the spot.

Green plants contain **chlorophyll**. This pigment **absorbs red light** for photosynthesis, so little red is reflected. Healthy leaves, on the other hand, reflect near infrared very strongly. This is due to the **cell structure inside the leaf**, where light is scattered between cells and air spaces. The healthier and denser the plants are, the bigger the difference between red and infrared.

The formula is: NDVI equals **(NIR minus red) divided by (NIR plus red)**. An example: a pixel has a reflectance of 0.5 in near infrared and 0.1 in red. Then the NDVI is (0.5 minus 0.1) divided by (0.5 plus 0.1), so 0.4 divided by 0.6. That gives **about 0.67**. The value always lies **between -1 and +1**.

Dense, healthy vegetation has high values, often above 0.6. Rock, sand or settlements lie close to zero. **Open water** typically shows **negative values**. With very dense forest, NDVI has a weakness: it **saturates** and hardly rises any more, even when still more leaves are added. With **time series** over a year you follow the leafing out in spring, the length of the growing season and **drought stress** in summer.

gewusst: NDVI was developed in the 1970s with data from the first Landsat satellites.
With NDVI you can see from above when spring arrives in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A mixed forest is a forest of broadleaved and coniferous trees growing side by side. Because many different tree species occur here, an especially large number of animals and plants find a home too. In Switzerland, mixed forests are very common.
wichtigste: A mixed forest is made up of broadleaved and coniferous trees.
Typical trees in Swiss mixed forests are beech, silver fir, spruce, maple and ash.
The forest is divided into layers: moss layer, herb layer, shrub layer and tree layer.
Mixed forests are more resilient than pure spruce forests, because pests and storms do not hit all the trees equally.
The hurricane Lothar destroyed large areas of forest in Switzerland on 26 December 1999.
In the Emmental there are selection forests, in which trees of all ages stand side by side.
Because of climate change, foresters now increasingly rely on mixed forests.

abschnitte.text: A **mixed forest** is a forest in which broadleaved and coniferous trees grow together. In Switzerland these are often beeches, silver firs and spruces, together with maple, ash, oak or cherry. In autumn the broadleaved trees turn colourful, while most conifers stay green. In the Swiss Central Plateau, without people, mostly beech forest and mixed beech and fir forest would grow.

A forest is built like a house with floors, which is called **layering**. At the very bottom lies the moss layer with mosses, fungi and leaf litter. Above it comes the **herb layer** with ferns, grasses and flowers such as the wood anemone. Then comes the shrub layer with elder or hazel, and at the very top the tree layer with the crowns of the big trees.

Because a mixed forest has many tree species and layers, it is especially rich in species. Woodpeckers hammer holes into old trees, squirrels collect beechnuts and fir seeds. Roe deer, foxes, badgers and many beetles live here. Deadwood, that is dead trees, is an important habitat for fungi and insects. It is said that the forest has a high **biodiversity**.

On 26 December 1999, the hurricane **Lothar** swept across Switzerland. On the Uetliberg, gusts of 241 kilometres per hour were measured. About 10 million trees were blown down, especially many spruces in pure spruce forests. After the storm, the bark beetle also multiplied strongly. This experience showed that mixed forests cope better with storms and pests.

In a **selection forest**, young, middle-aged and old trees of all sizes stand in a colourful mix side by side. The forester only ever fells individual trees, instead of clearing whole areas. In this way the forest stays permanently closed and protects the soil. In the Emmental and in other Pre-Alpine areas, this kind of forest management with silver fir, spruce and beech has a long tradition.

Because of climate change it is getting warmer and drier. The spruce suffers especially from heat and drought. That is why foresters increasingly plant tree species that cope better with warmth, such as oak, Douglas fir or silver fir. A well-mixed forest spreads the **risk**: if one species fails, others stay standing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The division of the forest into layers from the ground up to the tree crowns.
The forest layer of grasses, ferns and flowers directly above the moss layer.
A forest in which trees of all ages stand mixed side by side.
A small beetle that lives under the bark and attacks weakened spruces.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
In Switzerland, Lothar blew down in a single day about as much timber as is otherwise harvested in two to three years.
Switzerland has had a law protecting the forest since 1876.

teile.einleitung: The speed of light states how fast light spreads, namely about 300,000 kilometres per second. Nothing in the universe is faster than light in empty space. This speed is one of the most important basic quantities of physics and is abbreviated with the letter c.
wichtigste: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second.
Exactly, in empty space it is 299,792,458 metres per second.
The speed of light is abbreviated with the letter c.
According to what we know today, nothing can move faster than light in a vacuum.
The light of the sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
In water and glass, light is slower than in empty space.
The Dane Ole Rømer was the first to estimate the speed of light, in 1676.

abschnitte.text: The speed of light is the speed at which light and other **electromagnetic waves** such as radio waves spread. In a **vacuum**, that is in empty space, it is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. That is about 300,000 kilometres per second or over a billion kilometres per hour. Physicists abbreviate it with the letter **c**, from the Latin word celeritas for speed.

In a single second, light could race about seven times around the whole Earth. From the Moon to the Earth, light needs only a little more than a second. The light of the **sun**, by contrast, is on its way for about 8 minutes and 20 seconds before it reaches us. An aeroplane would need almost 20 years for the same distance.

For a long time many scholars believed that light was infinitely fast. In 1676 the Danish astronomer **Ole Rømer** observed that the eclipses of Jupiter’s moon Io occurred earlier or later depending on the distance between Earth and Jupiter. From this he concluded that light needs time to cover a distance. Later, ever more exact measurements succeeded, and since 1983 the **metre** has even been defined through the speed of light.

In transparent materials light becomes slower; in water, for example, it travels at only about 225,000 kilometres per second. When light passes at an angle from air into water, it therefore changes direction, which is called **refraction**. That is why a spoon in a glass of water looks bent. Lenses in spectacles, magnifying glasses and cameras also use this effect.

In 1905 **Albert Einstein**, who was then working at the patent office in Bern, published his special **theory of relativity**. In it, the speed of light is the same for every observer, no matter how fast he himself is moving. From this it follows that no object with mass can reach the speed of light. The famous formula E equals m times c squared also comes from this theory.

Because light is so fast, we see a flash of lightning almost at once, but we hear the thunder only later, for sound is almost a million times slower. Internet data travels as light signals through **fibre-optic cables** around the world. Navigation systems such as GPS also have to calculate the travel time of the radio signals exactly. When researchers talk to space probes at Mars, they wait a few minutes for an answer, depending on the distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: An empty space in which there are almost no particles, as in outer space.
Light changes its direction when it passes from one material into another.
A theory by Albert Einstein about space, time and motion.
A very thin glass thread through which light signals carry data.

gewusst: When you see the sun, you see it as it was about 8 minutes ago.
Albert Einstein developed his famous theory of relativity in Bern, where you can visit his flat of that time today.
If after a flash of lightning you count the seconds until the thunder and divide by three, you get roughly the distance of the storm in kilometres.

teile.einleitung: In the past, mires were seen as useless, dangerous land. That is why they were drained with ditches and pipes to gain fields and meadows. In Switzerland, most mires have disappeared in this way.
wichtigste: Mires were drained to gain land for fields and meadows.
The mire area of Switzerland has shrunk by about 90 per cent since the 19th century.
In the Second World War, many mires were drained during the Battle of Cultivation.
The first Jura Water Correction lowered the lake levels in the Seeland.
In a drained mire, the peat breaks down and the ground sinks.
Animals such as the tree frog and the snipe lost their wet habitat.

abschnitte.text: To drain a mire, **ditches** are dug through which the water runs off. Later, **drainage pipes** were also laid in the ground. They carry the water away underground, and the area above can be farmed. In this way wet mires became **fields and meadows**. **Peat** was also mined and used as fuel.

In the **Second World War**, Switzerland was surrounded by other countries that were at war. Food became scarce. With the **Battle of Cultivation**, also called the Wahlen Plan, the country was to produce more of its own food. For this, parks were ploughed up and many **mires were drained**. In all, the mire area of Switzerland has shrunk by **about 90 per cent** since the 19th century.

In the **Seeland** there used to be a large mire plain that was often flooded. The **first Jura Water Correction** in the 19th century led the Aare into Lake Biel and **lowered the water levels** of the Jura lakes. In this way the plain could be drained. Today the **Grosses Moos** is an important **vegetable-growing area** and is often called the “vegetable garden of Switzerland”.

Peat is made of plant remains that were hardly broken down in the wet mire. When air gets into the ground after draining, the **peat breaks down**. Carbon dioxide escapes, and the **ground sinks**. In the Grosses Moos, the peat layer has shrunk badly in many places. That is why in some places the ground there is now too wet again, or the peat layer has almost gone.

With the mires, the habitat of many animals and plants disappeared. The **tree frog** needs wet meadows and ponds, and the **snipe**, a wading bird with a long beak, probes the soft mire ground for food. Both became rare in Switzerland. Today the remaining mires are protected, and some are being made wet again.

gewusst: In the past, dried peat was burned for heating in many households.
In their peat, mires store a great deal of carbon, which is released when they are drained.

teile.einleitung: Mars has two small moons, called Phobos and Deimos. They are not round like our Moon, but look like irregular, potato-shaped lumps of rock full of craters. They were only discovered in 1877, because they are so small and dark.
wichtigste: The two moons of Mars are called Phobos and Deimos.
Both moons were discovered in 1877 by the American astronomer Asaph Hall.
Phobos means fear, Deimos means terror.
The moons are small and irregularly shaped like potatoes.
Phobos is bigger and orbits much closer to Mars than Deimos.
Phobos is slowly approaching Mars and will break apart or crash in many millions of years.
The moons may be captured asteroids or debris from an impact.

abschnitte.text: Mars has exactly two natural **moons**: Phobos and Deimos. They are among the smallest moons in the Solar System. Phobos is about 27 kilometres long, Deimos only about 15 kilometres, so both would fit comfortably inside a small Swiss canton. Both are very dark and have a surface covered in **craters**.

In August 1877, the American astronomer **Asaph Hall** discovered the two moons with a large telescope in Washington. He named them after the sons of the Greek god of war Ares, who was called Mars by the Romans. **Phobos** means fear and **Deimos** means terror. In legend, the two accompanied their father into battle.

Phobos orbits at a height of only about 6,000 kilometres above the surface of Mars and needs less than 8 hours for one lap. Because it orbits faster than Mars turns, it rises in the west and sets in the east, and does so twice a day. Deimos is further away and needs about 30 hours for one orbit. Phobos gets about two centimetres closer to Mars every year and, in many millions of years, will be torn apart by **tidal forces** or crash onto Mars.

On Phobos the huge crater **Stickney** stands out. It is about 9 kilometres across, a third of the length of the whole moon. The impact that made it almost broke Phobos apart. Long grooves also run across the surface of Phobos. Deimos looks smoother, because many craters are filled with fine **dust**.

How the moons of Mars were formed is still not clearly settled. One idea is that they are **asteroids** that Mars captured with its gravity. Another idea is that they formed from debris that a huge **impact** on Mars flung into space. The Japanese mission MMX is meant to bring soil samples from Phobos to Earth and help settle this question.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavenly body that orbits a planet.
A bowl-shaped dip, usually made by the impact of a lump of rock.
Forces that arise from the different pull of a heavenly body and that can deform other bodies.
A small body of rock that orbits the Sun.

gewusst: The writer Jonathan Swift wrote about two moons of Mars as early as 1726 in his book about Gulliver’s travels, over 150 years before their discovery.
On Phobos gravity is so weak that a strong jump would carry a person very far up.
Seen from Mars, Deimos looks hardly bigger in the sky than a bright star.

teile.einleitung: A meteoroid is a small lump of rock or metal that flies through space. If it hits the Earth, it usually burns up as a glowing shooting star. Only rarely does a remnant survive and land on the ground as a meteorite.
wichtigste: A meteoroid is a small body of rock or metal that orbits the Sun.
Meteoroids are smaller than asteroids, and many are only as big as a grain of sand.
The meteoroid is the body in space, the meteor is its glow as it enters the atmosphere.
A meteorite is the remnant that reaches the ground.
In everyday speech, meteors are also called shooting stars.
Many meteoroids come from comets or from broken-up asteroids.
In meteor showers such as the Perseids in August, you see especially many shooting stars.

abschnitte.text: A **meteoroid** is a small lump of rock or metal that flies through our Solar System. Most are tiny, only a few millimetres across. Bigger lumps of many metres are usually called asteroids. Meteoroids orbit the Sun like the planets, but on very different paths.

These three words sound similar, but mean different things. The **meteoroid** is the body in space. When it races into the Earth’s envelope of air, the air in front of it is squeezed and heated so strongly that it glows: this glow is called a **meteor**. What is left of it and reaches the ground is called a **meteorite**.

Meteoroids hit the Earth’s atmosphere at 11 to over 70 kilometres per second. That is much faster than a rifle bullet. They begin to glow at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres. Most burn up completely before they get lower than 50 kilometres. Especially bright meteors are called **fireballs** or bolides.

Comets lose dust and small stones along their path. If the Earth crosses this trail of dust every year, a **meteor shower** results. The Perseids in August come from the comet Swift-Tuttle. In December you can watch the Geminids. On dark nights you then sometimes see dozens of shooting stars per hour.

Meteorites are roughly divided into stony meteorites, iron meteorites and stony-iron meteorites. The biggest known meteorite is the Hoba meteorite in Namibia, which weighs about 60 tonnes. In Switzerland, many pieces of an iron meteorite have been found at the **Twannberg** in the canton of Bern. Meteorites are valuable for research because they show what the young Solar System was made of.

Very big lumps can leave craters. In 2013, an object about 20 metres across exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk, and the shock wave broke many window panes. About 66 million years ago, a huge asteroid hit Mexico and helped to wipe out the dinosaurs. But events like this are extremely rare.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small lump of rock or metal flying through space.
The streak of light in the sky when a meteoroid burns up in the air.
A piece from space that has fallen all the way to the ground.
Many shooting stars that come at the same time of year from the same direction of the sky.

gewusst: Every day, tonnes of tiny grains of dust fall from space onto the Earth.
Most shooting stars are made by grains smaller than a grain of rice.
Some meteorites come from Mars or from the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Neobiota are living things that people have brought into a new area, on purpose or by accident. They include plants, animals and fungi. Most hardly stand out, but some spread strongly and cause damage.
wichtigste: Neobiota are species that reached an area only through humans.
In Europe the year 1492, when Columbus arrived in America, counts as the cut-off year.
New plants are called neophytes, new animals neozoa, new fungi neomycetes.
Plants that were brought in as early as prehistoric times are called archaeophytes.
The spread of species by humans is called hemerochory.
In Switzerland, Info Flora keeps the Black List of invasive alien plants.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek **neos** for new and **bios** for life. It means species that did not occur naturally in an area. Humans brought them along, with ships, trade, gardens or farming. This kind of spread is called **hemerochory**. In Europe the cut-off is the year **1492**: after that a lively exchange between the continents began.

Depending on the group, there are separate terms. Alien plants are called **neophytes**, animals **neozoa** and fungi **neomycetes**. Plants that came much earlier are called **archaeophytes**. They reached central Europe, for example, with early arable farming, such as the cornflower and the corn poppy. Species that spread strongly and do harm are called **invasive**.

In Switzerland the organisation **Info Flora** keeps the Black List of invasive plants. The **Canadian goldenrod** comes from North America and forms dense stands. The **Japanese knotweed** sprouts anew even from small pieces of its underground shoots, the rhizomes. The **yellow nutsedge** is a troublesome arable weed. It is mostly carried from field to field with soil on farm machinery.

Some neophytes can harm health. The sap of **giant hogweed** makes the skin sensitive to light. If sunlight then falls on the skin, painful blisters appear, as with a burn. So you should never touch the plant without protective clothing. If you find a suspicious plant, you can report it to the municipality or Info Flora.

gewusst: Many neobiota are harmless or even useful, such as the potato or maize.
You cannot see fungi when they are brought in: a neomycete caused ash dieback here.

teile.einleitung: The **oil palm** is a palm whose fruits supply a great deal of oil. Palm oil is in many foods, soaps and cosmetics. Growing it brings in money, but also causes disputes, because rainforest is cleared for it.
wichtigste: The oil palm originally comes from West Africa.
Indonesia and Malaysia together produce the largest part of the world’s palm oil.
Palm oil is obtained from the fruit flesh, palm kernel oil from the seeds.
Raw palm oil is orange-red.
No other oil plant supplies so much oil per hectare.
Rainforest is cleared for plantations, which harms the orangutan, for example.

abschnitte.text: The oil palm grows in warm, damp regions near the equator. It originally comes from **West Africa**, and today it is grown in many tropical countries. A young palm bears its first fruit after about **3 years**. The fruits grow in large, heavy **fruit clusters** with many single fruits. Each fruit has flesh on the outside and a hard kernel with the seed inside.

From the **fruit flesh** you press the **palm oil**. Raw palm oil is **orange-red**, because it contains many pigments that are also found in carrots. From the seed in the kernel you obtain **palm kernel oil**, which is pale. Both oils are used for food, but also for soaps, detergents, candles and cosmetics.

The food industry likes palm oil because it is **cheap** and stays **semi-solid** at room temperature. So it is well suited to chocolate spread, baked goods, margarine or ready meals. The oil palm supplies **more oil per hectare than any other oil plant**, for example more than rape, soya or sunflowers. If palm oil were replaced by other oils, much more farmland would be needed for it.

The largest part of palm oil comes from **Indonesia** and **Malaysia**. There large areas of **rainforest** were cleared or burned for plantations. As a result many animals lose their habitat, especially the **orangutan** on Borneo and Sumatra. In addition, when peat soils are burned and drained, a lot of carbon dioxide gets into the air. There are labels for more sustainable palm oil, but experts disagree about how much they achieve.

In **March 2021** Switzerland voted on a **free trade agreement with Indonesia**. One main topic was palm oil. Supporters pointed to new opportunities for the economy and to rules for sustainable growing. Opponents feared that more rainforest would be destroyed. The voters narrowly approved the agreement.

gewusst: A single fruit cluster of the oil palm can weigh several dozen kilograms.
Palm oil is one of the most widely used vegetable oils in the world.

teile.einleitung: A cloud forest is a forest that is very often in cloud or fog. The air there is almost always moist, and countless mosses and ferns grow on the trees. Such forests are among the richest habitats in species on Earth.
wichtigste: Cloud forests lie where clouds regularly get caught on mountain slopes.
Most cloud forests grow on mountain slopes in the tropics, for example in the Andes.
Leaves, mosses and lichens comb water droplets out of the fog.
The trees are thickly covered with mosses, ferns and epiphytes.
Cloud forests store water like a sponge and release it slowly to streams.
Well known are the Monteverde reserve in Costa Rica and the laurel forests of the Canary Islands.

abschnitte.text: Moist air rises on mountains and cools as it does so. The water vapour forms clouds that bank up on the slopes. In this **cloud zone** the cloud forest grows. The sun rarely shines there, and it is mostly cool and very damp. For the tropical forests, experts speak of **montane cloud forests**.

Cloud forests get not only rain. Tiny fog droplets stick to leaves, mosses and lichens, run together and drip off. This **fog precipitation** is also called combing out. It can make up a large part of the water. Mosses and soils soak up water and release it bit by bit to streams. Some cities in the tropics get part of their **drinking water** in this way.

The constant moisture is ideal for plants that grow on other plants. They are called **epiphytes**. They include mosses, ferns, bromeliads and many orchids. Trunks and branches look as if they were covered with green fur. The epiphytes take water straight from the air and need no soil.

Cloud forests are very rich in species. In Central America lives the **quetzal**, a bird with shimmering green feathers. The males have very long tail feathers, and the quetzal is the national bird of Guatemala. A famous protected area is the **Monteverde** cloud forest reserve in Costa Rica. On the **Canary Islands** the moist trade-wind clouds bank up on the mountains. On La Gomera, in Garajonay National Park, a fog-moist **laurel forest** grows.

Cloud forests cover only a small area of the Earth. They are threatened by clearing for pastures and fields. **Climate change** is also a danger: if the clouds rise higher, the forest lacks the fog. Many animals and plants occur in only a single cloud forest. That is why protecting them is especially important.

gewusst: In a cloud forest a single tree can carry hundreds of epiphytes.
The quetzal is so important to Guatemala that the national currency is also called the quetzal.

teile.einleitung: Net primary production, NPP for short, tells you how much new biomass plants build up in a given time. It is the food basis for almost all animals and humans. Experts usually measure it in grams of carbon per square metre per year.
wichtigste: Gross primary production is everything that plants make by photosynthesis.
Net primary production is gross primary production minus the respiration of the plants.
Plants typically use up about half of their gross primary production in respiration themselves.
Worldwide, NPP is about 100 billion tonnes of carbon per year.
Just under half of it comes from the oceans.
Only NPP is available to animals as food.

abschnitte.text: Plants use sunlight to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. This whole achievement is called **gross primary production**. But the plants need part of it themselves for their **respiration**, that is, for the energy to live. What is left is the **net primary production**. The rule is: NPP equals gross primary production minus respiration of the producers. Typically plants use up about half.

A forest makes 2,400 grams of carbon per square metre in a year. The plants use up 1,300 grams of it in respiration. So net primary production is 2,400 minus 1,300, which is **1,100 grams of carbon** per square metre per year. This amount is contained in new wood, new leaves and roots. It can be eaten by animals or broken down by fungi.

Worldwide, plants and algae build up about **100 billion tonnes of carbon** a year as new biomass. **Just under half** of it is made in the oceans. There it is mainly tiny algae, the **phytoplankton**. On land, tropical rainforests are especially productive, deserts and ice regions hardly at all. According to a study by Haberl and others from 2007, humans take for themselves about **a quarter** of the possible NPP, for example through farming and the use of timber.
