Animals can only eat what plants have really built up. What the plant has used up itself in respiration is gone. That is why for animals **NPP is what counts** and not gross primary production. If you also subtract the respiration of all animals, fungi and bacteria, you get the **net ecosystem production**. It shows whether an ecosystem overall stores or gives off carbon.

gewusst: The tiny algae in the sea build up almost as much biomass as all land plants together.
Today satellites help to estimate the net primary production of the whole Earth.

teile.einleitung: With a light microscope you can see tiny things greatly magnified, for example plant cells. Light shines through a thin specimen, and lenses magnify the image. In school it is an important tool in the subject of biology.
wichtigste: The total magnification is eyepiece times objective, for example 10 times 40 equals 400.
The eyepiece is the lens at the eye, the objective sits above the specimen.
The image is upside down and reversed left to right.
With the diaphragm you regulate the amount of light.
You begin with the lowest magnification and the coarse focus.
Images magnified at most about 1,000 to 2,000 times are useful.

abschnitte.text: At the top of the tube sits the **eyepiece**. You look in through this lens with your eye; the name comes from the Latin oculus for eye. Close above the specimen sits the **objective**. It produces the first magnified image. Several objectives are fixed to a turning part, the **nosepiece**. The specimen lies on the **stage**. Beneath it sits the **diaphragm**, which lets through more or less light.

You work out the **total magnification** by **multiplying** the magnifications of eyepiece and objective. An eyepiece with 10 times magnification and an objective with 40 times magnification give 10 times 40, that is **400 times**. Because of the wavelength of light, with a light microscope only images magnified at most about **1,000 to 2,000 times** are useful. For even smaller things you need an **electron microscope**.

You always begin with the **lowest magnification**. In this way you see the largest section and find the interesting spot more easily. With the large **coarse focus** you first set an approximately sharp image. After that you set it exactly sharp with the **fine focus**. Only then do you switch to stronger objectives. With the diaphragm you adjust brightness and **contrast**.

The light microscope shows the image **upside down** and **reversed left to right**. If you push the specimen to the left, the image moves to the **right**. So the image always moves in the opposite direction. At the beginning this is unfamiliar, but with a little practice you quickly find your way.

In the 17th century researchers began to look into the tiny world with lenses. The Englishman **Robert Hooke** looked at thin slices of cork and called the small chambers **cells**. The Dutchman **Antoni van Leeuwenhoek**, with lenses he ground himself, was one of the first to see tiny living things in water. Since then the microscope has been indispensable in biology.

gewusst: The word cell for the building blocks of living things comes from Robert Hooke and his look at cork.
A light microscope cannot magnify as much as you like, because light itself sets a limit.

teile.einleitung: Paclitaxel is an important drug against cancer. It originally comes from the bark of a tree, the Pacific yew. Its story shows how plants can help medicine.
wichtigste: Paclitaxel was discovered in the bark of the Pacific yew.
It is a cytostatic drug, that is, an agent that inhibits cell division.
Paclitaxel stabilises the microtubules and so blocks the division of cancer cells.
Today it is made semi-synthetically from a precursor obtained from yew needles.
Chemically, paclitaxel is a diterpene and belongs to the taxanes.
A common side effect is hair loss.

abschnitte.titel: An active substance from the yew
abschnitte.text: In the 1960s the US National Cancer Institute searched many plants for substances against cancer. In the bark of the **Pacific yew** (Taxus brevifolia) an especially effective substance was found. This yew grows in the west of North America. The active substance was given the name **paclitaxel**, and it also became known under the trade name Taxol.

When a cell divides, it builds a spindle apparatus from fine tubes, the **microtubules**. This pulls the genetic material apart into two daughter cells. Normally the microtubules are constantly built up and broken down. Paclitaxel prevents the breakdown, the spindle freezes, and the division gets stuck. Because cancer cells divide especially fast, it hits them hard.

Paclitaxel is a **cytostatic drug**, that is, an agent of chemotherapy. It is used, among other things, for breast cancer, ovarian cancer and lung cancer. Unfortunately it also hits healthy cells that divide quickly, for example in the hair roots. That is why **hair loss** is a common side effect. After the treatment the hair usually grows back.

abschnitte.titel: Where the substance comes from today
abschnitte.text: The bark contains very little paclitaxel, and a tree that has been stripped dies. For a single treatment the bark of several trees would have been needed. So other ways were sought. Today a precursor is obtained from the **needles of the European yew** and chemically converted into paclitaxel. This is called **semi-synthetic**. The needles grow back, and the tree stays alive.

Paclitaxel belongs to the **terpenes**, more precisely to the **diterpenes** with a framework of 20 carbon atoms. This basic framework is called the taxane framework. The whole group of active substances is called **taxanes**, after the Latin name of the yew, Taxus. A close relative is the drug **docetaxel**.

gewusst: The European yew also grows in Swiss forests. Almost all its parts are poisonous to humans.
In the 1990s chemists managed to build paclitaxel completely in the laboratory. For production, however, this route is far too costly.

teile.einleitung: New plant varieties come about through breeding. In mutation breeding, random changes in the genetic material are deliberately triggered, and then plants with useful features are looked for. In this way thousands of varieties have been produced since the 20th century.
wichtigste: In mutation breeding, changes in the genetic material are triggered with radiation or chemicals.
A commonly used chemical is ethyl methanesulfonate, EMS for short.
Lewis Stadler showed in 1928 that X-rays trigger mutations in barley.
The FAO and the IAEA keep a database of over 3,000 mutation varieties.
The mutations arise at random, so many plants have to be searched through.
In the EU and Switzerland, such plants are exempt from the regulation of genetic engineering.

abschnitte.text: A **mutation** is a change in the genetic material. In nature, mutations happen by themselves, but rarely. In **mutation breeding**, seeds or parts of plants are treated with **radiation** such as X-rays or gamma rays. You can also use **mutagenic chemicals**, that is, substances that trigger mutations. **Ethyl methanesulfonate**, **EMS** for short, is often used.

The American researcher **Lewis Stadler** showed in **1928** that **X-rays** trigger mutations in plants such as **barley**. After that, breeders around the world began to use the method. Some research stations set up so-called **gamma gardens**. These are test fields with a **radiation source** in the middle. The plants all around are irradiated over a long period.

The food organisation **FAO** and the International Atomic Energy Agency, the **IAEA**, together keep a database of **over 3,000 mutation varieties**. These include the grapefruit varieties **Star Ruby** and **Rio Red** with dark red flesh. The barley variety **Golden Promise** came about through irradiation. For a long time it was especially important for **Scotch whisky**.

abschnitte.titel: Like looking for a needle in a haystack
abschnitte.text: The biggest disadvantage of the method: the mutations arise **at random**. You do not know beforehand which genes will change. Most changes are useless or harmful. That is why breeders have to grow and search through **very many plants** until they find one with a good feature. With the newer **genome editing**, on the other hand, a particular spot in the genetic material can be changed on purpose.

Plants from classical mutation breeding are legally **not** counted in the **EU** and in **Switzerland** as genetically modified organisms that have to be labelled. They are **exempt from the regulation of genetic engineering**, because the method has been used for a long time. New breeding methods such as genome editing, on the other hand, are discussed politically, and opinions about them differ.

gewusst: Many people eat food from mutation varieties without knowing it, because it does not have to be labelled.
Irradiated seeds are not radioactive after the treatment.

teile.einleitung: A forest is much more than a collection of trees. It is an ecosystem in which plants, animals, fungi and tiny soil creatures live closely together. In Switzerland the forest even protects whole villages from avalanches.
wichtigste: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered by forest.
The forest is an ecosystem of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria that depend on one another.
Protective forests in the mountains protect against avalanches and rockfall.
If forest is exceptionally cleared in Switzerland, replacement forest has to be created in the same area.
The concept of sustainability originally comes from forestry.
In principle every forest in Switzerland may be entered, even if it belongs to a private person.
Forests store carbon, filter water and produce oxygen.

abschnitte.text: An **ecosystem** is a community together with its habitat. In the forest it includes trees, shrubs, mosses, birds, roe deer, beetles, fungi and bacteria. All of them are linked with one another by **food chains**. Plants make food with sunlight, and animals eat plants or other animals.

A forest is built like a house with several storeys. At the very bottom lies the ground layer with leaves, fungi and worms, above it follow the moss layer, the herb layer and the shrub layer. At the very top the treetops form the **tree layer**. Each storey has its own light, its own moisture and its own inhabitants.

In autumn leaves fall to the ground, and trees die at some point. **Decomposers** such as earthworms, woodlice, fungi and bacteria turn this dead material into fertile **humus**. From it the plants take their nutrients again. In this way almost nothing is lost in the forest.

About half of the Swiss forest has a protective function. A dense **protective forest** holds snow on the slope, slows rolling stones and prevents landslides. Without it many mountain villages, roads and railway lines would be at risk. Looking after it is therefore an important task for foresters.

In 1713 the Saxon mining official Hans Carl von Carlowitz wrote that you should fell only as much timber as can grow back. From this the term **sustainability** arose. In Switzerland strict forest protection has applied since the 19th century, now regulated in the **Forest Act**. Clearing is in principle forbidden, and for exceptions, replacement forest must be planted in the same area.

The Swiss Civil Code allows everyone to enter forest and pasture, even if they belong to private persons. This **right of access** applies, however, with consideration: you stay quiet, leave no rubbish behind and do not disturb wild animals. The most common tree species in Switzerland are spruce and beech. The forest supplies timber, clean drinking water and recreation for millions of people.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living things and their habitat that together form a system.
Dark, fertile soil made of decomposed plant remains.
A forest that protects people and buildings from natural hazards.
The permanent removal of forest in order to use the area in another way.
Using only as much as can grow back.

gewusst: In a handful of forest soil live more living things than there are people on Earth.
The forest area of Switzerland has been growing for many years, mainly in the Alps, because pastures are no longer used.
Many trees are linked through their roots with fungal threads and exchange substances through them.

teile.einleitung: Table, chair, bed and shelf: in every home there is **furniture**. A lot of it is made of **wood**, a raw material from the forest. Wood is sturdy, warm and easy to work.
wichtigste: A chair has a seat and a back.
A table usually has four legs and a top.
Anyone who builds furniture from wood is a joiner.
Pieces of wood are joined firmly with screws and glue.
Oil, wax or varnish protect wooden furniture and make it shine.
Books stand on the shelf; clothes and things lie in the drawers of a chest of drawers.

abschnitte.text: For sitting there is the **chair** with a seat and a back. At the **table**, with its top and usually four legs, we eat, play and learn. For sleeping we need a **bed**. Books are usually kept on the **shelf**. A **chest of drawers** has drawers in which you can put clothes or toys.

Different kinds of wood are used for furniture. **Spruce** and **fir** are pale and rather soft. **Beech** and **oak** are hard and very sturdy. **Walnut** has a beautiful, dark pattern. In Switzerland a lot of wood grows, and it is also used for furniture. Wood is a **renewable raw material**, because new trees keep growing in the forest.

Anyone who builds furniture from wood is a **joiner**, called a **“Schreiner”** in Swiss German. In Germany a joiner is also called a “Tischler”. In the workshop stands a **workbench**, a sturdy work table. There wood is sawn, planed and sanded. The pieces of wood are joined with **screws and glue**, and sometimes with wooden dowels. Today machines that cut very precisely help with this too.

Untreated wood soon gets stained and soaks up water. That is why furniture is protected with **oil, wax or varnish**. Oil and wax sink into the wood and bring out the grain beautifully. Varnish forms a hard layer on the surface. In this way wooden furniture stays beautiful for many years and can even be handed down.

gewusst: The lines in wood are called the grain. They come from the tree’s annual rings.
Good wooden furniture can be repaired and sanded down again if it is scratched.

teile.einleitung: The weather is not the same everywhere, even when places lie close together. In a hollow, on the wall of a house or in a wood, there is often a climate all of its own. This is called a microclimate.
wichtigste: A microclimate is the climate in a small space, such as a garden, a wood or a street.
On clear nights, cold air collects in hollows, where there is often ground frost.
A large lake smooths out temperature swings on its shore.
In a wood it is cooler and damper on summer days than in an open field.
Between tall buildings the wind is speeded up: the funnel effect.
Weather stations usually measure the air temperature 2 metres above the ground.

abschnitte.text: The **microclimate** describes temperature, humidity, wind and sun in a small space. It depends on how the ground is shaped, what grows on it and which buildings stand there. A south-facing slope is warmer than a north-facing one. A dark asphalt square heats up more than a meadow. So that measurements can be compared, **weather stations** usually measure the air temperature **2 metres** above the ground.

Cold air is heavier than warm air. On clear, still nights the ground cools strongly, and the cold air flows downhill like water. In **hollows** and **depressions** it collects into a **cold-air pool**. There you often get **ground frost**, while it stays milder on the slope above. A well-known example is the high valley of **La Brévine** in the Jura, which is called the “Siberia of Switzerland”.

Water warms up slowly and cools down slowly. A large **lake** therefore makes the climate on its shore more even. In **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva, vines grow on steep terraces. It is said that **three suns** work there: the sun in the sky, its light reflected from the **lake**, and the warmth of the **walls**. Lavaux has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

In a **wood**, the tree crowns give shade, and the leaves give off water. That is why it is **cooler and damper** there on summer days than in a field. In the garden, people use the microclimate on purpose. Fruit trees are often trained as **espaliers** on a **south-facing wall**. The wall stores heat in the day and gives it off again at night, so the fruit ripens better.

Cities are often warmer than the land around them, because concrete and asphalt store a lot of heat. This is called a **heat island**. Between tall buildings the wind is squeezed together and so gets faster. This is called the **funnel effect**. Trees, parks and fountains help to cool the city on hot days.

gewusst: On the Glattalp in the canton of Schwyz, in a hollow full of cold air, about minus 52 degrees was measured in the winter of 1991.
The difference between a sunny south-facing slope and a shady north-facing slope can decide the plant life of a whole valley.

teile.einleitung: Meteorology is the science of the weather and of the Earth’s envelope of air. Meteorologists measure temperature, wind and rain and predict what the weather will be like in the coming days. Without them we would not know whether we need an umbrella tomorrow.
wichtigste: Meteorology is the study of the weather and of the processes in the atmosphere.
A meteorologist forecasts the weather on television, for example.
Among other things, temperature, air pressure, humidity, wind and precipitation are measured.
Weather forecasts are calculated today with high-performance computers.
In Switzerland, the federal office MeteoSwiss is responsible for weather and climate.
The further into the future a forecast reaches, the less certain it becomes.
Meteorology also warns of dangers such as storms, thunderstorms or heat.

abschnitte.text: **Meteorology** investigates what happens in the Earth’s envelope of air. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “the study of things in the air”. Over 2,300 years ago, the Greek scholar Aristotle already wrote a book about clouds, rain and wind. Meteorology deals with the weather of today and tomorrow, **climatology** with the weather over many decades.

For a good forecast you need many measurements. A thermometer measures the temperature, a **barometer** the air pressure, a hygrometer the humidity and an anemometer the wind speed. Weather balloons rise to over 30 kilometres and take measurements on the way. Weather satellites photograph the clouds from space, and weather radars detect rain and hail.

All the measurements from around the world are fed into **weather models**. These are computer programs that use the laws of physics to calculate how air, heat and moisture move. This takes extremely fast supercomputers. Then experts look at the results and write the forecast from them. For the next two to three days, forecasts are usually quite reliable today.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, is responsible for weather and climate. It runs a dense network of automatic measuring stations and five weather radars, including on the Albis and on Monte Lema. In Payerne, weather balloons are released every day. The weather station on the Säntis has been taking measurements since 1882.

Meteorologists warn of severe weather such as thunderstorms, hail, storms, heavy rain or heatwaves. In Switzerland the warnings have five levels. Aircraft, ships, farming and ski resorts also need accurate weather data. In the mountains, the **avalanche warning** is closely tied to the weather forecast.

begriffe.erklaerung: A prediction of what the weather will be like in the future.
An instrument for measuring air pressure.
A computer program that calculates how the weather will develop.
A warm, dry wind that blows down the slopes into Alpine valleys.

gewusst: A weather balloon gets bigger and bigger at great height until it bursts.
The weather station on the Säntis has been taking measurements for over 140 years.
The barometer was invented in 1643 by the Italian Evangelista Torricelli.

teile.einleitung: In nature, many species live closely together. When both partners benefit from the relationship, it is called **mutualism**. Such partnerships exist between animals, plants, fungi and tiny micro-organisms.
wichtigste: Mutualism is a relationship to the benefit of both partners.
Cows can use grass only thanks to micro-organisms in their rumen.
In mycorrhiza, plants swap sugar for water and mineral salts from the fungus.
Nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air for clover, peas and other legumes.
Cleaner wrasse free larger fish of parasites.
If the relationship is vital to survival, it is called obligate mutualism.

abschnitte.text: The word **mutualism** comes from the Latin “mutuus”, which means “mutual”. Both partners give something and get something back, for example food, protection or help with spreading. If the relationship is essential for the partners’ lives, it is called **obligate mutualism**. If it is only useful but not essential, it is called **facultative mutualism**. Mutualism is a form of symbiosis in the wider sense.

Cows, sheep and goats are **ruminants**. Their biggest part of the stomach is the **rumen**. There live countless bacteria and single-celled organisms. They break down the **cellulose** in grass and hay, which vertebrates cannot digest themselves. In return, the micro-organisms get a warm habitat with constantly new food. Without these helpers, the many cows on Swiss alps could hardly make use of the grass.

Many forest trees live together with fungi. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The fine fungal threads wrap around the roots and supply water and minerals such as **phosphate**. In return the tree gives off **carbohydrates** from photosynthesis. Clover, peas and beans have small nodules on their roots with **nodule bacteria**. These make nitrogen from the air usable for the plant and get sugar in return.

On the coral reef there are proper **cleaning stations**. There the small **cleaner wrasse** waits for customers. Larger fish come by and let it eat parasites and dead skin off their bodies. Even predatory fish open their mouths and let the cleaner in. The cleaner fish gets food, and the big fish is made clean and healthy.

Certain **acacias** in Central America have hollow thorns in which ants live. The plant also supplies them with food. In return, the ants attack plant-eaters and even remove plants that take light away from the acacia. The **yucca** is pollinated by the **yucca moth**. The moth brings the pollen deliberately to the stigma and lays its eggs in the flower. Its caterpillars eat part of the seeds, and the rest of the seeds ripen. The two depend on each other.

gewusst: Lichens are a partnership made up of a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium.
Bees and flowers also form a mutualism: the bee gets nectar, and the flower is pollinated.

teile.einleitung: A monsoon forest is a tropical forest with a rainy season and a dry season. In the rainy season it is dense and green, in the dry season many trees stand bare. It is especially widespread in South and Southeast Asia.
wichtigste: In a monsoon forest, the rainy season and the dry season take turns.
Many trees drop their leaves in the dry season to save water.
It is also called a rain-green forest.
The teak tree is a typical tree of monsoon forests.
The tiger lives in the monsoon forests of India.
The word “monsoon” comes from Arabic.

abschnitte.text: The **monsoon** is a wind over a large area that changes its direction over the course of the year. In summer it brings damp air from the sea and heavy rainfall. In winter it blows from the land and is dry. The word comes from **Arabic** and means roughly “season”. The monsoon shapes the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

In the **rainy season**, the trees put out new leaves, and the forest is lushly green. In the **dry season**, many trees drop their leaves. In this way they lose less water through their leaves. Because the forest has leaves mainly in the rainy season, it is also called a **rain-green forest**. It is lighter and less rich in species than the always-damp rainforest.

Monsoon forests are especially widespread in **South and Southeast Asia**, for example in India, Myanmar and Thailand. Similar forests with a rainy and a dry season are also found in parts of Africa, South America and northern Australia. Many monsoon forests have been cleared to make room for fields, plantations and settlements.

A typical tree of the monsoon forests is the **teak tree**. Its wood is hard, heavy and very resistant to water and pests. That is why **teak** is used for ships, garden furniture and floors. Because teak wood is so sought after, it is now often grown on plantations.

In the monsoon forests of **India** lives the **tiger**, the biggest cat in the world. Asian elephants, leopards, deer and many species of monkey are also at home there. The animals have to adapt to the change of seasons. In the dry season they often gather at waterholes.

gewusst: In some areas of India, almost the whole year’s rain falls in a few months of the monsoon.
Teak wood contains natural oils that protect it from rot.

teile.einleitung: A monoculture is the growing of only a single plant species over a large area, often for many years. In this way huge amounts of maize, wheat or palm oil can be harvested efficiently. But monocultures also have big disadvantages for soil, animals and plants.
wichtigste: A monoculture is the growing of a single plant species over a large area.
Examples are huge fields of maize or soya, oil palm plantations and pure spruce forests.
Monocultures can be worked and harvested easily with machines.
Pests and diseases can spread very quickly in monocultures.
The soil loses nutrients when it is always used in the same way.
Monocultures offer a home to only a few animals and plants.
Crop rotation and companion planting are alternatives to monoculture.

abschnitte.text: The word **monoculture** is put together from the Greek “mono” for alone and “culture” for growing. It means that only a single plant species grows in a field or a forest. Often the same plant is even grown in the same place year after year. In the USA there are maize fields that reach to the horizon.

Monocultures are easy to farm. All the plants are sown, fertilised and harvested at the same time, so large **machines** can be used. In this way a lot of food can be produced with little work. A uniform harvest is also convenient for trade.

In a monoculture, **pests** and disease-causing organisms find plenty of food and spread rapidly. That is why a lot of pesticides are often needed. The soil is drained of nutrients in a one-sided way, and without a protective plant cover, rain and wind can carry the soil away, which is called **erosion**. There is also little habitat for insects, birds and wild plants.

Between 1845 and 1849, a fungal disease, **potato blight**, destroyed almost the whole potato harvest in Ireland. Because many people lived almost only on potatoes, a severe famine followed. Bananas have this problem too: the once popular variety Gros Michel was almost wiped out by a fungal disease in the 20th century. Today the Cavendish variety is also under threat.

For palm oil, huge areas of rainforest were cleared in Indonesia and Malaysia and replaced by **plantations**. In Brazil, soya beans grow over vast areas, mainly as animal feed. As a result, orangutans and many other species lose their habitat. Pure spruce forests are also monocultures and suffer badly from storms and bark beetles.

In **crop rotation**, the plant species in a field is changed every year, for example wheat, then potatoes, then clover. In companion planting, several species grow side by side at the same time. In Switzerland, farms that receive direct payments have to follow a regulated crop rotation. The rather small fields make the Swiss landscape more varied than many farming landscapes abroad.

begriffe.erklaerung: Growing only one plant species over a large area.
The yearly change of the plants grown in a field.
The wearing away of soil by wind and water.
A large farm on which usually only one crop grows.

gewusst: Almost all the bananas in the supermarket belong to the same variety and are nearly identical genetically.
Because of the famine in Ireland, over a million people emigrated, many to America.
Even a perfect English lawn is really a small monoculture.

teile.einleitung: Soil is the basis for plants, animals and our food. So that we know how it is doing, Switzerland has the **National Soil Monitoring Network**, **NABO** for short. For decades it has regularly measured the condition of soils.
wichtigste: NABO is run by Agroscope, the federal centre of competence for agricultural research.
It has been measuring the condition of Swiss soils since the mid-1980s.
The network comprises a good 100 permanent observation sites.
The sites are sampled again every 5 years.
On grassland with a lot of farmyard manure, copper and zinc have built up.
Cadmium reaches arable soils mainly through mineral phosphate fertiliser.
The soil samples are kept in an archive.

abschnitte.text: The National Soil Monitoring Network is run by **Agroscope**, the federal agricultural research institute. It works on behalf of the Federal Office for the Environment and the Federal Office for Agriculture. NABO has been measuring the condition of Swiss soils **since the mid-1980s**. In this way changes can be followed over many decades. This is important, because soils often change only very slowly.

The network includes **a good 100 permanent observation sites** all over Switzerland. They lie on fields, meadows, pastures, in forests and in other places. These sites are sampled again **every 5 years**. Experts take soil samples at precisely fixed spots. In the laboratory they then examine, for example, heavy metals, nutrients and the humus content.

NABO has shown that on **grassland sites** with a lot of **farmyard manure**, such as pig slurry, the heavy metals **copper and zinc** have built up. These substances come from animal feed and reach the meadows through the slurry. The heavy metal **cadmium** reaches arable soils mainly through **mineral phosphate fertiliser**. Heavy metals do not break down in the soil and stay there for a very long time.

In Switzerland the **Ordinance on Soil Pollution** sets the guide values for pollutants in soil. If such a value is exceeded, the authorities look more closely. NABO keeps its soil samples in an **archive**. In this way they can be **examined again later with new methods**, for example for substances that cannot even be measured today.

gewusst: A handful of healthy soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
It often takes hundreds of years for a soil layer of a few centimetres to form anew.

teile.einleitung: When leaves, roots and dead animals rot in the soil, they do not simply disappear. Tiny living things break them down into simple substances. In soil science, this process is called mineralisation.
wichtigste: Mineralisation is the breakdown of organic matter into inorganic compounds.
Bacteria and fungi in the soil do this work.
In the process, nutrients become available to plants again.
In mineralisation with oxygen, the carbon escapes as carbon dioxide.
It runs fastest in warm, damp, well-aerated soil.
In waterlogged raised bogs it is held back, which is why peat forms there.

abschnitte.text: Organic matter is material that comes from living things, such as dead leaves or roots. In **mineralisation**, **micro-organisms** such as bacteria and fungi break these remains down. What is left is simple **inorganic compounds**: carbon dioxide, water, ammonium, nitrate, phosphate and other minerals. Earthworms and woodlice help by first chopping up the remains.

Plants are the **producers** in an ecosystem. They take up nutrients from the soil and build their bodies from them. When they die, mineralisation makes sure these nutrients become **available again**. Without this breakdown, the nutrients would stay locked in dead remains. The living things that do the breaking down are called **decomposers**.

When mineralisation runs with oxygen, it is called **aerobic**. The carbon from the remains then gets into the air as **carbon dioxide**. How active the micro-organisms are is therefore measured by the amount of carbon dioxide a soil gives off. This measurement is called **soil respiration**. A living soil “breathes” strongly.

Micro-organisms work best when it is **warm**, **damp** and **well aerated**. In cold, dry or very wet soils, the breakdown is slow. In **raised bogs** the ground is permanently wet, and there is no oxygen. That is why plant remains are hardly broken down there and pile up into thick **layers of peat**.

Not all remains are broken down completely. Part of them is turned into stable **humic substances**, which form the dark **humus**. This process is called **humification**. If a farmer works a lot of **straw** into the soil, it contains a lot of carbon but little nitrogen. It is said to have a **wide C/N ratio**. The micro-organisms then take nitrogen from the soil for a while, so it is missing for the plants.

gewusst: In a handful of soil live more micro-organisms than there are people on Earth.
In the peat of bogs, you sometimes find plant remains that are thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: In everyday life we call many hard fruits nuts. For botanists, though, a true nut is a very particular kind of fruit. In it the whole fruit wall turns woody, and it usually contains only one seed.
wichtigste: In a true nut, the whole fruit wall turns woody.
A true nut usually contains only one seed.
Nuts are indehiscent fruits: they do not open when ripe.
The hazelnut is a true nut.
The three-edged nuts of the beech are called beechnuts.
An acorn sits in a cup-shaped cupule.

abschnitte.text: A fruit forms from the flower and encloses the seed. In a **true nut**, the whole **fruit wall becomes hard and woody**. Inside lies usually only **one seed**. Nuts belong to the **indehiscent fruits**: they do not open by themselves when ripe. The seed is freed only when the shell breaks open or rots away.

The **hazelnut** is a prime example of a true nut. The fruits of beech and oak are also nuts. The three-edged nuts of the beech are called **beechnuts**. The acorn of the oak sits in a cup-shaped **cupule**. The sweet chestnut also forms nuts, which are enclosed in a prickly husk.

There are also smaller forms of nuts. The kernels of the **sunflower** are one-seeded fruits whose fruit wall is not fused with the seed. This form is called an **achene**. In the **cereals** such as wheat and maize, the fruit wall and seed coat are firmly fused together. This nut-like fruit is called a **caryopsis**. A grain of cereal is therefore, botanically, a whole fruit.

Many well-known “nuts” are something else, botanically speaking. The **walnut** and the almond are really stone fruits, like cherries, except that in them the kernel is the part you eat. The **peanut** is a legume and related to peas and beans. The **coconut** is also a stone fruit. In everyday speech, though, we call all these fruits nuts.

gewusst: Squirrels bury hazelnuts as a store and do not find them all again, which is how new hazel bushes grow.
The strawberry also bears many tiny nutlets on its surface.

teile.einleitung: Firs, spruces and pines belong to a very old group of plants: the **gymnosperms**. Their name reveals a special feature. Their ovules are not enclosed in an ovary, but lie open.
wichtigste: In gymnosperms, the ovules lie open on scales.
Gymnosperms include conifers, ginkgo, cycads and Welwitschia.
Most conifers are pollinated by the wind.
Ginkgo and cycads still have sperm cells with flagella that swim.
The yew is poisonous almost everywhere, except for its red seed covering.
The Swiss stone pine has needles in fives and edible seeds.

abschnitte.text: In flowering plants such as the apple tree, the ovules are hidden in an **ovary**. In the **gymnosperms**, on the other hand, they lie **open on scales**, for example on the scales of a cone. That is where the name comes from, “gymnosperm” meaning “naked seed”. Gymnosperms do not make true fruits. The **nutritive tissue** in the seed of a conifer is made of the **haploid female gametophyte**, that is, tissue with a single set of chromosomes.

Most **conifers** are pollinated **by the wind**. In spring their male cones release huge amounts of pollen. In May there is sometimes yellow dust on cars and puddles. The wind carries the pollen grains to the female cones. **Ginkgo and cycads** are especially ancient: they still have **sperm cells with flagella that swim**.

The **cycads** look like small palms on the outside, but belong to the gymnosperms. The **ginkgo** from China has fan-shaped leaves and is seen as a living fossil. A particularly strange plant is **Welwitschia** from the **Namib Desert** in Africa. Throughout its whole life it makes only **two leaves**. These keep growing, are shredded by the wind and lie like ribbons on the sand.

In Switzerland many conifers grow, such as spruce, silver fir, larch and pine. The **yew** is **poisonous** in almost all its parts. Only the **red seed covering** around the seed is not poisonous, but the seed inside is. The **Swiss stone pine** grows high up in the Alps. It has **needles in fives** in bundles and **edible seeds**, the stone pine nuts. The nutcracker hides these seeds as a store and so helps the Swiss stone pine to spread.

gewusst: Some Welwitschia plants are probably over 1,000 years old.
Gymnosperms existed long before the first flowering plants; in the time of the dinosaurs they were widespread.

teile.einleitung: Macroinvertebrates, known in science as macrozoobenthos, are the small invertebrate animals on the bed of streams, rivers and lakes that can still be seen with the naked eye. They tell us a lot about how clean a body of water is.
wichtigste: They include insect larvae, snails, mussels, worms and small crustaceans.
Mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies make up the EPT taxa.
Many of their larvae need clean, oxygen-rich water.
Caddisfly larvae build a case out of small stones or plant parts.
The Swiss index IBCH assesses bodies of water using these animals.
The freshwater shrimp is a crustacean and chops up fallen leaves.

abschnitte.text: The word is put together from Greek: **makro** means large, **zoon** animal and **benthos** bed. It means invertebrate animals that you can see without a microscope and that live on and in the **bed of a body of water**. They include **insect larvae**, snails, mussels, worms and **small crustaceans**. You find them under stones, in sand and among water plants.

Three groups of insects are seen as indicators of good water quality: **mayflies**, **stoneflies** and **caddisflies**. Their scientific names Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera and Trichoptera give the abbreviation **EPT**. Many of their larvae need clean, oxygen-rich water. Stonefly larvae have **two** tail filaments, while most mayfly larvae have three. Caddisfly larvae glue sand, small stones or plant parts together with silk to make a **case** that protects their soft abdomen.

The animals feed in different ways. The **shredders** eat leaves that have fallen into the water. They include the **freshwater shrimp** Gammarus and some caddisfly larvae. The freshwater shrimp is a **crustacean** and, despite its name, is not related to fleas. Shredders make the energy in the leaves of the trees along the bank available to the whole body of water.

Many animals that live on the bed let go of it and drift downstream with the current. This drifting with the water is called **drift**. It happens mostly **at night**, when fish find it harder to see the animals. In this way the animals spread out through the body of water.

In Switzerland there is the index **IBCH**, the **Indice Biologique Suisse**. It is part of the federal government’s **modular stepwise procedure** for investigating bodies of water. Experts work out which **families** of invertebrates living on the bed are present in a sample. From this they calculate how good the condition of the water is.

gewusst: Some mayflies live as adult insects for only a few hours to days, but as larvae they live in the water for much longer.
The larvae often spend most of their lives in the stream.

teile.einleitung: A nutrient-poor meadow is a meadow with poor soil that is hardly fertilised. Precisely for that reason it is especially colourful and full of different flowers and insects.
wichtigste: A nutrient-poor meadow gets little or no fertiliser.
It is mostly mown only once or twice a year.
The grass stays low because the soil has few nutrients.
That is why many species of flower have room, also rare orchids.
Especially dry nutrient-poor meadows are called dry meadows.
Switzerland protects the most important dry meadows in an inventory.

abschnitte.text: A **nutrient-poor meadow** is hardly or not at all **fertilised**. That is why its soil has few **nutrients**. Plants need nutrients to grow, so the grass grows slowly and stays low. Because no tall grass overgrows everything, many different flowers have enough light and room. Nutrient-poor meadows are therefore very **rich in species** and colourful.

On a nutrient-poor meadow little fodder grows. It is mostly mown only **once or twice a year**. If it is mown only after flowering, the flowers can form seeds. In this way they come back the next year.

Nutrient-poor meadows are often found on **sunny, dry slopes**. Steep slopes are hard to fertilise and farm. That is why nutrient-poor meadows were often preserved there. Especially dry nutrient-poor meadows are called **dry meadows**. There many special plants and insects live, such as butterflies, grasshoppers and wild bees.
In Switzerland wild **orchids** also grow. Many of them need nutrient-poor meadows. They are rare and therefore **protected**. You may not pick or dig them up.

Many dry meadows have disappeared in recent decades, for example through fertilising or building. The **Confederation** has entered the most important dry meadows and dry pastures in an **inventory**. In this way the rare plants and animals are to be protected. Farmers receive payments if they look after such meadows gently.

gewusst: On a single nutrient-poor meadow, many dozens of different plant species can grow.
If you fertilised a nutrient-poor meadow heavily, many of its flowers would disappear in time.

teile.einleitung: An ecosystem is a community of living things together with their habitat. Plants, animals, fungi and bacteria depend on one another and on soil, water, light and climate. A forest, a lake or a coral reef are examples of ecosystems.
wichtigste: An ecosystem consists of a community and its habitat.
The community is called the biocoenosis, the habitat the biotope.
Examples of ecosystems are forest, meadow, lake, moor, desert and coral reef.
In an ecosystem, energy flows from the sun through plants to animals.
Nutrients are used again and again in cycles.
Ecosystems can regulate themselves, but can also get out of balance.
Healthy ecosystems supply humans with clean water, food and fresh air.

abschnitte.text: An **ecosystem** is a piece of nature in which living things and their environment work closely together. It consists of two parts: the **biotope**, that is, the habitat with soil, water and climate, and the biocoenosis, the community of all plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. The British researcher Arthur Tansley introduced the term in 1935. An ecosystem can be as small as a puddle or as big as an ocean.

Ecosystems on land include forests, meadows, moors, deserts and the tundra. In water there are lakes, rivers, seas and coral reefs. In Switzerland you find very different ecosystems in a small space, from the riverside woodland on the Aare through alpine pastures to the glacier. A town or a field is also an ecosystem, one that is strongly shaped by humans.

Almost all ecosystems are driven by the **sun**. Plants use the light and make nutrients, plant-eaters eat the plants, meat-eaters the plant-eaters. Fungi and bacteria break down dead living things and give the substances back to the soil. In this way **cycles** arise, such as the carbon or the water cycle, in which nothing is lost.

An ecosystem can usually balance out small changes. If there are many mice, for example, foxes and owls find more food and multiply, after which the number of mice falls again. Big disturbances such as fires, storms, pollution or introduced species can, however, change the **balance** greatly. Afterwards the system often recovers only slowly.

Ecosystems provide many services for us without our paying for them. Forests filter drinking water, store carbon and protect against avalanches. Insects pollinate fruit trees and vegetables. Moors and floodplains hold back water in floods. These services are called **ecosystem services**.

When species die out, links are missing in the web of life. That is why protecting **biodiversity** is so important. In Switzerland there are protected areas for this, such as the Swiss National Park in the Engadine, where nature has been left to itself since 1914. Small things help too, for example a flower meadow in the garden or a pile of branches for hedgehogs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A community of living things together with their habitat.
The habitat with soil, water and climate.
All living things that live together in a habitat.
The variety of species, habitats and genes.

gewusst: Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor but are home to about a quarter of all marine species.
The human gut also has its own small ecosystem of trillions of bacteria.
The Swiss National Park is the oldest national park in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: High above the Earth, a layer of ozone protects us from harmful rays of the sun. Over Antarctica this layer is strongly thinned every spring. This hole in the protective shield is called the ozone hole.
wichtigste: The ozone hole is a strong thinning of the ozone layer, mainly over Antarctica.
It occurs every year in the southern spring, that is, from about September to November.
It was caused mainly by chlorofluorocarbons, CFCs for short.
British researchers made the ozone hole known in 1985.
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 banned the harmful substances step by step.
The ozone layer is recovering slowly and should largely recover by about the middle of this century.
The fight against the ozone hole is regarded as a great success of worldwide environmental protection.

abschnitte.text: The **ozone hole** is not a real hole, but an area where much less ozone is present than normal. It lies in the **stratosphere**, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground. Over Antarctica it is sometimes bigger than the whole of North America. Over the Arctic, too, the ozone layer becomes thinner in some years, but mostly less strongly.

The main culprits are **CFCs**, artificial gases that used to be in spray cans, fridges and foams. They slowly rise as far as the stratosphere. There sunlight releases chlorine, which destroys ozone. A single chlorine atom can break down thousands of ozone molecules.

In the Antarctic winter it becomes extremely cold at height, below minus 78 degrees. Then **polar stratospheric clouds** form, on which the chemical reactions run especially well. When the sun returns in September, a great deal of ozone is broken down in a short time. A strong whirl of winds stops air rich in ozone from flowing in.

The chemists Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland researched how substances destroy ozone. For this they received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry in 1995. The researchers Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey published their measurements over Antarctica in 1985. Satellite images then confirmed the huge extent.

In 1987 the states agreed in the **Montreal Protocol** to reduce the production of CFCs sharply and later to ban it. Today every country in the world has signed it, Switzerland too. Since then the amount of these substances in the air has slowly been falling. Because CFCs last a very long time, recovery nevertheless takes decades.

Less ozone means more **UV radiation** at the ground. It can cause sunburn, skin cancer and eye damage and also harms plants and plankton. People in South America, Australia and New Zealand were especially affected. In Switzerland too the rule holds: sun cream, a hat and sunglasses protect against UV rays.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas made of three oxygen atoms that absorbs UV rays.
Artificial gases that used to be in spray cans and fridges and destroy ozone.
The layer of air about 15 to 50 kilometres above the Earth.
A worldwide treaty of 1987 to protect the ozone layer.

gewusst: The researchers at first did not trust their readings, because they were so unusually low.
The Montreal Protocol was the first environmental treaty that all states on Earth joined.
Many CFCs are also strong greenhouse gases, so banning them helps the climate too.

teile.einleitung: A squirrel on a branch, a butterfly on a flower: there is a lot to photograph in nature. In **nature photography** you need patience and a good eye. Most important of all, though, is that animals and plants are not disturbed.
wichtigste: You photograph animals quietly and from a distance.
With the zoom you bring an animal closer without going nearer.
Early in the morning the light is soft and many animals are awake.
If an animal gets nervous, you walk away slowly.
Very close photos of small things are called macro photos.
To stop blurred photos, hold the camera steady or prop it up.
A flash frightens animals, so it is better to leave it off.

abschnitte.text: When photographing animals you behave **quietly and from a distance**. Otherwise animals flee or leave their young alone. If a bird gets **nervous**, calls loudly or flutters up, you **walk away slowly**. A good photo is never more important than the animal’s welfare. You stay on the paths and **do not walk into a flower meadow**, or you trample the plants.

With the **zoom** you bring an animal closer in the photo without going closer yourself. Many nature photographers use long lenses for this. Some hide in a **camouflage tent**. In it they wait quietly until animals come by. A car, a hedge or an observation hut can also serve as a hide.

Nature photographers like to be out **early in the morning**. Then the **light is soft** and warm, and **many animals are awake** and looking for food. Evening is also a good time. At midday the sun is harsh and makes hard shadows. With animals it is better to do without a **flash**, because **the bright flash frightens** them.

Photos of very small things such as insects, dewdrops or parts of flowers are called **macro photos**. For these the camera goes right up close. Even a small movement makes the picture blurry. To stop **blurred photos**, it helps to **hold the camera steady** or **prop it up**, for example on a stone, a rucksack or a tripod. Breathing out slowly as you press the button also helps.

gewusst: In Switzerland special rules often apply in protected areas, such as a requirement to stay on paths or a ban on drones.
Many nature photographers wait for hours for a single good picture.

teile.einleitung: Every flower has a **pistil** in the middle. Its very top is called the **stigma**. It is the landing place for pollen and so an important part of the flower.
wichtigste: The stigma is the top tip of the pistil and catches the pollen.
Many stigmas are sticky so that the pollen stays put.
Wind-pollinated grasses mostly have feathery stigmas.
A pollen tube grows from a pollen grain on the stigma.
Saffron consists of dried stigmas, and one flower has three stigma branches.
Saffron is harvested in Mund in the Valais.
The threads at the top of a young corn cob are styles with stigmas.

abschnitte.text: The **pistil** has three parts: the **ovary** at the bottom, the **style** in the middle and the **stigma** at the top. The stigma **catches the pollen** that insects or the wind bring. In many flowers it is **sticky**, **so that the pollen stays put**. Only pollen of the right plant species can germinate properly on the stigma.

Grasses and cereals are pollinated by the **wind**. Their stigmas mostly look **feathery**. They have many fine branches and a large surface. In this way they can comb pollen grains out of the air well. In **maize**, long “hairs” hang from the top of the young cob. These are **styles with stigmas**, and later a maize kernel forms at each thread.

When a pollen grain lands on a suitable stigma, it begins to germinate. A fine **pollen tube** grows. It grows down through the style as far as the ovary. There fertilisation can then take place, and seeds form. So the stigma is the start of a long journey.

The expensive spice **saffron** consists of the dried **stigmas** of the **saffron crocus**. Each flower has **three** red stigma branches. They are picked by hand in autumn. A great many flowers are needed for one gram of saffron. In Switzerland saffron is grown in **Mund** in the **Valais**. The village is known for its saffron.

Stigmas look very different depending on the plant. In the **corn poppy** the stigma sits **like a star** directly **on the ovary**. In the lily it has three parts, in many daisy family plants two. Some stigmas are smooth, others have fine hairs or papillae. Their shape always suits the way the plant is pollinated.

gewusst: By weight, saffron counts as one of the most expensive spices in the world.
In some plants the stigma can recognise whether the pollen comes from the same plant, and then rejects it.

teile.einleitung: In almost every cell of plants, animals and fungi there are tiny parts that provide energy. They are called mitochondria. They are often called the power stations of the cell.
wichtigste: Mitochondria gain energy through cellular respiration.
In the process they use up oxygen.
They make the energy carrier ATP.
Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste.
A mitochondrion is surrounded by two membranes; the inner one forms folds, the cristae.
Plant cells have mitochondria too, not only animal cells.

abschnitte.text: Every cell needs energy to grow, to move or to make substances. This energy is gained by the **mitochondria**. That is why they are often called the **power stations of the cell**. A single mitochondrion is so small that you can only see it under the microscope. A cell can contain many hundreds of them.

**Cellular respiration** takes place in the mitochondria. Sugar is broken down with **oxygen**. The energy that is released is stored by the cell in the molecule **ATP**. ATP is like a small battery that can be used anywhere in the cell. **Carbon dioxide** and **water** are produced as waste. We breathe the carbon dioxide out again with the air.

A mitochondrion is surrounded by **two membranes**. The outer one is smooth. The inner one is strongly folded; these folds are called **cristae**. The folds make the surface bigger, and there is more room for the parts that make ATP. The space inside is called the **matrix**.

Many people think plants do not need mitochondria because they carry out photosynthesis. But **plant cells** have mitochondria **just like animal cells**. In the **chloroplasts**, plants use light to make sugar. In the mitochondria they break this sugar down again to gain energy. They do this day and night.

Mitochondria have a small **genetic material** of their own, like bacteria. Researchers assume that a very long time ago they arose from bacteria that were taken into another cell. This explanation is called the **endosymbiotic theory**. Today it is seen as well supported.

gewusst: Muscle cells and heart cells contain especially many mitochondria, because they need a lot of energy.
Human red blood cells have no mitochondria.

teile.einleitung: A plant grows only as well as the scarcest nutrient allows. This rule is called the law of the minimum. It is important for farming and for understanding lakes and other ecosystems.
wichtigste: The law of the minimum says: the factor that is most lacking limits growth.
Carl Sprengel formulated it as early as 1828.
Justus von Liebig made it well known in the 19th century.
In the minimum barrel, the shortest stave stands for the limiting factor.
Besides nutrients, light, water and temperature can also be at the minimum.
In many Swiss lakes, phosphorus is the minimum factor for the growth of algae.

abschnitte.text: The agricultural scientist **Carl Sprengel** described the law of the minimum as early as **1828**. But it became well known through the chemist **Justus von Liebig**, who wrote a great deal about plant nutrition and fertiliser in the 19th century. That is why people often speak of **Liebig’s law of the minimum**. Today it is sometimes also called the law of Sprengel and Liebig.

The **minimum barrel** is used to illustrate it. A wooden barrel is made of many boards, the **staves**. Each stave stands for a growth factor. If the staves are of different lengths, the water spills over at the **shortest** one. In the same way, the scarcest factor limits how high the yield will be. A longer stave elsewhere is no use.

If a soil lacks **phosphorus** but has enough nitrogen, extra **nitrogen fertiliser** hardly brings any **extra yield**. First the missing phosphorus must be added. The researcher **Eilhard Alfred Mitscherlich** also showed that every further dose of fertiliser brings a smaller and smaller **extra yield**. For farming this means: fertilise in a targeted way and in moderation.

**Light**, **water** and **temperature** can also be at the minimum. In a desert, water usually limits growth; in a dark wood, it is often light. Victor **Shelford’s** **law of tolerance** extends the law of the minimum: not only a lack but also **too much** of a factor can limit growth, for example too much heat or too much water.

In many lakes, **phosphorus** is the factor that limits the **growth of algae**. In the 20th century, when a lot of phosphorus from waste water and agriculture got into Swiss lakes, algae grew in huge numbers there. When the algae were broken down, oxygen ran short. With sewage treatment plants and the ban on phosphate in detergents in 1986, the amount of phosphorus was greatly reduced, and many lakes recovered.

gewusst: The law of the minimum applies in cooking too: if one ingredient is missing, it is no use taking more of another.
When you fix the minimum factor, another factor often becomes the new minimum.

teile.einleitung: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland. It stretches along the southern foot of the Jura between Yverdon-les-Bains and the city of Neuchâtel. On its southern shore lies the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland.
It is about 218 square kilometres in area, around 38 kilometres long and up to 152 metres deep.
In French it is called Lac de Neuchâtel.
The cantons of Neuchâtel, Vaud, Fribourg and Bern border on it.
Together with Lake Biel and Lake Murten it forms the Three Lakes Region.
Through the Jura Water Correction, the lake level was lowered by about 2.5 metres.
On the shore many remains of pile dwellings were found, which belong to the UNESCO World Heritage.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Neuchâtel** lies in the west of Switzerland at the foot of the Jura, at about 429 metres above sea level. It is about 38 kilometres long and up to 8 kilometres wide. Its area is about 218 square kilometres, and the deepest point is at 152 metres. Lake Geneva and Lake Constance are bigger, but partly belong to France, Germany and Austria.

Important inflows are the Orbe, which flows into the lake at Yverdon as the Zihl, and the Areuse from the Jura. Through the Broye Canal the lake is linked with **Lake Murten**. Its water flows through the Zihl Canal into Lake Biel and from there on via the Aare. The three lakes together form the **Three Lakes Region**.

In the past the Seeland between the lakes was regularly flooded, and many areas were marshy. In the first **Jura Water Correction**, from 1868, the Aare was diverted into Lake Biel and new canals were built. As a result the level of Lake Neuchâtel fell by about 2.5 metres. The marshes became fertile farmland, which today is regarded as the vegetable garden of Switzerland.

When the lake level fell, many wooden piles of ancient settlements came to light on the shore. These **pile dwellings** have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage since 2011. At La Tène at the north-eastern end of the lake, many weapons and tools from the Iron Age were found. The Celtic **La Tène period** is named after this site. In the Laténium museum in Hauterive you can marvel at the finds.

On the southern shore between Yverdon and Cudrefin stretches the **Grande Cariçaie**. It is the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland, with reeds, sedge meadows and riverside woodland. Thousands of plant and animal species live here, including many rare waterbirds. In winter numerous migratory birds rest here.

On the north shore lies the city of **Neuchâtel** with its castle and old town, at the south-west end the spa town of Yverdon-les-Bains. The medieval little town of Estavayer-le-Lac also lies on the lake. Around the lake people mainly speak French. On the north shore vines grow, and in the lake whitefish and perch are caught, which appear as egli on many menus.

begriffe.erklaerung: A big building project that diverted the waters in the Seeland and prevented floods.
Houses from the Stone Age and Bronze Age that stood on piles on the lake shore.
A habitat with very wet ground, such as fen, marsh or reedy shore.
A part of the Celtic Iron Age, named after a site on Lake Neuchâtel.

gewusst: Before the Jura Water Correction, Lake Neuchâtel was almost 24 square kilometres bigger than today.
A whole epoch of European history, the La Tène period, bears the name of a place on this lake.
In a strong bise the lake can become so stormy that high waves form.

teile.einleitung: On almost every farm there is a manure heap. What smells like rubbish is very valuable for farming. Manure is a natural fertiliser for fields and gardens.
wichtigste: Manure is made of animal dung, urine and straw from the stable.
Farmers use manure to fertilise their fields.
A manure heap is warm inside, so it steams on cold days.
By hand, manure is loaded with a pitchfork.
Fresh manure is not put directly on young plants, because it is too harsh.
The scarab beetle is a beetle that shapes balls out of dung.

abschnitte.text: In the stable, **straw** lies as bedding. It soaks up the animals’ **dung** and urine. This mixture is called **manure** or **solid manure**. The liquid mixture of dung, urine and water, on the other hand, is called **slurry**. Both together are called **farmyard manure**, because they are produced right on the farm. In Switzerland the manure heap is also called a **“Miststock”**.

Manure contains important **nutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Farmers spread it on the fields with a **manure spreader**. There it is broken down by living things in the soil, and the plants take up the nutrients. Manure also improves the **humus** in the soil. By hand, manure is loaded onto the wheelbarrow with a **pitchfork**.

Inside a manure heap, countless **micro-organisms** are at work. They break down the manure and produce **heat** in the process. That is why a manure heap is warm inside. On cold days you can see **steam** rising. In the past this heat was used for **hotbeds**: under the soil of a cold frame lay fresh horse manure, which warmed the ground.

**Fresh manure** is **too harsh** for young plants. It can damage their delicate roots. That is why it is first left to stand for a few months, until it has rotted well. Gardeners like to use **horse manure**, for example for **roses**. It is loose and warms up quickly. Manure from cows, sheep or hens is also used.

A manure heap is a habitat for many animals. In summer, **flies** often buzz around it and lay their eggs there. Worms and beetles live in the manure. The **scarab beetle** shapes balls out of dung and rolls them away. Its larvae grow up inside them. In ancient Egypt this beetle was sacred as the **scarab**.

gewusst: The heat in a large manure heap can get so high that you would hardly want to leave your hand in it.
On pastures, dung beetles help to get the animals’ dung quickly into the soil.

teile.einleitung: The lotus effect is the ability of some surfaces to clean themselves with water. The most famous example is the leaf of the lotus flower, from which water and dirt simply roll off.
wichtigste: Wilhelm Barthlott from Bonn studied the lotus effect and made it known.
The basis is superhydrophobicity, an extreme water repellence.
From a contact angle of over 150 degrees, a surface counts as superhydrophobic.
Tiny bumps with wax crystals form the rough surface.
Rolling drops take dirt particles with them.
Self-cleaning facade paints use the effect.

abschnitte.text: The lotus flower, also called the **sacred lotus**, has the scientific name **Nelumbo nucifera**. It belongs to the genus **Nelumbo**. Water lilies of the genus Nymphaea look similar but belong to a different family. Although the lotus flower grows in muddy waters, its leaves stay clean.

The Bonn botanist **Wilhelm Barthlott** studied plant surfaces with the **scanning electron microscope**. In doing so he recognised how the self-cleaning works. Later he had the term “Lotus-Effect” protected as a trademark. His research disproved a widespread assumption: for a long time people believed that the **smoothest surfaces** stay cleanest. The lotus effect shows that it is precisely a **rough microstructure** that makes self-cleaning possible.

The leaf surface carries tiny **bumps**, which are in addition covered with **wax crystals** nanometres in size. This double structure greatly reduces the area that a drop of water touches. This is called **superhydrophobicity**. From a contact angle of 90 degrees a surface counts as hydrophobic, above **150 degrees** as superhydrophobic. The drops are then almost perfectly round, roll off and take **dirt particles** with them.

Clean leaves offer **pathogens** such as fungal spores hardly any hold. In addition no film of dirt blocks the light that the plant needs for **photosynthesis**. In this way the leaf stays healthy and can work well.

Researchers transfer the effect to materials. An example from the building trade is **self-cleaning facade paints**. Their water-repellent, microstructured surface is cleaned by the rain. In this way house walls stay clean for longer. When you use ideas from nature for technology, this is called **biomimetics**.

gewusst: Nasturtium and kohlrabi also have leaves from which water rolls off.
A drop of water on a lotus leaf touches the leaf at only a few points.

teile.einleitung: Mycorrhiza is the name for the close partnership between fungi and the roots of plants. The fungus supplies the plant with water and nutrients, and in return the plant gives it sugar. Without this invisible cooperation in the soil, many trees could not grow healthily.
wichtigste: Mycorrhiza is the symbiosis between fungi and plant roots.
The word comes from Greek and means “fungus root”.
The fungus supplies water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
The plant gives the fungus sugar, which it makes by photosynthesis.
Most land plants live together with mycorrhizal fungi.
Well-known mycorrhizal fungi are the porcini, the chanterelle and the fly agaric.
Trees in the forest can be linked to one another by fungal threads.

abschnitte.text: The word **mycorrhiza** is put together from the Greek words for fungus and root. It describes a partnership in which both partners benefit, a **symbiosis**. The German researcher Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1885. Today we know that the great majority of all land plants have such fungal partners.

In the soil, fungi form a network of hair-thin threads, the **hyphae**. These threads reach much further and into much finer cracks in the soil than roots can. In this way they gather water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen and pass them on to the plant. In return, the fungus gets sugar, which the plant makes in its leaves by photosynthesis. A tree gives a considerable part of its sugar to the fungi.

In **ectomycorrhiza**, the fungus wraps around the fine root tips like a stocking. This form is typical of forest trees such as spruce, beech, oak, birch and pine. In endomycorrhiza, the fungal threads grow into the root cells. This form is found in many grasses, herbs and crops such as wheat or maize.

Many popular edible fungi are mycorrhizal fungi, such as the **porcini**, the chanterelle and the truffle. The poisonous fly agaric likes to grow under birches and spruces. That is why certain fungi are always found with certain trees. Because they need a living tree partner, porcini can hardly be grown artificially.

The fungal threads can link several trees to one another. Researchers suspect that nutrients can also travel between trees through this network. Some people therefore jokingly call it the **Wood Wide Web**, after the Internet. How much trees actually exchange through it is still being researched.

With mycorrhiza, plants grow better, survive drought more easily and are better protected from disease. For healthy forests it is indispensable. Air pollution, too much fertiliser and compacted soils can harm the fungi. In Switzerland, many cantons have rules on **mushroom picking** to protect the fungi.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living together of two living things in which both benefit.
The fine threads of which a fungus in the soil is made.
The whole web of fungal threads in the soil.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.

gewusst: The fungus that we collect is only the fruiting body; most of it lives unseen in the soil.
The very first land plants, over 400 million years ago, probably lived together with fungal partners.
Truffles grow underground on tree roots and are searched for with dogs.

teile.einleitung: In the forest, on stones or between paving stones, you often find soft, green cushions. These are mosses. A moss cushion is made up of many tiny plants that grow close together.
wichtigste: A moss cushion is made up of many small moss plants.
It feels soft like a pillow.
Most moss plants grow only a few centimetres high.
Mosses like to grow in damp, shady places.
Mosses have no flowers; they reproduce with spores.
Tiny animals such as water bears live in moss cushions.

abschnitte.text: A **moss cushion** is not a single plant, but is made up of **many small moss plants**. They stand so close together that they form a **soft pillow**. Most moss plants grow only **a few centimetres** high. Instead of real roots they have fine holding threads with which they cling to the ground, to stones or to tree bark.

Mosses especially like to grow in **damp, shady places**, for example in the forest or on the north side of walls. They take up water directly through their little leaves. A dense cushion can **store** a lot of water, like a sponge. If it dries out, it turns brown and hard. When rain comes again, it often quickly turns green again.

Mosses have **no flowers** and make no seeds. They **reproduce** with **spores**. These are tiny grains that form in small **capsules** on thin stalks. The wind carries the spores away. Mosses are among the oldest land plants on Earth.

A moss cushion is a small habitat. In it live tiny animals such as **water bears**, which can only be seen well under the microscope. They have eight stubby little legs and look like small bears. Water bears can dry out completely and later come back to life. Mites, springtails and roundworms also live in moss.

Many **birds** collect moss to **line** their **nests** softly. In the **city** you can often spot moss in the **cracks between paving stones**, on roofs or on old walls. There it is damp and shady enough. Moss is also important for the forest, because it keeps the soil damp and holds back rainwater.

gewusst: Water bears from moss cushions are among the toughest animals in the world and even survive great cold.
Sphagnum mosses can take up many times their own weight in water.

teile.einleitung: Fog is a cloud that reaches right down to the ground. It consists of tiny water droplets that hang in the air and make it harder to see. In the Swiss Central Plateau, in autumn and winter there is often a grey blanket of fog for weeks.
wichtigste: Fog forms when a cloud reaches down to the ground.
It consists of many tiny water droplets hanging in the air.
Fog forms when moist air cools and the water vapour condenses.
We speak of fog when you can see less than a kilometre.
In the Swiss Central Plateau there is often high fog in autumn and winter.
From the mountains you then see a sea of fog with the sun shining above it.
In road traffic, special care is needed in fog.

abschnitte.text: **Fog** is really a cloud lying on the ground. It consists of billions of tiny water droplets that are so light that they hang in the air. The droplets scatter the light, so everything looks grey and blurred. By definition there is fog when the **visibility** is under one kilometre. If visibility is a little better, we speak of haze.

Air always contains invisible water vapour. When the air cools, it can hold less water vapour. When the **dew point** is reached, the vapour turns into small droplets, which is called **condensation**. This is the same thing you see on a misted-up mirror after a shower.

On clear, still nights the ground cools strongly and also cools the air above it, which creates **radiation fog**, often in hollows and valleys. When warm, moist air moves over cold water or cold ground, advection fog forms, for example on sea coasts. Over warm lakes, steam fog can rise on cold mornings. High fog is a layer of fog that does not quite reach the ground.

In autumn and winter the Swiss Central Plateau is one of the foggiest regions in Europe. Cold air collects between the Jura and the Alps like water in a bowl, with warmer air above it. This weather situation is called an **inversion**. Then the fog sometimes stays for days, while it is sunny and warm on the Rigi, Pilatus or Chasseral and you look down on a white **sea of fog**.

In fog you see cars, bikes and pedestrians much later. So you have to drive more slowly and keep more distance. Cars switch on dipped headlights and, in very thick fog, the **rear fog light**. Airports and ships also have special instruments so that they can land and navigate safely in fog. For children on the way to school, bright clothes and reflective strips are especially important.

In very dry regions such as the Atacama Desert in Chile, people catch water with large **fog nets**. The droplets stick to the mesh and drip into gutters. Some beetles in the Namib Desert also drink in this way. In autumn you can also see fog on spiders’ webs, which then hang full of glittering droplets.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water vapour turns into tiny water droplets as it cools.
The temperature at which moist air is so cold that droplets form.
A weather situation in which cold air lies below and warmer air above.
A blanket of fog that you see from above like a white sea.

gewusst: It takes about a million fog droplets to make one raindrop.
In winter, walkers deliberately go up mountains to get above the sea of fog into the sun.
The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco is famous for often disappearing in fog.

teile.einleitung: To grow, plants need not only light, water and carbon dioxide, but also nutrients from the soil. Some of these they need only in tiny amounts. These are called micronutrients or trace elements.
wichtigste: Plants need micronutrients only in very small amounts, macronutrients in large amounts.
Micronutrients include iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, nickel and chlorine.
Molybdenum is a component of the enzyme nitrogenase.
Manganese takes part in the splitting of water in photosynthesis.
If a micronutrient is missing, the plant shows typical symptoms of deficiency.
Too much of a micronutrient can be poisonous.

abschnitte.text: Plant nutrients are divided up by the **amount needed**. **Macronutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed by the plant in plenty. **Micronutrients** it needs only in traces, which is why they are also called **trace elements**. They are indispensable all the same. If just one is missing, the plant cannot grow properly.

Many micronutrients sit in **enzymes**, which are proteins that speed up chemical processes in the cell. **Molybdenum** is found in **nitrogenase**, with which nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air. **Nickel** is needed by the enzyme **urease**, which splits urea. **Copper** is contained in the protein **plastocyanin**, which carries electrons in photosynthesis.

In photosynthesis, water is split, and oxygen is produced. **Manganese** takes part in this **splitting of water** in **photosystem II**. The plant needs **iron** to make chlorophyll. If iron is missing, young leaves turn yellow while the leaf veins stay green. This yellowing is called **chlorosis**. It often occurs on soils rich in lime.

In **sugar beet**, a **lack of boron** leads to **heart rot and dry rot**: the inner leaves die, and the beet goes rotten. A **lack of zinc** shows in fruit trees as **small leaves** standing in rosette-like tufts. Farmers can tell from signs like these what the soil is missing. Then they can fertilise in a targeted way.

With micronutrients, too little and too much often lie close together. Too much copper or boron can damage the plant. That is why trace elements are only applied when there is really a deficiency. The soil plays a part as well: if it is very rich in lime or very acid, the plant may take up some substances poorly even though they are there.

gewusst: Humans also need trace elements such as iron, zinc and iodine, but only in tiny amounts.
Without the enzyme nitrogenase and its molybdenum, beans and clover could not use nitrogen from the air.

teile.einleitung: Mosses are small, green plants without true roots and without flowers. They form soft cushions on forest floors, stones, roofs and tree trunks. Although they look unremarkable, they are among the oldest land plants on Earth.
wichtigste: Mosses are small land plants without flowers, seeds and true roots.
They hold on to the ground with fine threads, the rhizoids.
Mosses reproduce with spores, which ripen in small capsules.
For fertilisation, mosses need water, because the male cells swim to the egg cell.
Moss cushions store many times their own weight in water and are important for the water balance in the forest.
Sphagnum moss forms the peat in raised bogs over thousands of years.
There are about 16,000 species of moss worldwide, and over 1,000 in Switzerland.
