abschnitte.text: **Mosses** are simply built land plants. They have no flowers, no seeds and no vessels like trees or flowers. That is why they usually stay small, often only a few centimetres high. A distinction is made between true mosses, liverworts and hornworts. Mosses were among the first plants to conquer the land, over 400 million years ago.

A little moss plant consists of a thin stem with tiny leaves. Instead of roots it has fine threads, the **rhizoids**. They hold the moss to the ground or stone, but hardly take up any water. Mosses soak up water directly through their little leaves, like a sponge.

Mosses reproduce with **spores**, which are tiny cells that the wind spreads. Before that, though, fertilisation is needed. For this, the male cells swim in a film of water, such as a dewdrop, to the egg cell. From the fertilised egg cell grows a stalk with a **spore capsule**, from which the spores later fall. That is why mosses thrive especially well in damp places.

Moss cushions can store many times their own weight in water. In heavy rain they soak up water and give it back slowly. In this way they protect the soil from drying out and from erosion. They are also a habitat for small animals such as mites, springtails and the tiny **water bears**.

**Sphagnum moss** keeps growing at the top while it dies at the bottom. The dead parts hardly rot in the wet, acid water and over thousands of years turn into peat. This is how raised bogs form. Sphagnum can store especially large amounts of water and makes the water around it acid.

Many mosses react sensitively to air pollution, so they serve as **indicator plants** for clean air. In the past, dried moss was used to seal timber houses and as dressing material. Today mosses are used to green roofs and walls. In many Swiss nativity scenes, moss is laid at Christmas, but collecting it is restricted in some areas.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine threads with which mosses hold on to the ground.
Tiny reproductive cells from which new moss plants grow.
A small capsule on a stalk in which the spores ripen.
A plant whose presence tells you something about the environment.

gewusst: Water bears that live in moss can even survive in space.
It is not reliably true that moss grows only on the north side of trees; as a compass it is no good.
Some mosses can dry out completely for years and wake up again as soon as they get wet.

teile.einleitung: The bog cranberry is a tiny plant that is easy to overlook in a raised bog. Its thread-thin stems creep over cushions of sphagnum moss, and in autumn it bears bright red berries. It is closely related to the American cranberry.
wichtigste: The bog cranberry grows on sphagnum cushions in the raised bog.
Its stems are very thin and creep along the ground.
The pink flowers have petals that curve backwards.
Ripe bog cranberries are red.
It belongs to the heather family and is closely related to the American cranberry.
Fungi on its roots help it to take up nutrients in the nutrient-poor mire.

abschnitte.text: The **bog cranberry** is a small, **evergreen** shrub, even if it does not look like a shrub at all. Its stems are **very thin** and **creep** across the ground. The leaves are tiny, narrow and slightly rolled at the edge. It grows on the **cushions of sphagnum moss** in the **raised bog**. Often the sphagnum grows so fast that the bog cranberry is half sunk in it.

In early summer, small **pink flowers** appear on long, fine stalks. Their **petals** are strongly **curved backwards**, so that the flower is a little like a small cyclamen flower. From them come round berries that turn **red** in autumn. They are quite large in proportion to the plant. The berries taste very sour.

The bog cranberry belongs to the **heather family**, like the bilberry and the cowberry. It is closely related to the **American cranberry** from North America, which is also called the large cranberry. American cranberries are grown on large plantations and made into juice and dried berries.

In a raised bog there are very few nutrients. The bog cranberry can survive all the same, because **fungi** live on its roots. The fine threads of the fungi help it to take up **nutrients** from the soil. In return, the fungi get sugar from the plant. Such a partnership is called a **mycorrhiza**.

The **raised bogs** of Switzerland are **strictly protected**. That is why you should not pick bog cranberries there. Even walking on them can damage the delicate sphagnum cushions. If you want to see the plant, it is best to stay on the paths and wooden boardwalks that some mires have.

gewusst: The bog cranberry is so delicate that among the sphagnum you often only spot it by its red berries.
American cranberries are harvested in fields that are flooded for the purpose. The berries then float on top.

teile.einleitung: Nitrification is a process in soil and water in which bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate. It is an important part of the nitrogen cycle. Without nitrification, plants could use far less nitrogen.
wichtigste: In nitrification, ammonium is oxidised to nitrate by way of nitrite.
It takes place only in the presence of oxygen.
In the classic model, the genus Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium to nitrite.
The bacteria gain energy from inorganic nitrogen compounds.
In 2015 comammox was described, complete nitrification by a single bacterium.
Nitrification makes the soil more acidic.

abschnitte.text: When plants, animals or manure are broken down, **ammonium** forms. In nitrification it is **oxidised** in two steps, that is, combined with oxygen. First **nitrite** forms, then **nitrate**. Oxygen is needed for this, so nitrification takes place only in well-aerated soils and waters. Plants can easily take up nitrate through their roots.

In the classic model, two groups of bacteria share the work. **Nitrosomonas** oxidises ammonium to nitrite, **Nitrobacter** turns nitrite into nitrate. These bacteria get their **energy** not from sugar but from the oxidation of inorganic nitrogen compounds. In 2015, researchers discovered bacteria of the genus Nitrospira that manage both steps alone. This process is called **comammox**, from English “complete ammonia oxidation”.

In nitrification, **acid particles** are released, so over time it **makes the soil more acidic**. Nitrate is also easily washed out into groundwater. Ammonium, on the other hand, sticks better in the soil. Some farmers therefore add **nitrification inhibitors** to the fertiliser. In this way the nitrogen stays longer in the soil as ammonium, and less is lost.

Sewage contains a lot of ammonium, for example from urine. For fish, ammonium in the form of ammonia is very poisonous. In **sewage treatment plants**, bacteria therefore carry out nitrification on purpose. For this, air is blown into the tanks. In this way the ammonium that is poisonous to fish is turned into nitrate before the cleaned water flows into streams and lakes.

gewusst: Nitrification also takes place in aquariums, which is why a new aquarium needs a few weeks before fish can move in.
The name nitrification comes from the Latin word for saltpetre, nitrum.

teile.einleitung: The downy birch is a birch that is at home on wet soils. It looks like the better-known silver birch, but differs from it in a few features. In Swiss mires it is a common tree.
wichtigste: The young twigs of the downy birch are finely hairy.
Its branches grow rather upright and do not hang down.
It tolerates wet and acid soils especially well.
Its species name “pubescens” means “downy, covered in fine hairs”.
It belongs to the birch family.
If many downy birches spread in a raised bog, the bog gets drier.

abschnitte.text: The **downy birch** has pale, white bark like other birches. But its **young twigs** are **finely hairy**, which you can feel if you stroke them. The twigs of the **silver birch**, on the other hand, are bare and covered with small warts. The branches of the downy birch grow **rather upright** and do not hang down. Its leaves are **rather egg-shaped and rounded**, while in the silver birch they are more triangular and pointed.

The scientific name of the downy birch is **Betula pubescens**. The word **pubescens** means “**covered in fine hairs**” and refers to the little hairs on the twigs and young leaves. The downy birch belongs to the **birch family**. Alders and hazels also belong to this family.

The downy birch grows on **wet** and **acid soils**, where many other trees struggle. It is found in mires, at the edges of mires and in damp woods. A forest on permanently wet boggy ground, in which downy birches and alders often grow, is called a **carr**. The downy birch is also very **tolerant of cold** and grows far into the north of Europe.

In a healthy **raised bog**, it is so wet and poor in nutrients that hardly any trees grow. If the bog is **drained** by ditches and gets drier, downy birches can spread. Many young birches in a raised bog are therefore a **warning sign**. The trees also draw extra water out of the bog. When looking after mires, they are therefore often removed.

gewusst: Birch seeds have small wings and are carried far by the wind, which is why birches settle open ground very quickly.
Downy birch and silver birch are sometimes so alike that even experts have to look closely.

teile.einleitung: The lily of the valley is a pretty, strongly scented spring flower with white little bells. But beware: the whole plant is poisonous.
wichtigste: The lily of the valley blooms mainly in May.
The white little bells all hang to the same side.
The plant usually has two broad leaves.
After flowering it forms red, poisonous berries.
After touching it you should wash your hands.
It grows wild in light deciduous forests.

abschnitte.text: As its German name “Maiglöckchen”, “little May bell”, says, the **lily of the valley** blooms mainly in **May**. On one stalk hang about **5 to 10** small, white **flower bells** in a row, all to the same side. The flowers smell **strong and sweet**. A lily of the valley usually has **two**, rarely three, broad leaves. Between them grows the flower stalk.
In nature the lily of the valley grows in bright, light **deciduous forests**. There it often forms large carpets, because the plants spread under the earth. Many people also plant it in the garden.
After flowering, the lily of the valley forms small, **red berries**. They look tempting but are likewise **poisonous**. You must on no account eat them.

All parts of the lily of the valley contain **poison**. After picking, some of it can also stick to the hands. That is why you should **wash your hands** if you have touched lilies of the valley. The poison can also get into the **vase water**. You must not drink this water, you pour it away. Anyone who thinks that somebody has eaten some of the plant calls the emergency number **145** of Tox Info Suisse in Switzerland.

gewusst: Young lily of the valley leaves look similar to the leaves of wild garlic, so you have to be very careful when gathering wild garlic.
Wild garlic smells of garlic, lily of the valley leaves do not.

teile.einleitung: A light year is the distance that light covers in a year. Although the word year occurs in it, the light year is not a time but a length. Astronomers use it because the distances between stars and galaxies are so huge that kilometres are far too small for them.
wichtigste: A light year is the distance that light covers in a year.
The light year is a unit of length and not a unit of time.
A light year corresponds to about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
The nearest star after the sun, Proxima Centauri, is a good 4 light years away.
The Milky Way has a diameter of about 100,000 light years.
The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light years from us.
Anyone who looks at the starry sky is looking into the past.

abschnitte.text: A light year is a **unit of length** in astronomy. It states how far light travels in empty space in a year. Because light covers about 300,000 kilometres per second, this comes to about **9.46 trillion kilometres**, that is a number with twelve zeros. Abbreviated, a light year is written as **ly**, from the English light year.

To work out a light year, you multiply the speed of light by the number of seconds in a year. A year has about 31.5 million **seconds**. Three hundred thousand kilometres times 31.5 million gives the enormous distance of almost ten trillion kilometres. A car driving non-stop at 100 kilometres an hour would need over ten million years for a single light year.

The star that is nearest to us after the sun is called **Proxima Centauri** and is a good 4 light years away. Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is about 8.6 light years away. Our home galaxy, the **Milky Way**, measures about 100,000 light years across. The Andromeda galaxy, which on dark nights you can just see with the naked eye, lies about 2.5 million light years away.

Because light takes time, we do not see distant heavenly bodies as they are today. A star that is 100 light years away appears to us as it looked 100 years ago. The light of the Andromeda galaxy has been on its way since the first ancestors of humans existed on Earth. With large **space telescopes** such as the James Webb Telescope, researchers can therefore look far back into the early period of the universe.

Within the solar system, astronomers prefer to use the **astronomical unit**, which is the mean distance between Earth and sun of about 150 million kilometres. For very large distances, experts often use the **parsec**, which corresponds to about 3.26 light years. For smaller distances, people sometimes also speak of light minutes or light seconds. The sun is, for example, a good 8 light minutes from the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure for distances, such as metres, kilometres or indeed the light year.
A huge collection of billions of stars, gas and dust.
The mean distance between Earth and sun, about 150 million kilometres.
A unit of length in astronomy, about 3.26 light years long.

gewusst: Some stars that you see in the sky could have gone out long ago, without their light giving this away yet.
A light year is so long that you would have to travel round the Earth about 236 million times for it.
The term light year was introduced in the 19th century, when for the first time the distance of a star could be measured.

teile.einleitung: Animals and plants need not only good habitats but also links between them. Ecological connectivity ensures that species can move and exchange. In Switzerland, farmers help with this too.
wichtigste: Through ecological connectivity, animals can move between habitats.
Roads and settlements cut up habitats.
Small, isolated groups of animals are threatened by inbreeding and dying out.
Stepping stones are small habitats that make the way across open land easier.
Bats like to fly along hedges and rows of trees.
Switzerland is building an Ecological Infrastructure of core areas and connecting areas.
Farmers receive additional payments from the Confederation if they take part in connectivity projects.

abschnitte.text: Many animals must be able to move: to look for food, to find a new territory or, in spring, to reach their spawning waters, like frogs and toads. **Ecological connectivity** means that habitats are linked so that animals can **move between them**. Plants benefit too, because their seeds are carried on by animals or by the wind. This is also called a **biotope network**.

In densely populated Switzerland, **roads and settlements separate** many habitats. This is called the **fragmentation of habitats**. A small group of animals living in an isolated area can no longer mix with other groups. It is threatened by **inbreeding** and, in the worst case, **dying out**. Connectivity helps to link such islands again.

Small habitats such as ponds, hedges, piles of stones or flower strips are called **stepping stones**. They make the way across open land easier for animals, just as stones in a stream help you to cross. **Hedges** and **rows of trees** also act as guiding lines. **Bats**, for example, like to fly along such structures at night, because they use them to find their way and find insects there.

In Swiss farming there are regional **connectivity projects**. In them farmers lay out biodiversity areas such as extensive meadows, hedges or wildflower fallows so that they are well linked with one another. Those who take part can receive **additional payments from the Confederation**. In this way farmland becomes more permeable again for hares, birds and insects.

At national level, Switzerland wants to build up an **Ecological Infrastructure**. This is a network of **core areas**, that is, valuable protected areas, and **connecting areas** between them. It also includes wildlife bridges over motorways and passages under roads. The Confederation, cantons and municipalities work on it together.

gewusst: On some roads, volunteers put up fences in spring and carry toads safely across the road in buckets.
Even a single hedge across a field can become an important link for many animal species.

teile.einleitung: The nival zone is the highest altitude zone in the mountains. There is a lot of snow and ice there all year round. Even so, there is life here too: lichens, a few flowering plants, algae and even tiny animals.
wichtigste: The nival zone is marked all year round by a lot of snow and ice.
In the Swiss Alps it begins at about 2,800 to 3,200 metres.
Flowering plants grow only in sheltered rock crevices and on ridges.
The glacier crowfoot is a typical plant of the nival zone.
Lichens often settle on bare rock first.
Snow algae sometimes colour snowfields reddish in summer.

abschnitte.text: The word **nival** comes from the Latin “nix” for snow. In the **Swiss Alps** the nival zone begins at about **2,800 to 3,200 metres**. Here the snow does not melt completely in many places even in summer. Below lies the **subnival zone**, a transition area with scree, rocks and small cushions of plants. Further down follows the alpine zone with grass and mats.

Where the wind blows the snow away or the sun melts it, single **flowering plants** grow. They stand in sheltered **rock crevices** and on ridges. Dark rock **warms up in the sun** and gives the plants a little warmth. Especially typical is the **glacier crowfoot** with white to pink flowers. It is among the flowering plants that climb highest in the Alps, above 4,000 metres.

On bare rock, **lichens** often settle first. A lichen is a partnership of a fungus and an alga. It endures great cold and long dryness. Lichens grow very slowly, some only a few millimetres in many years. In time they loosen the rock very slightly and so prepare the ground for other plants.

On glaciers and snowfields lives the **glacier flea**. It is not a real flea but a tiny **springtail**. It eats pollen, algae and dust that the wind brings. In summer some snowfields turn **reddish**. This comes from tiny **snow algae**, which make a red pigment against the strong sunlight. This is also called **watermelon snow**.

gewusst: The glacier crowfoot has been found in the Swiss Alps at over 4,000 metres.
The glacier flea can stand temperatures below freezing point.

teile.einleitung: In the Solothurn Jura lies a valley of forests, pastures and steep rocks: the **Thal**. Here is the **Thal Nature Park**. It is known, among other things, for its **European bison**, the largest land mammals in Europe.
wichtigste: The Thal Nature Park lies in the canton of Solothurn.
It lies in the Jura mountains.
Balsthal is the main town of the district of Thal.
Near Balsthal, narrow valleys called klusen cut through the Jura chain.
The Dünnern flows through the Thal and joins the Aare near Olten.
Since 2022, European bison have lived in a woodland enclosure in the nature park.

abschnitte.text: The Thal Nature Park lies in the **canton of Solothurn**, in the middle of the **Jura**. The Jura is a limestone mountain range with long mountain chains. The main town of the district of Thal is **Balsthal**. The **Dünnern** flows through the valley. It joins the **Aare** near **Olten**. The park is a regional nature park in which people live, work and farm.

Near Balsthal there is a special landscape form: the **klus**. This is a **narrow gorge** cutting through a **Jura chain**. Over a very long time the water has dug its way through the mountain. Steep rock walls rise on the right and left. Roads and railway lines often run through such klusen, because they open a way through the mountain chains.

Since **2022**, **European bison** have lived in a large **woodland enclosure** in the Thal Nature Park. The bison is the **largest land mammal in Europe**. It looks like a mighty bull or cow with dark, shaggy fur and a hump. Bison eat grass, leaves, bark and twigs. In the project, experts are studying how the animals change the forest and whether there could be room for them in Switzerland again.

In the past, bison lived in many forests in Europe, including in what is now Switzerland. They **were hunted** and **lost** their **habitat**, because forests were cleared and turned into fields and pastures. In Switzerland they disappeared many centuries ago. In the early 20th century the last wild bison died out completely. Only thanks to animals in zoos and enclosures could the species be saved.

gewusst: A fully grown bison bull can weigh almost a tonne.
All bison alive today are descended from only a few animals that survived in enclosures.

teile.einleitung: If you climb a mountain in Switzerland, you pass through different altitude zones, each with its own climate and plants. The montane zone is the zone of mountain forests and mountain meadows. It shapes large parts of the Pre-Alps and the Jura.
wichtigste: The term “montane” comes from the Latin word for mountain.
On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone lies roughly between 600 and 1,200 or 1,400 metres.
Typical are forests of beech and silver fir, with spruce added further up.
The climate is cooler and wetter than on the Central Plateau.
Dairy farming on meadows and pastures is typical.
In the Jura there are wooded pastures, where trees stand scattered loosely.

abschnitte.text: It gets cooler as you go higher. That is why mountains are divided into **altitude zones**. At the very bottom lies the **colline zone**, and above it follows the **montane zone**. Higher up come the **subalpine**, the **alpine** and the **nival zone**. The name “montane” comes from the Latin word **mons**, which means “mountain”. On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone reaches roughly from **600 to 1,200 or 1,400 metres**.

Many natural forests of the montane zone are made up of **beech** and **silver fir**. They are called **beech and fir forests**. In the upper montane zone, **spruce** is often added. Still further up, in the subalpine zone, spruce becomes the most important tree. Today many forests have been changed by forestry, and there are often more spruces than would be natural.

In the montane zone it is **cooler** and **wetter** than on the Central Plateau. Snow stays on the ground longer in winter, and the growing season for plants is shorter. It is often too cool and too steep for arable farming. But grass grows well, because there is enough rain.

Typical of the montane zone are **meadows and pastures** with **dairy farming**. The cows graze in summer, and the grass of the meadows is made into hay for the winter. In many places, cheese is made from the milk. Landscapes such as the Emmental or the Toggenburg lie largely in this zone. In the **Pre-Alps** and in the **Jura** it takes up most of the slopes.

abschnitte.titel: The wooded pastures of the Jura
abschnitte.text: In the **Jura** there is a special landscape: the **wooded pastures**, called **“Wytweiden”** in German. On these pastures, single trees or small groups of trees stand scattered loosely, often mighty spruces. The areas are used as pasture and as forest at the same time. The animals find food and, in the shade of the trees, shelter. Wooded pastures are varied habitats.

gewusst: On the southern side of the Alps the altitude zones lie somewhat higher than on the northern side, because it is warmer there.
The limits of the altitude zones are not sharp lines, but merge gradually into one another.

teile.einleitung: Beneficial animals are animals that help humans by eating pests. In the garden they keep aphids, caterpillars and slugs in check, for example. If you encourage beneficial animals, you need less poison.
wichtigste: Ladybirds and their larvae eat many aphids.
The larva of the lacewing is called the aphid lion because of its appetite.
Tits collect very many caterpillars for their young.
The hedgehog eats slugs, beetles and worms.
The slow worm likes to eat slugs but is not a snake.
Insect hotels offer wild bees and other insects nesting places.

abschnitte.text: The best-known beneficial animal is the **ladybird**. It and its larvae eat very many **aphids**. The larva of the **lacewing** is also a greedy aphid hunter, which is why it is called the **aphid lion**. **Hoverflies** look like small wasps but do not sting. Their larvae also eat aphids. Earwigs go hunting for aphids at night.

In the garden the **hedgehog** eats slugs, beetles and worms, and hibernates in winter. **Ground beetles** are mostly dark and shiny and hunt slugs and insects on the ground at night. The **slow worm** looks like a snake but is a legless lizard. It likes to eat **slugs**. All these animals need hiding places such as piles of leaves, piles of stones or dense hedges.

Many birds are important beneficial animals. **Tits** especially help: for their young they collect very many **caterpillars** every day. A nest box in the garden attracts tits. Robins and blackbirds also eat insects and snails. If you do without poison, you find more birds in the garden.

You can offer beneficial animals a home. An **insect hotel** serves wild bees and other insects as a **nesting place**. For earwigs you hang an **upturned flowerpot with wood wool** in a fruit tree. A pile of branches or leaves offers the hedgehog shelter. Native flowers and shrubs provide food. In this way a balance arises in which pests do not get out of hand.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids in its life.
In greenhouses, beneficial animals such as parasitic wasps are used on purpose against pests.

teile.einleitung: Flour is found in bread, cakes, pasta and many sauces. It is made when grains of cereal are finely ground. Depending on which parts of the grain stay in the flour, it is light or dark.
wichtigste: Flour is made from ground cereal grains, for example wheat, spelt or rye.
White flour is light because the dark husk of the grain has been removed.
In Switzerland people distinguish between white flour, half-white flour, Ruch flour and wholemeal flour.
Ruch bread is baked from the dark Ruch flour.
Flour is mostly starch, which gives the body energy.
Flour is stored dry and well sealed.

abschnitte.text: A grain of cereal has three important parts: the **husk**, the small **germ** and the pale **endosperm** inside. In the **mill** the grain is crushed between rollers or stones and then sieved. The separated parts of the husk are called **bran**. In the past a water wheel often drove the millstones. Today big mills work with machines and very fine sieves.

For **white flour**, almost only the pale endosperm is used. **Half-white flour** contains a little more of the grain and is therefore medium-light. **Ruch flour** still has more of the husk in it, so it is darker and tastes stronger. For **wholemeal flour**, the whole grain is ground. Dark flours contain more **dietary fibre** and minerals than white flour.

The most important part of flour is **starch**. It gives the body energy. Added to this are protein, a little fat, water and minerals. In wheat and spelt flour there is a special protein, the **gluten**. It makes the dough stretchy, so that bread can rise nicely.

From flour, eggs and milk you stir a runny batter for **omelettes**, which are fried thin in the frying pan. With water, salt and yeast it becomes bread dough. If you stir a little flour into a sauce, it becomes **thicker** as it cooks. The starch takes up water and swells. This is called **thickening** the sauce.

Flour belongs in a **dry**, cool place and in a well-sealed container. If it gets damp, it can go **mouldy**. Small animals like to settle in old, open stores. A well-known example is the **mealworm**: it is the larva of the mealworm beetle and eats flour and grain.

gewusst: Fine flour dust in the air can catch fire and explode. That is why strict safety rules apply in mills.
Mealworms are bred and sold as food for birds and reptiles.

teile.einleitung: Littering means carelessly throwing away rubbish or leaving it lying. This dirties streets, parks and nature and can harm animals.
wichtigste: Rubbish belongs in the bin or is taken home.
PET bottles go into the PET collection, from which new bottles are made.
Cigarette stubs contain poison that gets into the water.
Animals can eat plastic or get tangled in it.
Plastic breaks down only after hundreds of years.
In many Swiss cantons and municipalities there are fines for littering.

abschnitte.text: The word **littering** comes from English: “litter” means rubbish. It means that you simply throw rubbish on the ground or leave it lying. This can be packaging, cans, bottles or even small things such as tissues. Even small rubbish belongs in a **bin**. If there is none nearby, you take it home with you.

In Switzerland a lot of rubbish is collected separately. **PET bottles** are taken to the PET collection, for example in the shop. From them new bottles can be made. Glass, aluminium, paper and cardboard are also collected and **recycled**, which means used again.

Many wild animals can get tangled in plastic or eat it. As a result they can become ill or die. Discarded **cigarette stubs** contain poisonous substances that get into the water and harm animals and plants. A **plastic bottle** needs hundreds of years in nature to break down. In the process tiny plastic particles arise, **microplastic**.

In many **cantons** and **municipalities** you can get a **fine** for littering. Anyone who throws rubbish on the ground then has to pay money. This is meant to help so that less rubbish lies around. Clearing up costs the municipalities a lot of money.

On a **clean-up day**, many people together collect rubbish in nature or in the town. School classes, clubs and families join in. In this way the surroundings become clean again. Anyone who does not leave any rubbish lying helps every day.

gewusst: A single cigarette stub can contaminate a lot of water with poisons.
In Switzerland, most of the PET drinks bottles are collected again.

teile.einleitung: Lignum, Holzwirtschaft Schweiz, is the umbrella organisation of the Swiss forestry and timber industry. It works to see that more wood is used, especially wood from Swiss forests. Its seat is in Zurich.
wichtigste: Lignum is the umbrella organisation of the Swiss forestry and timber industry.
It was founded in 1931 as a working group for wood.
Its seat is in Zurich.
Lignum awards the Swiss Wood mark of origin.
Since 2009 Lignum has awarded the Prix Lignum every three years.
Technical publications appear in the Lignatec series.

abschnitte.text: Lignum unites numerous **associations and organisations** under one roof. These include **forestry**, **sawmills**, **timber construction** and **wood processing**, but also planners, architects and research institutions. In this way the whole chain from the forest to the finished wood product is represented. Lignum represents the common concerns towards politics and the public. The organisation was founded in **1931**, and its head office is in **Zurich**. In addition there are regional organisations, for example in French-speaking Switzerland.

A main aim of Lignum is to promote the **use of wood**, especially **Swiss wood**. To this end Lignum informs, advises and does public relations work. Products made of wood that has grown in Switzerland and been processed here can carry the **Swiss Wood mark of origin**. So it shows where the wood comes from. The well-known **FSC** mark, by contrast, certifies forest management worldwide. Forest covers about a third of the area of Switzerland.

Since **2009** Lignum has awarded the **Prix Lignum** every three years. It honours innovative and high-quality use of wood in building, interior fitting and design, and is awarded regionally and nationally. For specialists Lignum publishes the **Lignatec** series. In it appear technical documents, for example on **fire protection** in timber construction. As early as the 1930s Lignum encouraged standardised **engineered timber construction**.

gewusst: The name Lignum is the Latin word for wood.
In 2006 Lignum celebrated its 75th anniversary.

teile.einleitung: When we see a mushroom in the forest, we see only a small part of it. Most of it lives hidden in the soil or in wood. This fine web of threads is called the **mycelium**.
wichtigste: The mycelium is a web of fine fungal threads.
It grows in the soil or in wood.
The part that we see is called the fruiting body.
Many mycelia break down dead leaves and wood into soil.
Many fungi and trees swap nutrients through the mycelium.
A mycelium is often white and can live for many years.

abschnitte.text: A fungus is made of very fine threads, the **hyphae**. Many hyphae together form a dense network, the **mycelium**. It is often **white** and looks a little like cotton wool or cobwebs. If you lift leaves or rotting wood in the forest, you can sometimes spot it. The mycelium grows **in the soil or in wood** and spreads slowly.

The mushroom with a cap and stalk is only the **fruiting body**. It grows out of the mycelium, often after rain in late summer and autumn. In the fruiting body, tiny **spores** form, with which the fungus spreads. The fruiting body is like the apple on an apple tree. If you pick a mushroom carefully, **the mycelium lives on** and can form new mushrooms next year.

In autumn, millions of leaves fall on the forest floor. The mycelium of many fungi **breaks down** the dead leaves and old wood. In this way, new, fertile **soil** gradually forms. The nutrients get back into the ground. Without fungi, a huge mountain of leaves and branches would pile up in the forest.

Many fungi live together with trees. Their mycelium wraps around the fine tree roots. The fungus gives the tree **water and minerals** from the soil. In return, the tree gives the fungus **sugar**, which it makes with its leaves. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The porcini and the fly agaric, for example, live with trees in this way.

gewusst: A mycelium can live to be **many years** old, some even hundreds or thousands of years.
The mycelium of a honey fungus in the USA covers several square kilometres and is considered one of the biggest living things on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The phases of the Moon are the different shapes that the Moon shows in the sky over the course of a month. Sometimes it is a thin crescent, sometimes half, sometimes perfectly round. The Moon itself does not change, only the part that we see lit up.
wichtigste: Over the course of a month the Moon shows different phases.
The four main phases are called new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter.
A complete cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon.
Depending on the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, we see more or less of this bright half.
The phases of the Moon are not caused by the Earth’s shadow.
The word “month” comes from the word “moon”.

abschnitte.titel: What are the phases of the Moon?
abschnitte.text: The Moon does not shine by itself, but is lit up by the Sun. Exactly one half of the Moon is always bright. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we look at this bright half from different angles. So we see sometimes a lot of it, sometimes a little: these are the **phases of the Moon**.

At **new moon**, the Moon stands between the Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, and we cannot see it. After that a thin crescent becomes visible, and the Moon is **waxing**. After about a week it is half lit, which is the first quarter. After about two weeks we see the whole bright side, and it is **full moon**. After that it wanes again, until it is new moon once more.

Here in the Northern Hemisphere, the right side is bright when the Moon is waxing. When the Moon is waning, the left side shines. An old German memory aid: if you add a line to the crescent so that it makes a written “z” (for “zunehmend”, waxing), the Moon is waxing; if you get an “a” (for “abnehmend”, waning), it is waning. In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

abschnitte.titel: When can you see the Moon?
abschnitte.text: The full moon rises at about sunset and sets at sunrise, so it can be seen all night long. The waxing half moon is in the sky in the evening. The waning half moon is seen mainly in the second half of the night and in the morning. That is why you can sometimes spot the Moon in the bright **daytime sky** too.

Thousands of years ago, people already based their calendars on the Moon. The word month comes from the word moon. The Islamic calendar is still a pure **lunar calendar** today. The date of Easter also depends on the Moon: Easter is on the Sunday after the first full moon in spring.

A **lunar eclipse** can only happen at full moon, when the Moon moves into the Earth’s shadow. A solar eclipse only happens at new moon, when the Moon covers the Sun. At new moon and full moon, the Sun and Moon pull on the oceans in a line. Then the tides are especially strong, which is called a spring tide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase of the Moon in which you cannot see the Moon, because its bright side faces away from us.
The phase of the Moon in which the Moon can be seen as a whole, bright disc.
The visible bright part of the Moon gets bigger from day to day.
The Moon moves into the Earth’s shadow and goes dark or reddish.

gewusst: A full moon near the horizon looks huge, even though it is the same size as when high in the sky.
At new moon the Moon is in the sky in the daytime with the Sun, we just cannot see it.
A full moon can sometimes occur twice in one calendar month; this is called a blue moon.

teile.einleitung: A **nature diary** is a notebook in which you write down what you observe outdoors. You can write, draw and stick in small finds. In time a very personal book about the nature around you is created.
wichtigste: A nature diary is a notebook for observations in nature.
Every observation has a date and a place.
You can also draw what you see.
Outdoors a pencil is useful.
The weather also fits well in a nature diary.
You can stick in a pressed leaf.

abschnitte.text: For every observation you first write down the **date and place**. Then you note what you saw or heard. The **weather** also fits well: sun, rain, wind or snow. Perhaps you even write down the temperature. In this way you can compare later when in the year something happened.

As well as writing, you can also **draw what you see**. A drawing does not have to be perfect. When you draw, you look more closely and discover more details. For outdoors a **pencil** is very useful, because it writes even in the cold and on damp paper. You can also stick in a **pressed leaf**, a feather or a blossom.

A nice idea is to draw **the same tree** all year round. In this way you see **how it changes with the seasons**. In spring the buds open, in summer it is thick with leaves. In autumn the leaves change colour, in winter it stands bare. At the end of the year you have a whole picture story about your tree.

In **spring** a typical entry is: **The first swallows are here.** In summer you can note butterflies or dragonflies. In autumn you see migratory birds and ripe fruit. In winter you may find tracks in the snow. Experts call such observations through the year **phenology**. In Switzerland the Confederation has been collecting such data for many decades.

gewusst: Many famous naturalists kept nature diaries.
If you keep your nature diary over several years, you can compare whether, for example, the first flowers appear earlier or later.

teile.einleitung: In a **nature reserve**, nature is meant to develop as undisturbed as possible. Rare animals and plants often live here. Visitors are welcome if they keep to a few simple rules.
wichtigste: A nature reserve is an area in which nature is protected.
You stay on the path so that animals and plants are protected.
In many nature reserves dogs are kept on a lead.
You take your own rubbish home with you.
Being quiet helps not to disturb the animals.
In Switzerland, moors and wetlands are often nature reserves.

abschnitte.text: A **nature reserve** is an area in which **nature is protected**. There rare animals, plants and habitats are meant to be kept. In Switzerland there are many such areas, small ponds as well as large landscapes. At the entrance there is often a **sign** with the **rules for visitors**. It is worth reading these rules beforehand.

In a nature reserve you **stay on the path**. In this way plants are not trampled and animals are not startled in their hiding places. **Dogs** are **kept on a lead** in many areas, because they could chase wild animals or disturb birds on the ground. You **take your rubbish home with you**. It is best to be **quiet**, because then you will also see more animals.

A **moor** is a landscape that is very **wet and soft**. The ground consists of **peat**, that is, plant remains that hardly decay because of all the water. Peat grows only very slowly. In moors live special plants such as bog moss, cotton grass or the sundew. Many moors in Switzerland are protected, because in the past many were drained.

A **wetland** on the shore of a lake is often full of **reeds**. Here **waterbirds** such as great crested grebes, moorhens or reed warblers breed. Fish lay their eggs in the shallow water. On some lakes there are **observation huts**. From there you can watch birds **without disturbing them**. With binoculars you then see them very close up.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps.
Some areas are completely closed during the birds’ breeding season.

teile.einleitung: The mimosa is a plant that moves when you touch it. Its feathery leaves fold up in seconds. That is why it is also called the sensitive plant.
wichtigste: If you touch the leaves of the mimosa, they fold up.
After a few minutes they open again.
At night the leaves also fold up.
The mimosa produces small pink flowers that look like little balls.
It originally grows in Central and South America.
A very sensitive person is sometimes called a “mimosa”.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of the mimosa are made up of many small **leaflets**. If a leaf is touched, the leaflets fold together in pairs, and sometimes the whole leaf stalk droops. It happens amazingly fast. After **a few minutes** the leaves slowly stand up again. In botany, such a movement in response to touch or a shock is called **seismonasty**.

At the base of the leaves sit small swellings, the **pulvini**. Their cells are normally full of water. When touched, water quickly flows out of certain cells. This makes the pulvini go limp, and the leaf folds up. Later the cells fill up again, and the leaf opens.

Even without being touched, the leaves fold up **at night** and open again in the morning. This is called a **sleeping position**. Why the mimosa reacts to touch is not entirely clear. It probably serves as **protection from animals**: a folded leaf looks small and wilted and is less tempting to plant-eaters.

The mimosa produces small, **pink** flower heads that look like fluffy **little balls**. It belongs to the **legume family**, like peas and beans. It originally comes from **Central and South America**. Today it grows wild in many tropical countries. Here we keep it as a houseplant.

Because the plant reacts even to a light touch, a very **sensitive** person is described in German with the words “Er ist eine Mimose”, “He is a mimosa”. It means that someone is quickly hurt or offended. People also say “mimosenhaft”, meaning “mimosa-like”.

gewusst: The yellow, sweet-smelling flowers that florists often call “mimosas” are really acacias.
If you touch the mimosa many times in a row, it reacts more weakly as time goes on.

teile.einleitung: The ozone layer is an invisible protective screen high in the air. It absorbs a large part of the dangerous UV radiation of the sun. Without it, life on land would hardly be possible.
wichtigste: The ozone layer protects the Earth from dangerous UV radiation.
It lies in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground.
Ozone is a gas made of three oxygen atoms.
If all the ozone were squeezed together at ground pressure, the layer would be only about three millimetres thick.
CFCs have damaged the ozone layer, especially over Antarctica.
In Arosa the ozone layer has been measured since 1926, the longest series of measurements in the world.
Ozone near the ground, on the other hand, is harmful and irritates the eyes and lungs.

abschnitte.text: The **ozone layer** is a region of the atmosphere in which an especially large amount of ozone occurs. It lies in the **stratosphere**, above the clouds and aeroplanes. Despite its name, it is not a solid layer but air with somewhat more ozone. The share of ozone in the air stays very small even there.

Normal oxygen consists of two oxygen atoms. Strong sunlight splits these molecules into single atoms. A single atom then combines with a normal oxygen molecule to form **ozone** with three atoms. Ozone is constantly being formed and broken down again, and in the process **UV radiation** is swallowed up.

The sun sends out different kinds of UV radiation. The most dangerous, **UV-C**, is almost completely absorbed by ozone and oxygen. Most of the UV-B is also held back. Only a small part reaches the ground and causes sunburn.

The French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson discovered the ozone layer in 1913. The Briton Gordon Dobson later built measuring instruments, and the unit of measurement **Dobson unit** is named after him. In Arosa in the Grisons, a series of measurements began in 1926 that is still continued today. Today satellites also watch the ozone layer all round the globe.

From the 1970s, researchers noticed that **CFCs** from spray cans and fridges destroy ozone. Over Antarctica an ozone hole formed every spring. With the Montreal Protocol of 1987 these substances were banned. Since then the ozone layer has been recovering slowly.

High up, ozone is a protective shield, but near the ground it is a pollutant. On hot summer days, **summer smog** forms from car exhaust and sunlight. Then the Swiss authorities sometimes warn of too-high ozone levels. People who are sensitive should then avoid strenuous outdoor sport in the afternoon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas made of three oxygen atoms with a sharp smell.
Invisible rays of the sun that cause sunburn.
The layer of air about 15 to 50 kilometres above the Earth.
A unit for the amount of ozone above a place.

gewusst: The word ozone comes from Greek and means roughly “the smelling one”.
After a thunderstorm you sometimes smell freshly formed ozone in the air.
Only when enough oxygen and ozone had formed in the atmosphere could living things move from the sea onto land.

teile.einleitung: Why are there so many more mice than foxes? The answer lies in the **ecological food pyramid**. It shows how much life and energy there is at each step of a food chain.
wichtigste: The food pyramid shows how numbers, mass or energy decrease from step to step.
The broad base is formed by the producers, that is, the plants.
There are pyramids of numbers, of biomass and of energy.
The energy pyramid can never be upside down.
Foxes are rarer than mice because less energy arrives at the top.
The food pyramid of the SGE, on the other hand, shows how to eat a balanced diet.

abschnitte.text: At the very bottom of the pyramid stand the **producers**. These are plants and algae that make food with sunlight. Above them come the **plant-eaters**, then the **meat-eaters**. At each step the amount gets smaller, because animals use a large part of their energy for movement, warmth and respiration. Only a small part becomes body mass that the next step can eat.

A fox has to eat very many mice to be full. The mice in turn eat large amounts of seeds and plants. So at the top of the pyramid **less energy arrives**. That is why in an area there are **far fewer foxes than mice**. For the same reason, large predators such as the wolf or the lynx are always rare and need large territories.

There are three kinds. The **pyramid of numbers** counts the living things at each step. The **pyramid of biomass** measures their weight. The **energy pyramid** shows how much energy there is at each step. Only the energy pyramid is **always** the right way up. Energy is lost from step to step, so more can never arrive at the top than at the bottom.

Pyramids of numbers and of biomass can sometimes stand **upside down**. A single **oak** feeds thousands of caterpillars. Here the pyramid of numbers is **narrower at the bottom than above it**. In the sea there is often less **phytoplankton** at any one moment than there are animals living on it. But the tiny plankton **multiplies very quickly** and constantly grows back. That is why the pyramid of biomass can be inverted there.

There is another well-known pyramid: the **food pyramid** of the **Swiss Society for Nutrition (SGE)**. It has nothing to do with ecology. It shows **how to eat a balanced diet**. At the bottom are drinks such as water, above them vegetables and fruit. At the very top are sweets and salty snacks, of which you should eat only a little.

gewusst: As a rule of thumb, only about 10 per cent of the energy passes from one step to the next.
That is why food chains rarely have more than four or five steps.

teile.einleitung: The lime fruit is a small, round nutlet that hangs on the lime tree in autumn and winter. With a wing-like bract it sails away on the wind.
wichtigste: Lime fruits are about as big as a pea.
They are round and often hang in several on thin stalks.
The fruit is a nutlet with a firm shell and a seed inside.
The shell is covered with fine hairs and feels felty.
Many fruits stay on the tree until winter.

abschnitte.text: The fruit of the lime is a **nutlet**. It has a firm shell in which a seed is held. Lime fruits are very small, only about as big as a **pea**, and mostly **round**. Their shell is covered with fine hairs. That is why it feels slightly **felty**.

Several nutlets hang together on thin stalks. These stalks are attached to a pale, flat **wing-like bract**. When the group of fruits falls from the tree, the bract spins like a propeller. In this way it falls more slowly, and the wind can carry it far away. From the seed a new lime tree can then grow.

Many lime fruits stay on the tree for a long time. They often still hang on the bare twigs when the leaves have long since fallen. Only the **winter wind** tears them loose bit by bit. In this way the seeds are spread over a long time.
Before the fruits form, the lime tree blooms in early summer. The **flowers** are collected and dried. From them **lime blossom tea** is made. Many people like to drink it when they have a cold.

gewusst: The lime fruit is an example of a flying fruit, similar to the fruits of maple or ash.

teile.einleitung: In a food chain, energy is passed on from one living thing to the next. In the process a lot of energy is lost at every step. Ecological efficiency describes how much of it actually reaches the next step.
wichtigste: From one step of the food chain to the next, roughly only about 10 per cent of the energy arrives.
Most of it is lost as heat from cell respiration.
Assimilation efficiency tells what share of the food is digested and taken up.
Warm-blooded animals usually have a lower production efficiency than cold-blooded ones.
In 1942 Raymond Lindeman described the energy flow between trophic levels.
That is why food chains are rarely longer than four to five links.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing in a food chain stands on a **trophic level**, a feeding step. At the very bottom are the **producers**, mostly plants, which store energy with sunlight. They are followed by the **primary consumers**, which eat plants, then the **secondary consumers** and the **tertiary consumers**. The American ecologist **Raymond Lindeman** described this energy flow in **1942** in the paper “The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology”.

As a rough rule of thumb, only about **10 per cent** of the energy of one step arrives at the next. A worked example: producers store **50,000 kJ**. At the primary consumers 5,000 kJ arrive, at the secondary consumers 500 kJ and at the **tertiary consumers** only **50 kJ**. That is why after a few steps the energy no longer suffices, and **food chains** are rarely longer than **four to five links**.

An animal does not digest everything it eats. The share that is digested and taken up is called **assimilation efficiency**. Part of the energy taken up is used in **cell respiration** and lost as **heat**. Only the rest becomes new body mass. Example: a caterpillar eats leaves with **200 J**. It passes 100 J out as droppings and uses up 67 J in respiration. So **33 J** become body mass.

The share of the energy taken up that becomes body mass is called **production efficiency**. **Warm-blooded animals** such as birds and mammals usually have a lower production efficiency than **cold-blooded animals** such as insects or fish. They need a lot of energy to keep their **body temperature** constant. A mouse therefore has to eat in proportion much more than a lizard.

These losses also affect farming. If grain is **eaten directly**, a field can **feed more people** than if the grain is first fed to animals. In turning it into meat, a lot of energy is lost. In Switzerland, though, a lot of grassland is used that is not suitable as arable land, and cows can turn grass into milk and meat.

gewusst: Actual ecological efficiency varies strongly between ecosystems, often between about 5 and 20 per cent.
Large predators are also rare because at the end of the food chain only little energy is left for them.

teile.einleitung: Cassava is a plant with thick, starchy root tubers. In many tropical countries it is an important staple food, but it is poisonous raw.
wichtigste: Cassava originally comes from the Amazon region of South America.
It is also called manioc or yuca.
Raw, it contains substances from which poisonous prussic acid can form.
Tapioca starch is obtained from cassava.
Fresh tubers go bad after just a few days.
In 2022 Nigeria harvested the most cassava.

abschnitte.text: **Cassava** was first grown in the **Amazon region** of South America. Portuguese sailors later brought it to **Africa** and **Asia**. It is also called **manioc** or, in Latin America, **yuca**. Its scientific name is Manihot esculenta, and it belongs to the **spurge family**, like the poinsettia.

Cassava contains substances from which poisonous **prussic acid** can form. That is why it must **not be eaten raw**. Peeling, soaking, boiling or roasting removes the poison. There is another problem: freshly harvested tubers often go bad after just **one to three days**. So they are processed quickly, for example into flour or dried pieces.

Almost pure **starch**, called **tapioca**, is obtained from the tubers. It is used to make, for example, the little balls in **bubble tea**. Tapioca is also used for puddings and for thickening dishes.

Cassava is very **hardy**. It also grows on poor soils and survives long **dry seasons**. The tubers can stay in the ground for a long time until they are needed. That is why cassava is an important staple food in many tropical countries. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the **FAO**, **Nigeria** was the world’s biggest producer in 2022.
Farmers usually do not grow cassava from seeds. They stick pieces of the woody stem into the soil, called **cuttings**. New plants grow from these. Seeds are used almost only in **plant breeding**.

gewusst: For hundreds of millions of people in Africa, Asia and South America, cassava is a staple food.

teile.einleitung: Nitrate is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen. Plants need it as an important nutrient, so it is in many fertilisers. But too much nitrate can get into groundwater and pollute drinking water.
wichtigste: The nitrate ion has the formula NO3- and is negatively charged.
Plants take up nitrate and build proteins from it.
In the 19th century, Chile saltpetre from the Atacama Desert was exported as fertiliser.
Because it hardly sticks to soil particles, nitrate is easily washed out into groundwater.
In Switzerland a maximum value of 40 mg nitrate per litre applies to drinking water (as of 2025).
From nitrogen fertiliser, the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide can escape from the soil.

abschnitte.text: The **nitrate ion** consists of one nitrogen atom and three oxygen atoms. Its formula is **NO3-**, so it is negatively charged. Nitrate occurs in soils, waters and many minerals. Salts of nitrate are also called **saltpetre**. In the 19th century **Chile saltpetre** was exported in large amounts from the Atacama Desert in Chile and used as fertiliser and for explosives.

Plants need nitrogen to build **proteins**. They mostly take it up as nitrate through the roots. In the plant, the enzyme **nitrate reductase** turns the nitrate into nitrite in the first step. For the further steps the plant needs energy from light. That is why **lettuce** from a winter greenhouse often contains more nitrate: in little light, less nitrate is converted into protein.

Soil particles are mostly also negatively charged. So nitrate hardly sticks to them and is easily **washed out** by rain. In this way it gets into the **groundwater**, from which much drinking water comes. In Switzerland a maximum value of **40 milligrams per litre** applies to drinking water (as of 2025). In areas with a lot of arable farming, the groundwater is in some cases heavily polluted. The cantons and the Confederation therefore support projects so that less nitrate seeps away.

In the body, or already in the water, **nitrite** can form from nitrate. Nitrite disturbs the **transport of oxygen** in the blood. Babies are especially sensitive to this, which is why clean water is important for them. Nitrogen also plays a role for the climate. Bacteria in the soil convert fertiliser, and in doing so **nitrous oxide (N2O)** can escape. Nitrous oxide is a strong greenhouse gas.

gewusst: Since the beginning of the 20th century, nitrogen fertiliser can be made artificially with the Haber-Bosch process.
Beetroot, spinach and rocket also contain a lot of nitrate naturally.

teile.einleitung: Macronutrients are the nutrients that plants need in large amounts. They include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
wichtigste: Plants need macronutrients in large amounts, but trace elements only in tiny amounts.
Nitrogen is the nutrient most needed by most crop plants.
Potassium controls the water balance and the stomata.
Magnesium sits at the centre of chlorophyll.
Sulphur is found in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
NPK 15-15-15 means 15 per cent each of nitrogen, phosphate and potash.

abschnitte.text: Plants need nutrients in very different amounts. **Macronutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus, **potassium**, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed in large amounts. **Trace elements** such as boron, zinc and molybdenum are needed by the plant only in tiny amounts. The roots take up the nutrients as dissolved **ions** from the soil solution. Potassium, for example, is taken up as the singly positively charged **K+ ion**.

Plants build most of their mass from **carbon**, **hydrogen** and **oxygen**. These come from the CO2 in the air and from water, not from minerals in the soil. Together they make up over 90 per cent of the dry mass. Among the nutrients from the soil, **nitrogen** is the most important. It is found in all amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and in chlorophyll.

**Potassium ions** regulate the osmotic pressure in the cells. In this way they control the opening and closing of the **stomata** and the water balance. Plants that get plenty of potassium suffer less from drought. **Magnesium** sits as the central atom in the ring-shaped **chlorophyll molecule**. Without magnesium, the plant cannot make chlorophyll.

**Sulphur** is a component of the amino acids **cysteine** and **methionine**, and so of many proteins. Oilseed rape and cabbage need an especially large amount of sulphur. **Calcium** strengthens cell walls and membranes. It is moved into the fruit only poorly inside the plant. In apples, a lack of calcium leads to **bitter pit**, with brown spots in the flesh.

abschnitte.titel: The numbers on a bag of fertiliser
abschnitte.text: Fertilisers often show **NPK** with three numbers, for example 15-15-15. The numbers give the share by mass in per cent: nitrogen as N, phosphate as P2O5 and potash as K2O. A 100 kg bag therefore contains 15 kg of each of these nutrients. The figures P2O5 and K2O are only values used for calculation; the plant takes up the substances as ions.

gewusst: If a plant lacks magnesium, its leaves often turn yellow between the veins.
Legumes such as clover can use nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria.
